title: Lions vs. Packers 5 Qs preview: Unpacking Jordan Love’s volatile numbers
summary: Fresh off their early-season bye, the Detroit Lions pick up where they left off against their first NFC North opponent: the Green Bay Packers. We had the pleasure of connecting with Justis Mosqueda, the Team Community Producer for Acme Packing Company, to give us some insight into this Packers team ahead of this week’s matchup. […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 27: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers prepares to throw during an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on November 27, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Fresh off their early-season bye, the Detroit Lions pick up where they left off against their first NFC North opponent: the Green Bay Packers. We had the pleasure of connecting with Justis Mosqueda, the Team Community Producer for Acme Packing Company , to give us some insight into this Packers team ahead of this week’s matchup. We learned about Jordan Love’s wild mix of quick releases and deep shots amidst Green Bay’s pass-protection woes, the ongoing O-line carousel and Josh Jacobs’ potential impact on the run game, as well as Jonathan Gannon’s hyper-aggressive blitz scheme—plus much more. 1. Jordan Love’s numbers are the most fascinating thing to unpack with this Packers offense. He has the shortest time to throw in the NFL among 37 qualifying quarterbacks (2.48 seconds), yet he sports the sixth-highest average depth of target (9.5 yards) and according to Pro Football Focus, leads the league in big-time throws (15) and passing attempts of 20+ yards downfield (33). Through six weeks of the season, what’s the story of Love between these numbers? In short: Heroics. The offensive line performed poorly in the pass-protection game outside of Weeks 4 and 5. He has absolutely no running game to speak of. Love is taking a massive pounding week to week. It really is just the Kobe stan in Love coming out and willing the team to victory. The team also leads the NFL in drops over this time period, too, and a lot of those are on what would have been explosives and/or touchdowns. It’s incredibly frustrating to watch Love play at such a high level with the rest of the offense playing poorly around him. 2. Likely associated with Love’s performance this season is the offensive line and the running game. Injuries have thrown Green Bay’s offensive line into the centrifuge. Since the start of the season, they’ve acquired some familiar faces in Laken Tomlinson and Kevin Zeitler, and they’ve done their fair share of shuffling to figure out the best combination. Is this the week Zeitler makes his season debut? What’s your level of confidence in this line solidifying itself by the time these two teams meet again in January? Meanwhile, the Packers have one of the worst rushing attacks in the league–but Josh Jacobs did come off the Commissioner’s Exempt List on Monday. How much do you anticipate Jacobs playing in this game based on Matt LaFleur’s comments this week, and do you think he’s the kind of difference maker who can single handedly get this run game out of the basement? I really think it could be. The running game has been bad all year, but at least Week 4 and 5 were games where the offensive line could at least protect Love. Last week, the Packers went into five-man protections for most of the game for the first time all season. This ended up exposing both guards a little more than anyone seemed to expect (Jacob Monk and Donovan Jennings started the year at guard before the team transitioned to Travis Glover and Laken Tomlinson). As of Thursday’s practice, the Packers were repping seven players to get ready for this game: the starting center (Sean Rhyan), the two tackles (Anthony Belton and Jordan Morgan) and four guard options (Glover, Tomlinson, Aaron Banks and Kevin Zeitler). I would not be shocked at all if we get Banks at left guard and Zeitler at right guard this week. If the Packers want to make that change before Week 9, they kind of have to do it now, because they have a short week against the Carolina Panthers after this. I 100 percent think Jacobs is going to play this week. LaFleur has really backed him at every opportunity to do so. The team has very much been in the business of getting Jacobs back on the field, even prior to the legal process playing out. They said he’s been working out with the team and in meetings the entire time. He just hasn’t been able to practice with them. They have three open roster spots on the 53-man roster that they’re keeping open right now, and two of those (Jacobs and PUP player Jordan Riley) are probably already filled in their minds. I think Jacobs can help turn some of those -2 runs into +2 runs, but I don’t think he’s just going to come into the lineup and fix all of Green Bay’s running game issues himself. 3. Former defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley left for a head coaching gig with the Miami Dolphins, and the Packers brought in Jonathan Gannon to replace him. What are some of the most notable differences you’ve noticed between the two coordinators, have said differences been mostly positive, negative or somewhere in between, and do you feel like the eventual return of Micah Parsons will end up making all the difference? The Hafley scheme was interesting, because it was mostly a scheme that disguised coverages, but didn’t do much on the pressure end, up until Micah Parsons came to town. When Parsons was on the field, teams obviously adjusted and ended up playing the Packers in more quick game and run game situations, which really forced Hafley to play more bland schemes—and Hafley went back to some “hidden” coverages once Parsons went down with an injury. Gannon’s defense really has been about bringing pressure. He’ll send seven guys on the first play of the game without blinking, and the cornerbacks have been playing pretty well this year (all three safeties have been great). They’ve done some interesting things with individual teams’ pass-blocking rules to get free rushers. It’s not uncommon for Gannon to scheme up a pressure where there are seven blockers on four rushers, one of the rushers is a free rusher, and the Packers still have seven coverage players for just three route-runners. The only time the defense hasn’t looked elite was against the Atlanta Falcons, which was a weird game. Bijan Robinson went crazy, and it seemed like everyone on both sides of the ball were slipping on the field that night other than Robinson. I think a lot of people are wondering if that was just a one-off or what the Packers’ defense looks like against a dynamic back. I think this week’s matchup will sort of answer that for us. Hopefully, Micah Parsons will be a big addition down the line, yes. Please, God. 4. Green Bay lost Edgerrin Cooper for the season after he suffered a torn Achilles in Week 4. Who has Gannon called on to replace Cooper, and how have the Packers adjusted on defense since the injury? Have you noticed any shifting in personnel groupings/deployment without their star linebacker available? EDITOR’S NOTE: This was asked and answered before Zaire Franklin suffered a mid-week injury and was declared out. The Packers use their linebackers a lot on special teams, because LaFleur’s offensive players hardly play teams—outside of the return positions. So they have Zaire Franklin at the Mike position (he doesn’t play teams) and now the Will role (previously Cooper) is being split by Isaiah McDuffie and Ty’Ron Hopper. My guess is they’re rotating McDuffie and Hopper (they change every two series or so) so that they can keep their legs fresh on special teams. Behind them, Green Bay rosters two linebackers who are functionally special teams-only players in Nick Niemann and Kristian Welch, if you want to know how important those linebackers are for the Packers’ special teams unit. Last week, they also called up Arron Mosby (a hybrid edge-linebacker who is basically another full-time special teamer) against the Cowboys. Both McDuffie and Hopper have played well, but the linebackers have never really been tested (outside of the run game against Atlanta) this entire season. No one is really throwing over the middle against us, in part because we’re sending blitzers so much. It’s sort of hard to evaluate the position right now. In the moments when you would expect…

title: What should become a Detroit Lions tradition at Ford Field?
summary: If you visit football stadiums around the country, you will notice that most everyone has their own thing. From the University of Michigan’s singing of “Mr. Brightside” to the way the Kansas City Chiefs cap off the singing of the national anthem, almost everyone has a unique flair to their gameday presentation. And that is […]
full_text: If you visit football stadiums around the country, you will notice that most everyone has their own thing. From the University of Michigan’s singing of “Mr. Brightside” to the way the Kansas City Chiefs cap off the singing of the national anthem, almost everyone has a unique flair to their gameday presentation. And that is no different for the Detroit Lions, as Ford Field has consistently been one of the toughest places for opponents to play. One of the biggest additions has been the arrival of the Lions stadium DJ, Djrayyadig , who does an amazing job of incorporating both modern and old-school Detroit-centric hits, especially during pre-game warmups. Then there is the massive presence of Theo Gridiron Spight . From leading the singing of “Gridiron Heroes” after the Lions score, to his countdown that gets the crowd amped up just before kickoff. Overall, the Lions’ gameday presentation at Ford Field is S-tier stuff. However, one thing that came up recently when talking to a friend is the fact that we don’t have anything that specifically signifies the start of the fourth quarter. That brings us to today’s question of the day—what fourth quarter tradition would you want incorporated into gamedays? My answer: I would go with something along the lines of a song that gets the players and fans going as the game turns to the fourth and final quarter. It could be the same song week-to-week, or it could be a rotation of tracks from Detroit’s history. One of the first that comes to mind is Tee Grizzley’s “ First Day Out, ” or Trick Trick and Eminem’s, “ Welcome to Detroit .” If we wanted to keep it old school, it could be a timeless, legendary classic like Marvin Gaye’s “Trouble Man.” I think this would be a great way to pay homage to the city while also getting the crowd ready for the fourth quarter. What do you think? What kind of fourth quarter or in-game tradition would you want implemented at Ford Field? Let us know in the comments below. Join the conversation! title: Detroit Lions TE Sam LaPorta’s full transcript on clarifying contract frustrations
summary: After his comments from the “Pardon My Take” blew up, Detroit Lions tight end Sam LaPorta met with the media on Friday afternoon to clarify and expand upon his thoughts, while he continues to seek a long-term deal in Detroit. Here is a full transcript of his session, with the media questions paraphrased. What was […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - DECEMBER 5: Sam LaPorta #87 of the Detroit Lions stretches prior to an NFL football game against the Green Bay Packers at Ford Field on December 5, 2024 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images After his comments from the “Pardon My Take” blew up , Detroit Lions tight end Sam LaPorta met with the media on Friday afternoon to clarify and expand upon his thoughts, while he continues to seek a long-term deal in Detroit. Here is a full transcript of his session, with the media questions paraphrased. What was your reaction to how people received your comments? “I feel bad if there was any sort of distraction to the team or my teammates or the coaches. But I think there was maybe a bit of a misconception with—I guess—my intentions are: I want to play for this team. I give everything that I have. My teammates do, as well. They all love me, respect me, and support me. And they want to see me be happy and compensated.” Where does your frustration stem from? “I guess I wouldn’t expect anybody else to really even care, but, emotionally, for me and my family, it’s an important thing for us. We want to have stability. We’re excited; in the upcoming months, we’re going to have our first kid, me and my wife. We’re going to welcome our baby girl into the world in Metro Detroit. We want to be here with the Lions. “And I guess I’m getting emotional about it, but in the grand scheme of things, it’s really a business. And you have to respect what the front office is doing, because they’re the ones calling the shots. They’re the ones that brought me in. It’s my first team. They’ve been nothing but supportive of me and my career.“ How do you compartmentalize contract negotiations and playing? “I guess you learn it early in your career that you’re being employed and you’re being compensated to do good work for this team, and if you’re not doing good work, you’re not going to be here.” Do you regret that emotional comments came out in the midst of business? “I don’t know if I regret it. I just don’t expect other people to understand. We’re very blessed. I’m getting paid millions of dollars this year. So you have to take it with a grain of salt. It’s coming from a stance of I want security for me and my family, but also when I reflect on other people in the league, I feel like I’m doing just as good of a job, if not better. And I want to be paid like those guys.” Any updates/progress in talks? “Um, no. I don’t think so.” Are you using these frustrations to fuel your play at all? “I don’t think so. I’ve not really changed the way I prepare. I’m going to give it my all every week. Starting with this weekend, huge game coming up. Trying to take a lead in the division, go 1-0. See what we can do there.” Did you expect comments to blow up? “I think the media will always take small stories and run with it and turn them into big ones. And when they splice together comments, anything can seem more harsh or bigger than the reality really is. I’m one person in a ginormous cog, ginormous machine in this building, and I want to continue to do my part, and hopefully something happens soon.” Where are the frustrations with negotiations? Not enough money? Guarantees? “I don’t know if I care to expand on that, because we could be here all day. (I) take that up with my agent.”

title: Final Dan Campbell takeaways before Detroit Lions vs. Green Bay Packers
summary: To close out his week of media availability, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell spoke to the press on Friday afternoon ahead of the team’s Week 7 game against the Green Bay Packers. It was a sprawling conversation, from Sam LaPorta’s recent comments to Detroit’s new punt returner. Here are my four biggest takeaways from his […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 27: Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell speaks to the media during the post-game press conference following the conclusion of an NFL regular season Thanksgiving Day football game between the Green Bay Packers and the Detroit Lions on November 27, 2025 at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images To close out his week of media availability, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell spoke to the press on Friday afternoon ahead of the team’s Week 7 game against the Green Bay Packers. It was a sprawling conversation, from Sam LaPorta’s recent comments to Detroit’s new punt returner. Here are my four biggest takeaways from his end-of-week presser. Note: Campbell’s comments on LaPorta’s contract negotiation frustrations were covered in a separate piece . Packers defense is balling out Green Bay has had to deal with a ton of injuries on defense. Micah Parsons remains out. Both starting linebacker Edgerrin Cooper and starting defensive tackle Javon Hargrave tore their Achilles in the past couple of weeks. And now linebacker Zaire Franklin will miss Sunday’s game against the Lions . Despite all of the hardships, the Packers are coming off of some of their best performances of the season, including holding the Cowboys to just 13 points last week, their lowest total of the season. Campbell had high praise for the unit: “They’ve been playing outstanding. That whole team has trended, I mentioned this, these last two weeks, they’ve really taken off and the defense is dangerous. I mentioned they play as one unit. That’s what you see. They play as one unit, and they all know where their help’s at. They play smart football. They play hard. They’re aggressive. They create disruption up front. They attack the run, they attack the pass. They give you multiple looks. It’s a physical, headsy unit. And look, seven takeaways in two weeks. That’s the thing. That’s huge.” What the Lions are getting in returner, DeAndre Carter Trust and dependability are so important when it comes to punt returners. That’s why I was a little surprised that Detroit is immediately handing the responsibilities to DeAndre Carter, who was signed earlier this week. But Campbell explained why he’s actually excited to see Carter—a player who has given him fits as an opponent before—play for Detroit. “What you notice on him is he is a catch-and-get downhill, and there is no taking your foot off the gas,” Campbell said. “This guy, there’s a naturalness to him locating the football, and when he goes, he doesn’t pitter-patter. He is running, and he will find the seam and hit it with speed. So that’s pretty exciting because when you have to defend it, it’s like, ‘Oh man, we’ve got to close these things down quick because he’ll hit it.’ So, I’m excited to watch him play. I think he’ll be good for us.” Packers offense, Jordan Love are rolling In my On Paper preview , I noted how Green Bay’s passing offense has been a different beast these last three weeks after making some shifts on the offensive line: Weeks 4-6: Ninth in passer rating (101.8) Seventh in yards per attempt (8.2) Sixth in dropback EPA (0.248) 14th in dropback success rate (47.1%) Campbell sees it, too. “Since they’ve kind of shored up this O-line, these last two games, it’s a lot different,” Campbell said. Later adding, “The protection is pretty dang good right now. [Jordan Love] is hanging in there. He can always make things happen. So now he’s able to facilitate and find his completions. Those guys are plucking, run after catch, and he’s still getting the bombs. So, he’s playing at a high level. I mentioned that. I think he’s playing as good as anybody right now at the quarterback position this year.” Cardinals’ performance was good, but not good enough The Lions played their best game of the season against the Cardinals in Week 5, blowing them out 45-21. And while that was a good performance on both sides of the ball, Campbell knows that won’t be good enough this week. Whether it was the three three-and-outs to start the game on offense or the coverage breakdowns on defense that continue to happen, Campbell doesn’t want to replicate that win; he wants to build on it. “I want to make sure we play better than we did against the Cardinals,” Campbell said. “Some of these little things we were talking about, we’ve got to be much cleaner on. And it was, it was really good. That was our best game, don’t get me wrong. But this opponent has got weapons, and they’ve been doing this for a while, and they’ve got an outstanding quarterback and an outstanding defense. And so, you don’t have the luxury of messing around or being a little off on a couple of plays because all of a sudden, you’re down 10 points.”

title: Dan Campbell responds to Sam LaPorta’s contract frustrations
summary: Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell spoke to the media Friday morning for the first time since tight end Sam LaPorta’s comments went viral. During an appearance on the “Pardon My Take” podcast, LaPorta expressed some clear frustration that he hasn’t received a contract extension yet, after talks broke off a few weeks ago. “I think […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - JANUARY 14: Head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions reacts with Sam LaPorta #87 during the second quarter against the Los Angeles Rams in the NFC Wild Card Playoffs at Ford Field on January 14, 2024 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell spoke to the media Friday morning for the first time since tight end Sam LaPorta’s comments went viral. During an appearance on the “Pardon My Take” podcast, LaPorta expressed some clear frustration that he hasn’t received a contract extension yet , after talks broke off a few weeks ago. “I think the combination of getting your heartstrings twisted as well as the violent sport we play—it sucks,” LaPorta said. “It’s disappointing that you go out there every week and you bear the risk of getting hurt. Like last year, whatever it was, Week 9, Week 10, I break my fucking back for this team. And then I’m going out there this year, and I’m ballin’, and maybe they’re just not showing the love.” Campbell was asked for his thoughts on the comments, and it’s clear he isn’t taking any of this personally. “I know what it may appear like. I know Sam. We all know Sam. Honestly, I don’t even think twice about those comments, because I know what he’s about, man,” Campbell said. “And we’re all good here. And we’re not going to let this be a distraction. He’s not. We’re not. We’re all good.” Campbell admitted they typically don’t want these things to bleed into the season, but said everyone involved is going about their business as normal. “On the outside world, it’s a distraction. In this building, it’s not,” Campbell said. “This kid’s locked in. He’s been locked in all year. He was locked in when he came in on Tuesday. He was locked in Wednesday, I mean Thursday. He was locked in today. So he’s ready to play, and we’re ready to use him. He’s a hell of a football player.” On the field, LaPorta is on pace to set career-highs. He’s currently fifth among tight ends in receiving yards (316) and t-fifth in touchdowns, despite playing one fewer game than most tight ends. As for the specific comments, Campbell chalked it up to some pent-up frustration from LaPorta, and not a knock on his character. “Look, I’ve said things that I regret—rarely, but sometimes it happens,” Campbell joked. “Sometimes you get into these spots, and you’re in a setting that feels a little bit more whatever. But it’s all good. That doesn’t mean that’s who the person is. You say something—sometimes you get something off your chest. But we picked the guys we picked for a reason, because we know their character, and we know what they’re about deep down. So, listen, man, Sam’s a stud. And he’s going to help us win games, and he’s an unselfish teammate, an unselfish player. Listen, sometimes things happen, things get said. It’s all good, man. “You can never take anything personal when you start talking business. That’s why business and football, they don’t belong with each other, but it’s the world we’re in, and it makes the world go around for all of us.” When asked if he believes LaPorta regretted the comments, Campbell had officially reached his limit on talking about the topic. “I’ve answered this I don’t know how many times. I said I didn’t want it to be a distraction, and now it’s becoming one, because you keep asking these things. That’s why.” LaPorta has not yet said anything to the media since his podcast appearance.

title: NFL predictions: 5 keys to a Lions victory over the Packers in Week 7
summary: The Detroit Lions (3-2) and Green Bay Packers (4-2) will square off in Week 7 in an NFC North divisional clash. “Division games are big, man,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said on Wednesday. “You talk about wanting to win a division, you have got to win division games. […] They’re really a game and a […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson (97) chases down Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love (10) for a sack during their football game on Thursday, September 28, 2023, at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wis. The Lions won the game, 34-20. Tork Mason/USA TODAY NETWORK-Wisconsin | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions (3-2) and Green Bay Packers (4-2) will square off in Week 7 in an NFC North divisional clash. “Division games are big, man,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said on Wednesday. “You talk about wanting to win a division, you have got to win division games. […] They’re really a game and a half if you want to look at it a certain way. But I mean, look, they’re (the Packers are) playing good football. They have got good players; they get good coaches. And so I respect that, man. This is a tough division.” Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will earn a victory over the Packers in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint. This week’s predictions preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook , who currently have the Lions listed at +1800 to win this year’s Super Bowl and are currently 3-point favorites in Week 7 . Packer s base scheme For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 7 preview: Breaking down the Packers’ offensive and defensive schemes . Prediction 1: Lions take the ball, get an early lead The Lions have struggled to get things going early in games this season. After scoring a touchdown on their second possession in Week 1 against the Saints, they’ve scored only three more points on their next nine first-quarter drives. Through five games, the Lions have scored just 10 first-quarter points, compared to 57 in the second quarter, 45 in the third quarter, and 52 in the fourth quarter and overtime. Here’s offensive coordinator Drew Petzing addressing the Lions’ slow starts: “Sometimes it’s play calls. Sometimes it’s execution. It’s always a combination of both. And honestly, and I’ve said it here before, anytime we don’t score, I’m a little irked whether it’s the first drive of the game or the last drive of the game. I was really excited that we have got it rolling and kind of saw it in the momentum carry into the next drive and the next drive and the next drive, which was excellent. [..] So again, it’s doing your job. It’s calling the right plays. It’s staying in the moment and doing it as hard and as fast as you can. I think that’s got to be the focus.” Petzing added that the team isn’t focusing too much on the slow starts because he doesn’t want the offense to strain to overcorrect, but there are subtle clues that the Lions are trying to gain an early advantage. For example, the Lions won the toss in Week 5 and elected to take the ball on offense first. While it didn’t work out in Arizona, the ideology made sense, and it wouldn’t be surprising to see them want the ball first against the Packers in this game as well. Green Bay’s offensive strength is in their aggressive approach in the passing game and willingness to take deep shots. However, as Anthony Balaj pointed out in his film study of the Packers’ passing attack , Packers coach Matt LaFleur calls a very different style of offense when his team has the lead vs. when they’re trailing. If the Lions can get an early lead on the Packers, LaFleur has a tendency to be less aggressive in his attack, take fewer deep shots, and deploy a more measured, cautious approach. Look for Detroit to want the ball first, score, and put LaFleur in an uncomfortable spot. Prediction 2: Detroit stretches the field with Jamo, softens the zone On defense, the Packers secondary is a strength, and they’ve posted impressive stats lately. This season, they’re allowing only 193.3 passing yards per game (6th best in the NFL), 5.9 yards per reception (3rd), -0.18 EPA per pass (3rd), and the fewest explosive passes allowed in the League. Now, they haven’t exactly faced a murderer’s row of quarterbacks this season. In Weeks 1, 4, and 5, the Packers faced backup quarterbacks, all of whom failed to throw for more than 200 yards: Vikings’ Carson Wentz threw for just 133 yards (though they scored 39 points), Bucs UDFA rookie Jalon Daniels threw for 148, and Chicago’s Tyson Bagent (87) and Case Keenum (108) combined for 195 yards. Against starters Geno Smith (Jets, 247 passing yards), Michael Penix (Falcons, 256), and Dak Prescott (Cowboys, 258), the Packers secondarily allowed closer to 250 passing yards per game. While the Packers are coming off a great performance against the best quarterback they’ve faced this season in Prescott, Jared Goff is arguably playing even better right now. Through five games, Goff is averaging 279.6 passing yards per game (3rd best in the NFL), 7.8 yards per reception (8th), an EPA of 0.25 per pass (2nd), and an 111.3 passer rating (3rd). Goff also has solid EPA results against the style of defense that the Packers run. For example, the Packers spend around 75% of the time in nickel defense, where Goff averages an EPA of 0.26 (4th), per SumerSports. The Packers also play zone coverage concepts roughly 78% of defensive snaps, and again, Goff’s EPA is very solid, averaging 0.20 (7th). And finally, the Packers run a two-high safety shell in their secondary, and Goff averages an EPA of 0.37 (4th) against this approach at safety. For Goff to keep producing at this rate, the Lions will need to soften the Packers’ zone, and despite the Packers running so many two-high safety looks, the Lions will need to keep them stretched out to create gaps underneath. The best way to keep the Packers’ defense honest and open is to test them deep with Jameson Williams. The Packers don’t want to give up explosives, and if the Lions even threaten to push the ball downfield to Williams, the safeties will need to respond accordingly, opening up the intermediate area of the field and allowing players like Amon-Ra St. Brown and Sam LaPorta to work. As accurate as Goff has been with the football this year, pushing the safeties back with Williams and taking what’s underneath should help the Lions sustain drives and stay consistent. But they’ll need one other component to make it all work … Prediction 3: Lions attack with Jahmyr Gibbs on outside zone runs While the Packers’ secondary has been solid, their defensive front has struggled with consistency against the run, allowing three opponents to rush for over 100 yards, including both of their losses: the Vikings ran for 107 yards, and the Falcons tuned them up with 242 rushing yards. With the Packers running a 34 front in base (25% of defensive snaps) and a 24 front in subpackages with stand-up edge rushers, teams have attacked them on the edges, running outside zone concepts on 62.2% of run calls (2nd highest rate in the NFL). Fortunately for the Lions, they lean on outside zone rushing as their primary blocking scheme; 45.6% of the time, with 54% of run calls going to the outside (10th most). When running outside zone, Jahmyr Gibbs has amassed 274 of his 504 rushing yards (4th most), 5.48 yards per carry (5th), a 50% rushing success rate (4th), eight “impact plays” (2nd), and 10 runs of 10+ yards (T-1st). Attack the edges in the run game to pinch the front, stretch them deep with Williams to expand the secondary, take what’s there in the intermediate zones, possess the ball, control the clock, keep the Packers offense on the sidelines. Prediction 4: Lions stay disciplined on deep shots The Packers’ deep ball has been a weapon in 2026, as quarterback Jordan Love has been aggressive in attacking downfield with both Matthew Golden and Christian Watson. Together, the pair account for nearly 50% of Love’s targets—Golden sees 26% of Love’s throws, Watson 22%—and the duo is amongst the most productive pairs in the NFL. The Chicago Bears handled the New England Patriots to move to 5-2 on the season. The win climbs them up to second place in an extremely competitive NFC North, and makes this week’s game between the Green Bay Packers and Detroit Lions even more important. Let’s take a very early look at the NFC playoff picture through six weeks and “Thursday Night Football.” NFC North standings: Vikings (5-0) Bears: (5-2) Packers: (4-2) Lions: (3-2) Chicago is looking like a Super Bowl contender with an offense that is much more under control with Caleb Williams under center, and a very disruptive defense. However, both of their losses have come against divisional foes, which could be a huge tiebreaker factor when it comes to playoff seeding. Meanwhile, the Vikings will take on the 2-4 Colts Sunday afternoon out of their bye week to try and keep their undefeated season alive. Whoever wins between the Lions and Packers will establish themselves as the third contender in the division. NFC playoff standings: Division leaders: 1. San Francisco 49ers (6-0) 2. Minnesota Vikings (5-0) 3. Carolina Panthers (3-2) 4. New York Giants (3-2-1) Wild Card teams (top three advance): 5. Chicago Bears (5-2) 6. Green Bay Packers (4-2) 7. Detroit Lions (3-2) 8. Seattle Seahawks (3-3) 9. Atlanta Falcons (2-4) 10. New Orleans Saints (2-4) 11. Philadelphia Eagles (2-4) 12. Dallas Cowboys (2-4) 13. Arizona Cardinals (2-4) 14. Los Angeles Rams (2-4) 15. Washington Commanders (1-4-1) 16. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (1-5) Currently, the Lions hold the final playoff spot in the NFC. Even if Detroit loses this week, they may keep their spot in the final Wild Card position, because the only team that could catch them—the Seattle Seahawks—is playing the Kansas City Chiefs. The Eagles, Cowboys, Rams, and Buccaneers have all been massive disappointments. title: To survive Detroit shootout, Packers should look to Thanksgiving win
summary: It’s no secret the Packers game against the Detroit Lions on Sunday is likely to be a shootout. As a byproduct of their stellar offense and inability to slow anyone on defense, Detroit hasn’t played a low-scoring game all year. In every Lions game so far this season, both teams have scored at least 21 […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 27: Dontayvion Wicks #13 of the Green Bay Packers scores a touchdown against Thomas Harper #12 of the Detroit Lions during the second quarter at Ford Field on November 27, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s no secret the Packers game against the Detroit Lions on Sunday is likely to be a shootout. As a byproduct of their stellar offense and inability to slow anyone on defense, Detroit hasn’t played a low-scoring game all year. In every Lions game so far this season, both teams have scored at least 21 points. In four of the five, both teams have scored at least 24. In two, both teams scored at least 30. If you like offense, you’ll probably like watching the Detroit Lions play football. The Packers, meanwhile, haven’t really been in a high scoring game this year. The Packers have only broken 30 once, and both times their opponents have done it, the Packers haven’t seemed super interested in keeping pace. Obviously they’ll have to avoid that outcome if they want a chance against the Lions. Fortunately, there’s a recent example of how the Packers should approach a game likely to result in a high-scoring shootout: their Thanksgiving day showdown with the Lions last year. That game alone should have showed the Packers exactly the kind of aggressive, playmaker-focused game they’ll need to play to beat the Lions this week. It starts with fourth down conversions. Matt LaFleur has trended back towards aggressiveness on fourth downs this year, and his choices against the Lions last November shows how that approach can pay off. The Packers converted all three fourth down tries last year, scoring two touchdowns (a 27-yard strike to Dontayvion Wicks and a one-yard score by Romeo Doubs) and putting the game away on their final drive. The third conversion deserves special attention. Facing a 4th and 3 on the Lions’ 45-yard line with just under two minutes to go, the Packers made the high-risk, high-reward decision to go for it. Given that the Lions had no timeouts, a conversion would end the game. But throw incomplete or come up short, and the Lions would have been in business, needing less than 20 yards to get into field goal range. Matt LaFleur put the ball in Jordan Love’s hands, and Love delivered, finding Wicks for a 16-yard completion. That sort of approach should again pay dividends against the Lions, who you can expect to be aggressive whenever they have the ball as well. The Packers’ aggressiveness should also extend to their playcalling. Last year, LaFleur and Love went deep often. Seven of Love’s 30 passing attempts that day were to targets more than 20 yards downfield. He completed four of those seven targets for 126 yards and two touchdowns. That’s not quite as good as Love’s heat check performance against the Bears, but it’s close enough,and considering how poor the Lions’ passing defense is by virtually every measure (in or near the bottom quarter in almost every stat you can find), I think we can reasonably assume he’ll have a chance to move the ball against the Lions this week. They should take advantage. They’ll need some defensive plays, though. Last year, Micah Parsons brought plenty. He came up with three sacks, two of which were on third down. On a second half third down, the Lions were lined up on the Packers’ four-yard line, trailing by 10. Parsons broke through and took down Jared Goff for a nine-yard loss, and the Lions kicked a field goal. If not for the sack, would Detroit have attempted a field goal or gone for it all? We’ll never know, but Parsons’ sack definitely changed the calculus. Parsons obviously won’t be on the field this week, but the need for playmaking is no less important, especially with Zaire Franklin on the sideline. Defensive stops may not forestall a shootout entirely, but a few crucial big plays could tilt the field. Looking to the past is no guarantee of success. The Packers have certainly changed quite a bit since last Thanksgiving. But the lessons learned in that widely watched game are still relevant today, and if the Packers can run the same script, they’ll be in great shape.

title: Packers’ simple pressure disguise creates chaos for the Cowboys
summary: In the last article, we broke down Evan Williams’ interception against the Dallas Cowboys. That play set the tone, but it was only the opening chapter of a long night for Dak Prescott. By halftime, Green Bay led 17-0, and Prescott had been picked off twice. The second interception wasn’t a product of disguise so […]
full_text: In the last article, we broke down Evan Williams’ interception against the Dallas Cowboys . That play set the tone, but it was only the opening chapter of a long night for Dak Prescott. By halftime, Green Bay led 17-0, and Prescott had been picked off twice. The second interception wasn’t a product of disguise so much as bad luck. Dallas was driving inside the Green Bay 30 when CeeDee Lamb lost his footing on a route, leaving the ball for rookie Brandon Cisse, who came away with the first interception of his career. Still, it fit the larger pattern. The Cowboys could move the ball in spurts, but every time they got close, something went wrong. And Gannon kept the pressure on in the second half, and the same theme kept showing up on tape: the look before the snap rarely matched what happened after it. From the above pressure package disguise, he shifted the defense into at least four different coverage rotations that the Cowboys were unable to decipher. Each of those above presents the same or similar pre-snap alignments. And each one has a different rotation behind and different zone droppers. After halftime, Gannon went back to what was working. On a third-and-7 in the third quarter, Green Bay lined up six defenders across the line, and Dallas set its protection to account for that front. Then Williams started walking down late in the play clock. Prescott saw it with roughly three seconds left, too late to reset the protection. The math was simple and bad for Dallas: four rushers coming off the weak side, three blockers to meet them. Prescott knew the ball had to come out immediately. It never had a chance to. The rush got home almost at once, and the quick throws Prescott was counting on weren’t there either. Behind the pressure, Green Bay dropped three players into the short zones, one of them traveling all the way across from the other side of the formation to plug a throwing lane. Pressure Dallas couldn’t block plus coverage it didn’t expect left Prescott with nothing, and the Cowboys punted. Few third-down calls are cleaner. The defense had the play beaten at the snap. Gannon’s creativity showed up on a drive in the fourth quarter. With Green Bay up 20-7 and Dallas needing to stay within striking distance, he called three straight plays that looked identical before the snap and played three different coverages after it. The sequence ended with the Cowboys running a fourth-down play that had little chance to succeed. It began on 2nd-and-7. The picture was a cover-0 pressure look: a loaded front, with four defenders in off coverage but sitting inside and off anywhere from press coverage to 10 yards. Green Bay had already brought real zero blitzes from that alignment earlier in the night, so Dallas had to respect it every time. On 2nd-and-7, the Packers showed it and then backed out into cover-4. The Cowboys had nothing designed to attack quarters and settled for 5 yards, making it 3rd-and-2. On third down, the look was identical, but this time the blitz was real. Green Bay sent everyone with no help behind it and got a rusher through untouched. Prescott was forced to throw before he could set, and the pass sailed incomplete. Once again the heat arrived so quickly that Dak had almost no time to deliver an accurate ball, and the pass fell incomplete. That set up 4th-and-2, and Dallas tried to take the blitz out of the equation by rolling Prescott out to his left. It’s a sensible answer to a zero blitz, because it moves the launch point away from free rushers. But Gannon had a counter. Green Bay didn’t rush extra at all and sat in cover-3. A rollout only gives the quarterback half the field, so once the first option to the left was covered, Prescott had nowhere else to look. He tried to force it, and the underneath defender knocked it away. Dallas called a play built to beat pressure, and Green Bay didn’t send any. Instead, the Packers dropped into cover-3. The downside of a sprint-out is that it eliminates half the field, and if the first read on a throw to the left isn’t there, there’s very little left to work with. Prescott tried to squeeze the ball in quickly, knowing his options were limited, and the underneath defender broke it up. Had Dallas known before the snap that cover-3 was coming, it almost certainly wouldn’t have called that play. That’s the true value of disguise. It keeps an offense from getting into its best call against what the defense is actually running. Green Bay added another field goal early in the fourth quarter to take a 23-7 lead not long after. The fourth coverage came on the very next Dallas drive. Same alignment, but this time the Packers rotated into cover-2. The corner at the top of the screen squatted on the short route because he knew he had a safety over the top. Prescott was a beat late recognizing it and nearly threw his third interception of the night. A hitch to the outside is about the worst throw you can make against a cover-2 corner, and it’s a throw Prescott likely never attempts if he reads the coverage before the snap. Prescott didn’t diagnose it fast enough and nearly threw a third interception. If he had known cover-2 was coming, he wouldn’t have thrown an outside hitch into a cloud corner, and he might have checked to a different play at the line. Dallas eventually got on the board late, with Prescott finding his receiver for a 6-yard touchdown pass with 44 seconds remaining, but a two-point try to Lamb fell incomplete and Green Bay recovered the onside kick. The final box score, with Prescott completing 34 passes for 258 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions, doesn’t capture how often the Cowboys were out of sorts. They ran too many non-competitive plays in critical moments, and that was the difference in the game. The loss dropped Dallas to 2-4, while Green Bay improved to 4-2. The Packers’ defense is rolling, and it’s doing so without Micah Parsons, who still hasn’t returned. The next test is a big one: Green Bay visits the NFC North rival Detroit Lions and a dangerous offense in Week 7.

title: How the Packers scheme an interception
summary: After giving up 35 points in their Week 3 meltdown against the Atlanta Falcons, the Green Bay Packers have allowed just 34 points combined over the three games since. Defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon’s disguises are a big reason why. On Sunday night against the Dallas Cowboys, he had quarterback Dak Prescott in a blender, forcing […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images After giving up 35 points in their Week 3 meltdown against the Atlanta Falcons, the Green Bay Packers have allowed just 34 points combined over the three games since. Defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon’s disguises are a big reason why. On Sunday night against the Dallas Cowboys, he had quarterback Dak Prescott in a blender, forcing him to read and react to a defense that hardly ever played its pre-snap shell. Gannon had defenders lining up in one spot and finished in another. They were mugging the front and showing cover-0 or single high man coverage all game long, forcing him to hesitate, resulting in three interceptions. Coverage players appeared out of nowhere. Free rushers got home. At times it must have felt to Prescott like Green Bay had 12 or 13 men on the field. No quarterback is immune to that. When the picture keeps shifting, it’s harder to get into the right call at the line, harder to trust what you see, and harder to process and react, because the pre-snap read may have nothing to do with what the defense actually plays. The result was a Dallas offense that never found a rhythm. The biggest play of the night may have come early in the second quarter, because it had planted doubt in Prescott’s mind and it kept the Cowboys from putting badly needed points on the board. The Packers offense had just turned the ball over on the previous drive and gave the Cowboys the ball on the wrong side of the field. The drive started at the Green Bay with Dallas getting into the red zone a few plays later, trailing only 7-0 at this point. View Link Here, Dallas faced 3rd-and-8 from the Green Bay 17 and came out of a 3×1 formation. The outside receiver and the middle slot receiver both ran shallow in-breaking routes, with the inside slot receiver running up the seam. View Link The Packers showed a single-high blitz look with seven potential rushers on the line, then rotated into red zone quarters at the snap. View Link Evan Williams ends up as the weakside safety playing “trix,” meaning that he’s reading the route of the #3 receiver inside and up. View Link The key was Williams (#33). He started on the line to Prescott’s left showing pressure, then knifed out to take away the #3 receiver inside and up. View Link Prescott never accounted for him and likely never saw. His only thought was likely that he’d need to get rid of the ball quickly and never really checked the post-snap rotation until it was too late. View Link The end zone angle shows Dak staring down the middle before working right to his inside receiver, never picking up Williams, who undercut the throw for an interception. Defenders materializing from nowhere like that is the kind of thing that can rattle a quarterback for the rest of the game.

title: Packers Injury Report: Franklin out, 4 questionable vs. Lions
summary: The big injury news out of Green Bay today: Head coach Matt LaFleur said linebacker Zaire Franklin, who was on the injury report Thursday with a shin issue, will miss Week 7 against the Detroit Lions. With Edgerrin Cooper, the team’s starting Will linebacker, already out, losing Franklin means both of the Packers’ linebackers against […]
full_text: (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The big injury news out of Green Bay today: Head coach Matt LaFleur said linebacker Zaire Franklin, who was on the injury report Thursday with a shin issue, will miss Week 7 against the Detroit Lions. With Edgerrin Cooper, the team’s starting Will linebacker, already out, losing Franklin means both of the Packers’ linebackers against Detroit—likely Isaiah McDuffie at Mike and Ty’Ron Hopper at Will —will be backups. Prior to Franklin’s injury, the Packers attempted to split the Will linebacker role between McDuffie and Hopper, so that both players could play special teams on top of their defensive contributions. With both players pushed into the starting lineup full-time now, Green Bay’s team will need to adjust in the kicking game. Beyond Franklin, the Packers listed four players as questionable on their final injury report of the week: guard Aaron Banks (knee/toe), receiver Bo Melton (back), defensive lineman Jordon Riley (Achilles) and cornerback Benjamin St-Juste (hamstring). Outside of Banks, who might have been in the running to start at left guard this week, these players are depth pieces for Green Bay. On Detroit’s end of the injury report, center Cade Mays and safety Brian Branch, who are both coming off time on the injury lists, are listed as questionable for the Lions. Both of these players are notable starters on the team, and it would be a shot in the arm for Detroit to get them back against the Packers. Packers ruled out Zaire Franklin, as LaFleur said earlier in the day, but have four questionable for Sunday. That includes G Aaron Banks. pic.twitter.com/lvmbu29nPq — Eric Boynton (@ericboynton) October 23, 2026

(Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images For a second straight week, the Green Bay Packers are playing in a game where the over/under on total points is set at 52.5. Last week, the team’s matchup with the Dallas Cowboys at Lambeau Field stayed well under the total, thanks in large part to an excellent effort by Jonathan Gannon’s defense. This week, however, could be a very different story. On Sunday afternoon, the Packers play the Detroit Lions at Ford Field, a venue that has been the site of several high-scoring games between these two teams in recent years. FanDuel Sportsbook has the total points line set at 52.5 once again, the highest line for a game between these two teams since 2020, when it was set at a whopping 55.5. But since 2020, these two teams have generally scored early and often on the fast turf in Detroit: 2020: Packers win 31-24 (total: 55) 2021: Lions win 37-30 (total: 67) 2022: Lions win 15-9 (total: 24) 2023: Packers win 29-22 (total: 51) 2024: Lions win 34-31 (total: 65) 2025: Packers win 31-24 (total: 55) That’s five of the last six games between these two teams in this venue going over 50 points, with four of them hitting 55 or more and two of them reaching a whopping 65 points. It’s just what these teams do — well, except for in 2022, a game that was a bizarre defensive slugfest. But look at those results starting in 2023, when Jordan Love took over at quarterback — the Packers haven’t scored fewer than 29 points at Ford Field with him behind center. Who will win the game? That’s less certain, as the results above show, with the two teams each taking three of the last six games at Ford Field. APC is a bit split on this one, as you’ll see in our picks below. But one thing we’re not split on is taking the over. Given the Packers’ issues defending against an elite running back earlier this year — and considering Jahmyr Gibbs is certainly in the Bijan Robinson echelon — plus the Lions’ abysmal passing defense, this game should shape up to be a wild one. Here are our picks for Sunday’s game, and give us your predictions in the comments!

title: Packers linebacker Zaire Franklin ruled out for Sunday
summary: The Packers will be without linebacker Zaire Franklin for Sunday’s game against the Detroit Lions. He’s been ruled out after taking a knee to the shin during practice. Franklin’s absence leaves the Packers perilously thin at linebacker, where they were already missing the services of Edgerrin Cooper. Now they’ll have to lean on Isaiah McDuffie […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 11: Zaire Franklin #44 of the Green Bay Packers celebrates after a play during the third quarter of the NFL football game against the Chicago Bears at Lambeau Field on October 11, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Packers will be without linebacker Zaire Franklin for Sunday’s game against the Detroit Lions. He’s been ruled out after taking a knee to the shin during practice. Zaire Franklin is OUT for Sunday after getting a knee to the shin in practice yesterday, per MLF. — Matt Schneidman (@mattschneidman) October 23, 2026 Franklin’s absence leaves the Packers perilously thin at linebacker, where they were already missing the services of Edgerrin Cooper. Now they’ll have to lean on Isaiah McDuffie and Ty’Ron Hopper to man the spot. McDuffie has historically been pretty good against the run, but he’s a liability against the pass. Teams have victimized his short stature (he’s just 6-foot-1) and limited lateral agility to attack him over the middle. One such team? The Detroit Lions. In their 2024 game against the Packers at Ford Field, the Lions’ Jared Goff competed all nine of his passes when he threw McDuffie’s direction, generating 68 yards and a touchdown. The Lions won, 34-31. Hopper, meanwhile, has been of a concept than a player since the Packers took him in the third round of the 2024 NFL Draft. Across 39 regular season games since then, he’s logged just 222 snaps on defense and has shown little when he’s been on the field. If he’s secretly a standout, now’s the time to show it. The injury couldn’t have been more poorly timed. The Packers are heading into a matchup with a Detroit Lions team that wants to run the ball out of heavy personnel , and Franklin would have been a big part of slowing down that attack, which is led by the near-supernaturally fast Jahmyr Gibbs. Any blow to that effort is a big problem. To make matters worse, the Packers will play on Thursday Night Football in Week 8, and it seems like a safe bet that Franklin will probably miss that game, too. That’s another tough blow for the Packers, but for Franklin as well; he had missed just one game in his NFL career to this point, and now the timing of a pretty random injury could keep him out for two.

title: Matthew Golden is outpacing other 2025 first round picks
summary: Nobody seems to think Matthew Golden is a bust anymore. After an admittedly uninspiring rookie season, Golden has bounced back in impressive fashion this year. With 30 catches and 501 yards, he has not only surpassed his 2025 output totals, his 2026 yardage is better than any wide receiver taken ahead of him in the […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 18: Matthew Golden #0 of the Green Bay Packers catches a pass during the second quarter against the Dallas Cowboys at Lambeau Field on October 18, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Nobody seems to think Matthew Golden is a bust anymore. After an admittedly uninspiring rookie season, Golden has bounced back in impressive fashion this year. With 30 catches and 501 yards, he has not only surpassed his 2025 output totals, his 2026 yardage is better than any wide receiver taken ahead of him in the 2025 NFL Draft. Through six weeks, the Panthers’ Tetairoa McMillan is Golden’s next closest competition, totaling 471 yards so far this season. McMillan is by far the most productive receiver from the 2025 class overall, though, after putting up 1,076 yards as a rookie. Emeka Egbuka is next on the list with 240 yards so far this season, though I’d argue he deserves a bit of a pass considering his quarterback has been out for most of the season. It’ll be interesting to see the extent to which his stats rebound when Baker Mayfield returns from his thumb injury. Travis Hunter is a distant fourth among 2025 first round wide receivers, though he too gets a pass on account of his significant other duties with the Jaguars. And it’s not like he isn’t doing interesting things! Just last Sunday he became the second player in the 21st century to catch a touchdown pass and an interception on the same day. The only other person to do it is Brian Dawkins, who caught his touchdown on a fake punt — hardly the same circumstances as Hunter. And none of this is to say Golden couldn’t be even better. He could! He leads the NFL in drops (according to Pro Football Focus charting) and could certainly stand to clean up that part of his game. But even still, he’s tied for third in the NFL with nine catches of 20 or more yards. (Christian Watson, for what it’s worth, is tied for the league lead with 10 such catches.) It all adds up to an exciting redemption tour for Golden. He may have been on the outside looking in for 2025, but he’s at the center of the Packers’ offense in 2026.

summary: When the Green Bay Packers and Detroit Lions meet on Sunday afternoon, it will be the first time that the two teams have played since last Thanksgiving. full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - SEPTEMBER 07: Green Bay Packers defensive end Lukas Van Ness (90) sacks Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) during a game between the Green Bay Packers and the Detroit Lions on September 7, 2025 at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, WI. (Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images When the Green Bay Packers and Detroit Lions meet on Sunday afternoon, it will be the first time that the two teams have played since last Thanksgiving. Much has changed since that day, when the Packers won 31-24, but in one sense, nothing has changed at all. Since that game, Micah Parsons suffered a torn ACL (one that he will not be back from in time for this game) and Zach Bako-Bewele injured his knee (twice) and is out for the season. Edgerrin Cooper also tore his ACL earlier this season. Then there’s the offensive line, where only two players who started for the Packers last Thanksgiving will be in the lineup again in this one, and one of them, Anthony Belton, is playing a different position. Likewise, the Lions also have just two players from last Thanksgiving’s starting offensive line on the team this week. And of the top 15 players on Detroit’s roster in terms of snaps played on defense in that game, just six are on the roster (seven if Brian Branch is activated off the PUP list by Sunday). But with all of that under consideration, this game looks like it should still be much the same as the Packers’ other recent games at Ford Field: a track meet with lots of points. This Sunday, the X-factors for both defenses should be their pass rush. If either unit hopes to slow down the opposition’s offense, it will need to get after the quarterback and, most importantly, get him on the ground. Jared Goff hasn’t thrown a pick yet this season while Jordan Love has been slinging the football like crazy despite heavy pressure. The two are both among the top five quarterbacks in the NFL in passing yards per game as well. Whichever team is able to get to the opposing quarterback more consistently should win this game, plain and simple. Packers fans will need to hope that defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon can keep confusing yet another offensive line on Sunday to help his players do just that. Packers winning with element of defensive surprise | Packers.com Gannon’s creative blitz looks are making it very hard for opposing offensive lines to identify who’s rushing, leading to plenty of pressure on opposing quarterbacks. Packers’ ball-hawking defense faces unique challenge against pick-free Jared Goff | Packers Wire Gannon’s goal will be to move Goff off his spot and force him to get the ball out quickly. So far this season, he has not thrown a single interception; will that change on Sunday? Can Lions get to Jordan Love before Packers receivers get loose? | Packersnews.com ($) On the other side of the ball, the pass rush is probably the one area where the Lions can actually slow down Green Bay’s offense. If Love has time to throw, he should be able to pick apart a porous secondary, so Aidan Hutchinson and company are Detroit’s best chance to keep the Packers’ passing game in check. Patriots-Bears on ‘Thursday Night Football’: What We Learned from Chicago’s 30-24 win | NFL.com Both Caleb Williams and Drake Maye had big games last night, but New England’s run game was MIA while the Bears managed to do enough on the ground late to grind out the win. Our own Tyler Brooke has reported that the Packers are calling about a quality veteran defensive tackle. It makes sense, too, given the injuries the team has suffered at the position so far. title: Five good Texans questions with Big Blue View
summary: The NFL has its scheduling quirks. Teams face an entire division every year from the opposing conference and by sheer definition you see them every four seasons unless there is some scheduling quirk involved. The New York Giants are one of those teams for the Texans. We don’t have a particular rivalry and we are […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 18: J.J. McCarthy #18 of the New York Giants passes the ball against the New Orleans Saints during the fourth quarter at MetLife Stadium on October 18, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images The NFL has its scheduling quirks. Teams face an entire division every year from the opposing conference and by sheer definition you see them every four seasons unless there is some scheduling quirk involved. The New York Giants are one of those teams for the Texans. We don’t have a particular rivalry and we are in opposite conferences, so we will not see them but every four years. By definition, I have done this feature once with Ed Valentine from Big Blue View in the last five seasons doing this feature. The Giants made it interesting by making a quarterback change midweek and that is where our conversation began. Battle Red Blog: The Giants have tabbed J.J. McCarthy to start this week. What should we expect to see from him? Are Giants fans confident that he can raise the level of play at the position and lead the Giants to the playoffs? Ed Valentine: I don’t think we really know what to expect. I do know Giants fans think this is the right choice . McCarthy hasn’t been with the team for a month yet, and how comfortable he is with the entire offense is anybody’s guess. He says he can run the entire playbook, but we will see. He gives the Giants’ offense a jolt of energy, and he brings the quarterback run game back into the offense. The Giants built an offense around Jaxson Dart, and the quarterback run game was a big part of it. That was out the window with Jameis Winston. McCarthy is not the runner Dart is, but he is young, athletic, can run, and puts that part of the playbook back into the arsenal. He also has a big arm, and isn’t afraid to use it. Can he get the Giants to the playoffs? That’s anybody’s guess. There is probably more upside with McCarthy than with Winston, but he did flop last year in Minnesota and he was No. 3 on the Vikings’ depth chart for a reason. BRB: Cam Skattebo did not get a lot of carries last week. Has he fallen out of favor following his fumble against Washington? EV: Cam Skattebo played six snaps and got ZERO carries Sunday against the Saints. He was held accountable for fumbling four times in five games, including three straight. His overtime fumble vs. the Commanders was inexcusable, and cost the Giants a chance to win. The Giants released Najee Harris this week, so Skattebo will most likely be right back in the mix this weekend. BRB: Malik Nabers is one of the top receivers in the NFL this season. How would you compare him to the other WR1s in the league? EV: I honestly don’t spend a lot of time studying Justin Jefferson, Ja’Marr Chase, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Puka Nacua, etc. That said, Nabers is a tremendous playmaker. He is a top 10 receiver, no doubt. BRB: Who are some names we haven’t heard of that could make an impact on Sunday? EV: The Giants don’t really have a bunch of out-of-nowhere guys you probably haven’t heard of. Maybe Trace Ford, a second-year edge defender who was just added to the 53 or kick returner/receiver Charlie Jones, who caught his first two passes with the Giants last week. BRB: The Texans opened as heavy favorites (7.5 advanced to 10 points) according to Fanduel. How do you see the game going? Are there any prop bets you feel comfortable recommending? EV: I think this is a difficult game for the Giants. I fear that the Texans defense, which has not been right this season, will have a get-right game. Prop bets are not my thing. I don’t pay much attention. We want to thank Ed so much for taking the time to answer our questions. This will be the rarest of occasions where yours truly will be in actual attendance at the Texans game. It will be the first time in my life to attend a Texans game although I did attend numerous Houston Oilers games back in the day. We want to wish Ed and the Giants luck for the rest of the season. As per usual, we hope that luck will begin on Monday morning.

title: The Colts Have More Paths to a Bright Future Than You Think
summary: The Colts finally did it. I think by now, anyone clicking on this article doesn’t need a full autopsy of the Chris Ballard era. I intentionally wait to do these long form pieces, because I like to take the emotion out of my analysis. However, when it comes to the end Chris Ballard era, there […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - OCTOBER 18: Carlie Irsay-Gordon co-owner and CEO of the Indianapolis Colts instructs fans the the Adam Venturi banner that was reviled at half time during and NFL game between the Tennessee Titans and the Indianapolis Colts on October 18, 2026 at Lucas Oil Stadium at Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Colts finally did it. I think by now, anyone clicking on this article doesn’t need a full autopsy of the Chris Ballard era. I intentionally wait to do these long form pieces, because I like to take the emotion out of my analysis. However, when it comes to the end Chris Ballard era, there isn’t much analysis needed. It was time, and anyone who followed the team realized it. You didn’t have to listen closely to hear the “Fire Ballard!” chants echoing throughout Lucas Oil Stadium during the team’s annual humiliating loss, this time to the winless Titans. While it was obvious, that this was going to be an end of the Chris Ballard era, one thing is certain: This is one of the most complex and nuanced tenures of any GM in NFL history. The reality is that there were numerous exits the Colts could have taken. 2021, certainly 2022, and 2024 all come to mind. Like a cat, Chris Ballard had 9 lives. If it wasn’t the epic choke in 2021 that caused the Colts to miss the playoffs, it had to be the year an ESPN analyst took over as head coach in one of the most embarrassing seasons in franchise history. After all that turmoil, surely he wouldn’t survive a season in which his handpicked quarterback tapped out of a game and was benched, while a team captain handed opponents free bulletin board material on his podcast, only for the Giants to whoop the Colts with a backup quarterback and end their season… Right? Wrong. Because the Chris Ballard tenure was never assessed on paper. He endured one of most shocking retirements in NFL history, which we all know by now. But also judging from some of the reporting, the health of late owner Jim Irsay played a role in his retention. It was more than the mediocre seasons and rosters with holes that the fanbase could identify in August. The Colts were loyal to him for as long as they possibly could be. That’s the gist of the story every Colts fan knows by now, perhaps all too well. But now that Chris Ballard has been fired, the Colts are closing a significant chapter in their franchise’s history and are grabbing the pen to start writing the next one. The funny part is that some people have already written it for them. There’s a narrative that the Colts are hosting a firesale, similar to what the Miami Dolphins did after firing Chris Grier around this time last year. Mock trades are flooding your social media feeds, with teams hoping to compete for a Lombardi Trophy raiding the Colts’ roster for just about every talented player they have. However, this is nothing like the 2025 Miami Dolphins. WHERE DO THE COLTS GO FROM HERE? This is may sound crazy to a portion of an understandably livid fanbase, but the first order of business has to be continuing to compete this year. And it’s a real possibility that they do. In the NFL, it’s fairly easy to see when teams are waving the white flag. You can see it in the press conferences and you can see it on the sidelines on Sundays. It’s pretty obvious. Typically, a coach is then fired. But the Colts didn’t fire a coach, they fired their GM. Carlie Irsay-Gordon is sending a message to everyone in that building that it’s time to wake up. Shane Steichen, Lou Anarumo, Daniel Jones, and the rest of the roster.. If they didn’t realize it already, they certainly realize it now. Everyone is playing and coaching for their jobs. The Colts can use this as an opportunity to roll over like they always have, or they can jumpstart their season and continue to keep fighting. The good news about having an owner that’s intimately involved with the organization? She gets a front row seat to see who quits on this team. Those are the people you can guarantee won’t be here next year. Maybe the roster was so poorly constructed that they’ll never be able to compete this season, but watch them this Sunday. I bet they show you some fight. 2026 FIRESALE? Circling back to the aforementioned firesale that everyone is convinced is about to occur. Ed Dodds, and certainly Carlie Irsay-Gordon, are going to do their due diligence to move some of the players that were never going to be apart of the team’s future this year. I think we can conclude that DeForest Buckner will eventually be one of those people. He’s on the last year of an expiring deal, is 32 years old, and wants to win. It’s about as natural a parting of ways as you’ll find in the NFL. He knows it, we know it, and 31 other teams know it. It would shock me to see him on the roster come mid-November. But everyone else? I’m not so sure. Like I said, the Colts are trying to win still. If they upset the undefeated Vikings, don’t things look a lot different? A win can do so much for a team in the NFL. Now I think we can be realistic to say that is still pretty unlikely. The Colts’ roster has plenty of flaws, as we’ve discussed all season, but that doesn’t mean the team should start trading away its best players. They would be wise to hold on to anyone who could still have a future with the franchise. That includes Jonathan Taylor, Quenton Nelson and Josh Downs. Is there a price for everyone? Of course. A massive overpay could completely change the equation. Just look at the Jets last year. But ask yourself this: Why would the Colts want to part ways with players that a potential new GM might view as building blocks for the future? You owe that the new GM to make that decision for himself. IS THIS AN ATTRACTIVE JOB? If you had asked me this question in January, I would have said no. Without a first-round pick and with an unsettled QB situation, I assumed they might be in stuck until they paid off the debts of the Sauce Gardner trade. But I underestimated one thing: The owner. I think Carlie Irsay-Gordon is a massive reason to take the job. Why? Because she’s deeply committed to process over results. She’s deeply invested in the team. And she’s willing to do what it takes to win. Also if you’re a GM taking over this job, are the standards If you zoom out to when she took over last year, it’s been quite the ride. The Colts were one of the hottest teams in the NFL, and while I did not agree with the move, she let Chris Ballard mortgage their future at the deadline to try and win. And then when things didn’t work out, she gave him a second chance. That goes a long way. Despite having quality ownership in your corner, it’s undeniable that the resources the Colts have to work with are probably not going to earn them the top job on the market this offseason. They don’t have the ammo to get a blue-chip prospect and they don’t have a QB that will entice many candidates to want to build a team around. That being said, while the roster might have some flaws, it can get better in a hurry. THE COLTS PATH MOVING FORWARD I’m positive that the Colts are going to get differing opinions in GM interviews about the state of the roster. Some people are going to love the young talent that’s on the roster and want to build around it. Others will look at an aging core that hasn’t accomplished anything and see an opportunity to sell high on its veterans and want to get younger quickly. Both give me a sense for optimism. While I don’t have a crystal ball, I really believe things can get better in Indianapolis quickly. Things in the NFL change fast and all it takes is one good offseason to completely change the trajectory of your team. Look at the 2024 Eagles who added Saquon Barkley and reinvented their secondary in the first two rounds of the draft. Look at the 2025 Seahawks who completely tore down their offense to the studs and built it all the way back up. The past guarantees nothing for the…

title: Stampede Blue Reacts results (Week 7): Colts fans show signs of optimism after Ballard firing
summary: According to this week’s results, 47 percent of Colts fans say they are confident the team is headed in the right direction. That number is still far from overwhelming, and it shows that a large portion of the fan base remains unconvinced, but it is also a notable sign that optimism has not completely disappeared […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Indianapolis Colts Owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon looks on against the Baltimore Ravens during the fourth quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to this week’s results, 47 percent of Colts fans say they are confident the team is headed in the right direction . That number is still far from overwhelming, and it shows that a large portion of the fan base remains unconvinced, but it is also a notable sign that optimism has not completely disappeared in Indianapolis. Just a few days ago, fan confidence felt like it had hit a breaking point following the Colts’ embarrassing collapse against the previously winless Tennessee Titans. Indianapolis looked firmly in control early, built a 13-0 halftime lead and still found a way to lose 26-20 in one of the most frustrating performances of the season. For many fans, it felt like another example of the same problems that have defined this era of Colts football: inconsistency, missed opportunities and an inability to take advantage of games the team should win. Then came the major change! Owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon fired general manager Chris Ballard less than 24 hours after the loss, ending a tenure that had increasingly become a source of frustration for much of the fan base. Ballard’s dismissal does not fix the roster overnight, and it does not erase the disappointing start to the season, but it clearly signaled a willingness from ownership to make a significant change rather than continue down the same path. That alone may have helped restore at least some belief that the franchise is capable of moving in a different direction. The 47 percent confidence mark reflects a fan base that is still conflicted. Colts fans are frustrated, and understandably so, but there also appears to be some renewed hope that meaningful change could lead to better days ahead. If Shane Steichen’s team can string together a few wins and climb back into the playoff picture, confidence could rise quickly. If not, this number could just as easily fall again. For now, though, nearly half of Colts fans still believe this franchise may be headed in the right direction. Elsewhere around the NFL, fans were also asked which head coach they believe will be the first fired this season, and Colts head coach Shane Steichen received 17% of the vote, tied with Tampa Bay’s Todd Bowles for second place behind Washington’s Dan Quinn (34%). Steichen’s inclusion should come as little surprise given Indianapolis’ disappointing start to the season and the recent dismissal of Chris Ballard. While ownership has already made one major organizational change, Steichen remains under considerable pressure to turn things around, particularly with the Colts still fighting to remain in the AFC playoff picture. A few victories over the coming weeks could go a long way toward improving his job security, but another extended losing streak could leave ownership facing another difficult decision before the season is over.

full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - OCTOBER 18: Head coach Shane Steichen of the Indianapolis Colts looks on against the Tennessee Titans at Lucas Oil Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts made a major decision when the Irsays chose to part ways with 10-year general manager Chris Ballard. It was a long time coming, but if things don’t shape up quickly, it won’t be the last move made in 2026. When it rains, it pours, and Shane Steichen better have his umbrella and poncho on because he is in danger of being the next to fall. The next two weeks could very well determine his fate. Offensively, the 5-0 Minnesota Vikings are one of the worst undefeated teams ever. They don’t put up a lot of yards or points. That’s all the good news there is for the Colts, though. As statistically bad as they may be on offense, they are coming off a bye, are at home, and have one of the league’s best defenses. Kyler Murray is back under center and is starting to get comfortable. In the building in which the Colts surrendered a 33-0 lead, anything is possible, but being a touchdown underdog implies this will be an uphill climb. If Steichen can rally the troops in the face of adversity and win, he can take a breath. It will only be a small gulp, however, because the test continues in Jacksonville against the Jaguars. Their record doesn’t matter. Whether Trevor Lawrence has his team rolling doesn’t matter. Great or horrible, the Colts don’t win in Jacksonville anymore. If Steichen wants to keep his job, this has to be the year to break the curse. These are two tough games to get the mojo back. Shane Steichen can script the first twenty or so plays, but after that, it falls apart. The Colts have already shown what “Find a Way” means when they released Ballard. It means win. Nothing else. Steichen’s leash was short to begin the year, and he is officially on notice as the next one on the chopping block. If he loses both, he will most likely be gone. This is a results-oriented league. Steichen must show those results or be shown the door.
