title: Raiders Week 7: How to attack the Rams stingy defense
summary: Klint Kubiak will have his hands full this Sunday when his Las Vegas Raiders matchup with the Los Angeles Rams. Ditto for Chris Schula as he’s the man in charge of the Rams defense trying to combat/quell Kubiak’s offense. That’s the high-level tale of the tape when the 3-3 Raiders host the 2-4 Rams within […]
full_text: (Photo by Jordon Kelly/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Klint Kubiak will have his hands full this Sunday when his Las Vegas Raiders matchup with the Los Angeles Rams. Ditto for Chris Schula as he’s the man in charge of the Rams defense trying to combat/quell Kubiak’s offense. That’s the high-level tale of the tape when the 3-3 Raiders host the 2-4 Rams within the confines of Allegiant Stadium for a Week 7 AFC West vs. NFC west matchup. Kubiak’s Raiders offense is the sixth-highest scoring unit in the NFL at 162 total points. Schula’s Rams defense, on the other hand, is quite stingy allowing the third-least amount of yards (1,764) but 17th in points allowed (138). But go deeper into the production — or lack thereof — and it’ll be intriguing to see how the strengths of the Las Vegas’ offense contends with might of Los Angeles’ defense. Case in point: The Raiders aerial attack is Top 10 in the NFL ranking seventh in yards (1,581) and second in touchdowns (14). However, the Rams air defense yields the second-least yards (1,002) and is 14th in touchdowns allowed (eight). Las Vegas’ highest output this season through the air was a 371-yard effort in a 45-17 loss to the New England Patriots in Week 5 and Los Angeles’ lowest air yards allowed on the year was 68 yards in a 24-20 win over the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 4. The Silver & Black’s strength offensively is an aerial attack and Kubiak has shown to be adept at getting targets open for his veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins — who leads the league with 14 passing touchdowns. Schula, meanwhile, is an air traffic controller with his Rams defense grounding flights. Which makes what I’m about to say next quite counterintuitive: The Raiders getting the ground game is going to be integral to Kubiak’s offensive success. If your eyebrow is raised, I don’t blame you. After all, Las Vegas has the 30th-ranked rushing production at 475 yards with only three touchdowns (ranking 25th amongst the 32 NFL teams), and a the 31st-ranked 3.0 yards per rush average. Los Angeles’ defense, though, has given up 762 rushing yards (seventh-most) and four touchdowns (fourth least) and a 4.4 yards per carry average (21st). The rest of Mike Washington's touches vs. #Bills Other than the draw play and a well-blocked play to the edge, not much room to run. Still a couple of runs where he overshot/rushed the development of double teams (1:47) or didn't press outisde-in as deep as he could have to… pic.twitter.com/VqtUtMlvfJ — Matt Waldman (@MattWaldman) October 19, 2026 Facing a leaky defense — with the Rams ailing with injuries, too — provides quite a get-right game for a Raiders team that’s dropped three-straight games. L.A. placed defensive tackle Poona Ford and Kobie Turner on injured reserve leaving the team light on the interior. Edge rusher Myles Garrett remains on IR, however, the Rams still have Aaron Donald in on the defensive line. That should give Kubiak and Co. ample opportunity to get the ground game going. The duo of Ashton Jeanty and rookie Mike Washington Jr. paced the Raiders running backs with 98 carries for 313 yards and one touchdown and 34 carries for 168 yards and one score, respectively. Las Vegas would be wise to test the interior of the Rams defensive line with gap- and power-run concepts with both Jeanty and Washington (the rookie did miss practice on Thursday with foot and back ailments, though). And also deploy the patented outside/wide zone that Kubiak prefers. Doing so should allow Las Vegas to have pulling guards pave the way for tailbacks. In their loss to the Arizona Cardinals last week and the Buffalo Bills the week prior, the Rams allowed 120 and 202 rushing yards in those two games. If the ground and pound continues to flop, however, we’ll get to see plenty of the air-to-air dogfight between Kubiak and Schula. Cousins has turned back the clock and is dropping dimes in Kubiak’s offense and Las Vegas would be wise to funnel the passing game through Brock Bowers and Tre Tucker. The elite tight end and fleet-footed wide receiver, respectively, are the most productive pass catchers with 28 receptions for 382 yards and three touchdowns and 2 catches for 371 yards and another three scores, apiece. Tight end Michael Mayer is coming into his own after signing a rich contract extension and is third with 28 receptions for 266 yards and a score. Opposing defenses have trouble matching up with Bowers — although the Bills did well putting their top cornerback Christian Benford on him last week — and the Raiders should exploit that until the wheels fall off. Filthiest route of the week: Brock Bowers on a blaze out pic.twitter.com/7YZWjIGKFF — Ted Nguyen (@FB_FilmAnalysis) October 19, 2026 That all said, Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard faces his own beasts of burden trying to stymie the Rams offense orchestrated by head coach Sean McVay. L.A.’s offense is 20th in points scored (135) and third in yards gained (2,408). The aerial attack is the most productive aspect ranking first in attempts (242) and second in yards (1,732). The 11 passing touchdowns ranks ninth with veteran Matthew Stafford completing 65.9 percent of his passes with 11 touchdowns to six interceptions. Las Vegas defense, in comparison, ranks 26th in points allowed (162) and 28th in yards yielded (2,230). The team allows the ninth-most passing yards (1,424) and the sixth-most passing touchdowns (13). Head-to-Head Sunday’s tilt marks the 17th game between the Raiders and Rams. The all-time series is tied at 8-8 (all regular season games) but it’s Los Angeles that is riding a four-game win streak dating back to November of 2014 (the 52-0 shellacking of the then Oakland Raiders in St. Louis). The most recent clash was in October of 2024 where the Rams dropped the Raiders 20-15 in a game where then-starting quarterback Gardner Minshew II threw three interceptions allowing L.A. to surge to a 20-6 lead. Quotes of Note “It’s just something we’re going to look to improve every week. Whether we have a game that we rush for 150, 200 yards, we’re still going to go back and say, ‘Okay, how can we get better?’ So, I don’t know that we’re looking at it in terms of it’s close. We’re looking for incremental improvement every week in everything we do.” —Las Vegas Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko on how close does he think the running game is to getting going. “Yeah, you’re trying to stress that all the time. He’s a gifted thrower, with the no looks and all those things. But that’s a point of emphasis every week, to finish through, stay with your guy, the play extends. But he’s a special talent.” —Las Vegas Raiders defensive coordinator on the biggest challenge Matthew Stafford presents on a defense.

title: Are the Los Angeles Rams a repeat of the Patriots game?
summary: Decimated by injuries and with a 2-4 record, the Los Angeles Rams have fallen far from being the Super Bowl favorites initially thought. Currently cellar-dwelling in the depths of the NFC West once again proving that “dream teams” are just a dream. All signs point to this being a very winnable game in Week 7 […]
full_text: . (Eric Thayer / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images) Decimated by injuries and with a 2-4 record, the Los Angeles Rams have fallen far from being the Super Bowl favorites initially thought. Currently cellar-dwelling in the depths of the NFC West once again proving that “dream teams” are just a dream. All signs point to this being a very winnable game in Week 7 for the Las Vegas Raiders. Precisely why Raider Nation and head coach Klint Kubiak should be concerned. Against the New England Patriots, missing four defensive backs and #1 wide receiver A.J. Brown, and with a host of banged-up players, the Raiders were soundly beaten 45-17. To be fair, they were also coming off a close, emotional loss with a comeback bid falling just short to Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs. Sounds kinda familiar, doesn’t it? This week, after a 33-30 loss to Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills, the Raiders have a chance to right the ship against a reeling Rams team and exorcise some demons. The Rams team, without Myles Garrett, recently placed the following players on injured reserve: Davante Adams, Poona Ford, Kobie Turner, and Blake Grupe, the replacement kicker. Nate Scheelhase, the Rams offensive coordinator, is experiencing some first-year coordinator growing pains. Last year under Mike Lafleur, the Rams had the number-one scoring and yardage offense; this year they have fallen all the way to 20th in scoring offense. Revisionist history on can’t-lose games hasn’t been kind to the Raiders. Whether it’s head coaches who have never coached before or quarterbacks who have been on the team for less than a week, or rosters missing 50% of their starters, these games never seem to work out for the Raiders. Concerns or sports fans masochism s Aaron Donald has yet to make the impact many thought he would coming out of retirement. Against the Raiders’ left side of the offensive line, which is their worst, he could finally get right. Spencer Burford has struggled mightily to block anyone who wasn’t a lower-caliber player; Tyler Linderbaum hasn’t been as good as advertised, nor has he played up to the contract he was awarded. Kolton Miller is getting pumped up by analytics charts from whoever is using AI to draw them up. When, in fact, his play has bordered on abysmal. Braden Fisk is facing a right guard situation where the position no longer has an entrenched starter. For as much as Kubiak has said there will be competition at the position, no player, be it Jackson Powers-Johnson or Caleb Rogers, has seized control. Rogers missed some key blocks last week and was blown up in a short-yardage situation, which ended a drive inside the red zone and under the shadow of the goalposts. Schematically, no teams deploy 13 personnel (one back, three tight ends) more than the Raiders’ current and last opponents. The Rams rank 1st at 29% of their offense and the Bills rank 2nd at 27%; realistically, that means a heavy emphasis on the run game and a lack of talent at the wide receiver position. The Rams have rushed for 676 yards, six rushing touchdowns and average 4.6 yards per carry. Ranking 12th in the NFL through six games. Too much to cover Covering tight ends continues to be a work in progress for the Raiders defense. Safeties Treydan Stukes and Jeremy Chinn continue to be up and down in terms of communication and execution. Stukes being the expected weakest link. Stukes, a rookie safety, struggles with in-breaking routes run by big ol’ tight ends. Chinn, the veteran, struggles with the out-breaking routes and lacks the twitch or long speed to keep up. Throwing in a third tight end puts a linebacker (Quay Walker or Nakobe Dean) on them, sometimes Taron Johnson, or leaves them open to a soft vacated zone. While the Raiders’ pass defense has prepared itself for wide receiver-heavy offenses, the tight ends and the running backs out of the backfield have been the Achilles’ heel. What’s problematic is that this plays right into Scheelhase’s and quarterback Matthew Stafford’s hands. Stafford has been without either Adams or Puka Nacua in every game except the game in Australia in Week 1 and last week. So sticking with power sets and standing tall in the pocket waiting to throw to tight ends and running backs is nothing new to him. Ultimately, it will be up to the Raiders’ offense to take advantage of the injuries to the Rams’ defense to get the win in Las Vegas, but the defense will have to be even better at getting to the quarterback and getting him on the ground. If not the song and dance of “the same old Raiders” will get louder and start to become unbearable.

title: What happened to Los Angeles Rams’ ‘Super Team’ ahead of Week 7 Las Vegas Raiders matchup?
summary: Heading into the season, who would have thought that the Week 7 matchup between the Las Vegas Raiders and Los Angeles Rams would be a “loser goes home” type of game when it comes to the playoffs? Not many, that’s for sure. But here we are. The 3-3 Raiders need to end a three-game losing […]
full_text: (Photo by Alika Jenner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Heading into the season, who would have thought that the Week 7 matchup between the Las Vegas Raiders and Los Angeles Rams would be a “loser goes home” type of game when it comes to the playoffs? Not many, that’s for sure. But here we are. The 3-3 Raiders need to end a three-game losing streak and beat a quality opponent to be legitimate postseason contenders, while the 2-4 Rams desperately need a win to keep pace in the NFC Wild Card race. To preview the game for Raider Nation, Silver and Black Pride reached out to our friends at Turf Show Times, and Kenny Arthur was kind enough to answer a few questions about the Rams. Q: Sorry, but I have to start with the elephant in the room. The Rams won the offseason and were billed as the heavy Super Bowl favorites heading into the campaign. Sitting at 2-4, how did the “Super Team” fall apart? A: For the record, I never thought the Rams were a super team, or even the best team in the NFC West. They spent the offseason doing what the Rams always do, which is chasing big names and brushing aside actual weaknesses. To be fair, Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson addressed a need at cornerback, and McDuffie was a much better use of a late first-round pick than anyone in the draft would have been. So kudos to L.A. for that, although Watson was an overpay. Even so, he was an overpay to replace one of the worst starters on the team. None of the other moves were that smart, and the non-moves were terrible miscalculations. Number one, the Rams had the worst special teams in the NFL last year, and it’s been a running theme for L.A. to have bad special teams for at least the last five years. Did they upgrade kicker Harrison Mevis? No. (Mevis was cut last week.) Did they hire a better special teams coordinator? No, they hired Bubba Ventrone, who was fired by the Broncos last year. Did they replace returner Xavier Smith, who fumbled the NFC Championship game away? No, they kept him. (Smith was released last month after the season started). So number one, the Rams had the 32nd-ranked special teams, and I would’ve predicted no change there. It’s extremely difficult to win the Super Bowl with the worst special teams in football, as the Rams found out last year. So no, I didn’t have a lot of respect for their disrespect of special teams . Number two, instead of using resources to upgrade obvious needs like a linebacker or a receiver (injuries to Puka Nacua and Davante Adams are NO surprise) or a safety or a defensive tackle, the Rams trade for Myles Garrett (???) and use a first-round pick on QB Ty Simpson (???). Are you pushing all-in or planning for the future? Garrett is a Hall of Famer, but he didn’t address a weakness, especially by trading away Jared Verse for him. Simpson felt like a reach — I understand the urge to draft a QB when your starter is 38 — but this is less about him. It’s more than the Rams always treat rookies like they couldn’t possibly help. That’s not true. Every year the Super Bowl teams have several key rookies. The Rams used their second-round pick on TE Max Klare, who is fifth string and has one snap this year. So that’s what I’d say about the “super team”. The Rams made headlines (like paying Aaron Donald $20-$30 million for one season and he’s having zero impact) but they ignored weaknesses. So yes, being 2-4 surprises me, but being far more beatable than they were predicted to be does not. Q: Matthew Stafford hasn’t looked anything like the guy who was last season’s MVP, from an outside perspective at least. What’s been the difference between this year’s version of Stafford and last year’s? Are the injuries starting to catch up to him? A: From 2022-2024, Stafford had a TD rate of 4% and an INT rate of 2%. That’s an average of 23 touchdowns and 11 interceptions per season and 7.3 Y/A, right? That’s three seasons; it’s a much larger sample size than one season. That’s who he is. That’s your basic Matthew Stafford. Then last season the Rams acquired Davante Adams, and he threw 46 touchdowns. Stafford’s TD rate went up to 7.7% and his Y/A went up to 8.8. He had a top-3 WR in Nacua helping him take chunks out of the field on the drive, and then at the goal line Sean McVay would call a pass for Adams. In 2025, Adams caught 11 goal-line touchdowns. McVay turned Stafford into a goal-line back, except with his arm. I say this all to say that Stafford won MVP because McVay changed the goal-line offense into one that favored passes instead of runs, which is what helped Stafford barely beat Drake Maye at the finish line. Now we’ve seen a normal Matthew Stafford season again. I think he struggled against the 49ers in Australia in Week 1, and then against the Eagles he wasn’t that good, and the goal-line touchdowns went to Kyren Williams. Otherwise, I actually think not much has changed. He’s Stafford. He’s good. He’s not elite. You’d rather have him than most quarterbacks. Puka missed two games; now Adams is out for 6-10 weeks. I think the Rams should have — as I said before — added another receiver in the offseason. Now they’re out of money. Q: A ruptured hamstring robbed us of the Davante Adams revenge game this weekend. So, who is expected to step up and fill the void as Los Angeles’ No. 2 pass-catcher behind Puka Nacua? A: Nobody will step up. Konata Mumpfield might get the reps, but he’s not that good. Jordan Whittington isn’t that good. Tyler Higbee might get the second-most targets, but he’s not that good. Tutu Atwell isn’t good. I might think it’s tight end Colby Parkinson, but he’s having an awful season. The Rams screwed up; they should have used their first-round pick to acquire a receiver somehow. Q: I’m going to cheat here and ask two defensive line questions. One, how has Aaron Donald looked since coming out of retirement? Two, besides Donald, with Myles Garrett, Kobie Turner and Poona Ford injured and out for Sunday, who is left on the Rams’ defensive line? A: Aaron Donald hasn’t looked good. Unfortunately for the Rams, he’s still been the best defensive lineman on the roster. The only other guy who might have that distinction is Turner, and he’s on IR. Ford could only stop the run; he’s arguably the worst pass-rushing defensive tackle in the league. Braden Fiske has regressed badly since his rookie season. Dare I say that Ashton Jeanty is going to look like a top-10 pick on Sunday? This might be the worst defensive line in football. You’ll see guys named Tyler Davis and Ty Hamilton. That’s about all I can say about them. Larrell Murchison too. Q: Los Angeles’ defense is interesting on paper because despite ranking third in yards allowed , the unit is 17th in points surrendered heading into Week 7. What’s led to that anomaly? If you were Klint Kubiak, how would you attack the Rams’ defense? A: Ask yourself when the Rams’ defensive stats improved. Against Jameis Winston in Week 2 (when he replaced Jaxson Dart) and against Jalen Hurts in Week 4. And against Bo Nix. Last week it was Jacoby Brissett. Josh Allen and James Cook had no problems. Brock Purdy and Christian McCaffrey had no problems. If the team has talent at QB and RB/OL, I wouldn’t think twice about having a banner day against L.A. Given how well Klint Kubiak seems to have done with Kirk Cousins this season (you know better than I do if that’s true), I expect an ugly day for the Rams defense. McDuffie was out last week; I’m not sure if he’ll be back this week. The Rams’ best players are McDuffie and Garrett, and both could be out. Without those two, the defense is downright bad. Attack them however you want. I’ll be called a “hater” by Rams fans, and “not a Rams fan” because of these answers. This is merely what I’ve observed from a 2-4 season with wins over the Giants and Eagles, and just losing to the Cardinals. In the same way that the Chargers are 0-6, should we say that the Chargers “aren’t that bad” because they looked better on paper? Or should we call a spade a spade? This is…

full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - OCT (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders’ lost a 33-30 home loss to the Buffalo Bills on Sunday Let’s review how their wide receivers fared: Tre Tucker Tucker played 46 snaps, which led the team Sunday and was a season high for him. He had his second big game of the season as he had five catches for 97 yards and two touchdowns. The Raiders need to find consistent production from Tucker and it’s on him, Kirk Cousins and the coaching staff to do so. He can be an impact player. Jalen Nailor: The starter returned from missing Week 5 with a concussion. He had one catch for 9 yards on four targets Sunday. He has 6 catches for 61 yards on 15 targets in five games after signing a three-year, $35 million contract in free agency. Cody White: White played 14 snaps after playing a combined 89 snaps the past two weeks because of injuries. He didn’t have a catch on two targets and couldn’t bring a pass at the goal line on third down. Malik Benson The rookie sixth-round pick played eight snaps. He wasn’t target. He has two catches on eight targets for 12 yards this season. Dareke Young: He played six offensive snap. He didn’t have any targets. Conclusion: As has been their recent trend, the Raiders threw more to their tight ends and running backs than their receivers with 26 targets. The Raiders’ tight ends and running backs have been targeted 82 times in the past three games. The Raiders’ wide receivers have been targeted 41 times, exactly half the number, in that time period.

title: Raiders entering a critical 2-game swing
summary: After the Las Vegas Raiders began the season with a 3-0 record, they began a mostly tough, season defining eight-game stretch. It has not started well. The Raiders have gone 0-3 during the first portion of this period and are now 3-3. However, they have a big opportunity in the next two games when the […]
full_text: (Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After the Las Vegas Raiders began the season with a 3-0 record, they began a mostly tough, season defining eight-game stretch. It has not started well. The Raiders have gone 0-3 during the first portion of this period and are now 3-3. However, they have a big opportunity in the next two games when the host the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday and play at the New York Jets in Week 8. Both teams are 2-4. The Raiders have feasted on poor competition this season. The three teams they have beaten are a combined 2-15. The three teams the Raiders lost to are 14-3. So, if Las Vegas can continue its trend of beating teams with poor records they can regain a cushion at 5-3. That would be important as they play at the San Francisco 49ers (6-0), host the Seattle Seahawks (3-3) and play at the Denver Broncos (4-2) to end this eight-game stretch. When this stretch started, I stated even if the Raiders went just 3-5 in the eight games, their 3-0 start created a cushion that would allow them to enter the stretch run at 6-5. That would likely put them squarely in the playoff mix doing into the final six games of the season. Because the Rams are battered and are not as good as expected, this gives Las Vegas a chance to make up for this three-game listing steak. The Jets’ game was always looked at an opportunity during this stretch. So, if the Raiders can swept the next two weeks, they will be looking pretty good doing into the final three games of this stretch. They can’t afford to blow this opportunity.

title: Raiders-Rams Week 7: 5 things to watch
summary: The 3-3 Las Vegas Raiders host the 2-4 Los Angeles Rams Sunday at Allegiant Stadium. Kickoff is at 1:25 p.m. PT. Here are five keys to victory for Las Vegas: Contain Puka Nacua: The Rams’ wide receiver is a game wrecker. The Raiders’ secondary has had its share of issues in recent weeks. Nacua cannot […]
full_text: (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 3-3 Las Vegas Raiders host the 2-4 Los Angeles Rams Sunday at Allegiant Stadium. Kickoff is at 1:25 p.m. PT. Here are five keys to victory for Las Vegas: Contain Puka Nacua: The Rams’ wide receiver is a game wrecker. The Raiders’ secondary has had its share of issues in recent weeks. Nacua cannot be allowed to take the game over. Don’t give up so many dang points: The Raiders have allowed 135 points (an average of 33.75 pints a game) in the past four games. During their current three-game losing streak, the Raiders have allowed, at least, 30 points in every game. That’s their longest such streak since 2019. The Rams are outgaining their opponents by a total of 644 yards, which leads the NFL. They are capable of hitting that 30-point mark. New Las Vegas defensive coordinator Rob Leonard has to figure out a way to stop this trend now. Control line of scrimmage: We know the Raiders’ offensive line has had its struggles and we know the Rams’ defensive front is beat up. The Raiders will not win this game if Aaron Donald and company take over. The Las Vegas offensive line must be stout. Be better in red-zone offense: The Raiders were two for five inside the red zone against Buffalo. Las Vegas coach Klint Kubiak lamented that fact after the game. The Bills, on the other hand, were three of five inside the Raiders’ 20-yard line. It was the difference in the 33-30 game. The Raiders can’t let for opportunities points be squandered against the Rams. Get Bowers involved earlier: The Bills tried to take Raiders’ superstar tight end Brock Bowers out of the game plan and it work for the most part as Bowers wasn’t target until their were less than five minutes remaining in the third quarter. Bowers did end up making an impact with four catches for 70 yards. But he is what makes this offense click. He needs to impact the game for four quarters.

title: Dolphins lack of pass rush must be fixed following bye week
summary: Save for a spark of a pass rush against the Minnesota Vikings in Week 4, the Miami Dolphins pass rush has been dormant for the 2026 NFL season. Against the Vikings, the Dolphins recorded four sacks, two by defensive tackle Zach Sieler and one each from edge rusher Josh Uche and Chop Robinson. A four […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - SEPTEMBER 13: Chop Robinson #44 of the Miami Dolphins gets set during the fourth quarter of an NFL football game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Save for a spark of a pass rush against the Minnesota Vikings in Week 4, the Miami Dolphins pass rush has been dormant for the 2026 NFL season. Against the Vikings, the Dolphins recorded four sacks, two by defensive tackle Zach Sieler and one each from edge rusher Josh Uche and Chop Robinson. A four sacks performance was impressive. The zero sacks in Weeks 1, 2, 3, and 5 were not. Miami’s four sacks against the Vikings are their total for the season. The Dallas Cowboys, Kansas City Chiefs, Los Angeles Rams, New York Giants, and Philadelphia Eagles are all tied for the second-fewest sacks this season, and they each have eight. The Dolphins are half the second-worst tally in the league. On a team where the defensive secondary was expected to be a major concern coming into the season, the pass rush was supposed to balance those concerns. Instead, the pass rush has not shown up. The Dolphins are coming off their bye week. They have had two weeks to watch the film, diagnose the issues, and get them fixed. Head coach Jeff Hafley discussed the pass rush this week, explaining, “We need to create more pressure, and we talked about it in the bye week. We looked hard at it at the bye week, and we’ll work on that in practice. There’s different ways to do that. Whether you try to move a guy off the spot to force some errant throws or whether you try to scheme some things up to get some one-on-ones or overload some protections to try to get hits on the quarterback, we need to do that. So we’re going to work really hard at that this week and hopefully put it on tape Sunday.” Miami is allowing a 115.0 passer rating against them this season, 31st in the league. The Dolphins’s defense has faced third-down plays by opposing offenses a league-low 58 times (which is also a concerning stat in-and-of itself as Miami does not force teams into third down situations), but they have allowed the 16th most conversions for first down. Teams are picking up first downs on 52 percent of the third down plays against Miami’s defense. Getting pressure on quarterbacks, especially in clear passing situations, would bring that conversion rate down. The Dolphins’ roster is the youngest in the league, and this season is a rebuilding year for the franchise. The top priority is the growth and development of the players, looking forward to a sustainable, winning club for years to come. This year is not the goal, but the start of the journey. The problem is, every position group on the team seems to be showing growth and development. The pass rush has stagnated with not a lot to show. If they cannot figure out how to generate pressure on opposing quarterbacks, this year will continue to be a struggle just to stay competitive. And, next year, there will be many questions that have to be answered for a position group that should have been a strong point for a rebuilding team.

title: Rewriting the Narrative: The Vikings’ New Story
summary: Narrative is a funny thing in the NFL. Sometimes I question where all of the different storylines come from or why the media focuses on certain aspects over others. Not to be a conspiracy theorist (even though it’s sometimes a hobby for me), but I am sure the NFL marketing department sends information out to […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - OCTOBER 11: Will Reichard #16 of the Minnesota Vikings kicks a field goal against the New Orleans Saints during an NFL football game at Cesars Superdome on October 11, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Narrative is a funny thing in the NFL. Sometimes I question where all of the different storylines come from or why the media focuses on certain aspects over others. Not to be a conspiracy theorist (even though it’s sometimes a hobby for me), but I am sure the NFL marketing department sends information out to certain insiders to cover the stories they want to be prevailing storylines. Maybe that’s not true, but there are no definitive facts that could convince me that there isn’t a possibility that most NFL storylines portrayed in the mainstream media are contrived from somewhere inside an NFL VP or executive suite. A new narrative that could pick up steam after this weekend is that the Vikings “chose the wrong quarterback.” People are losing their minds over J.J. McCarthy coming into a game in the fourth quarter, down by 24 points, and leading a feverish comeback that ultimately felt short. It looked all too familiar to Vikings’ fans. For some reason, J.J. McCarthy has always thrived in the 4th quarter. The narrative that is already forming is that Kevin O’Connell’s system wasn’t right for McCarthy and that things are simplified in John Harbaugh’s offense. While that may be true, I didn’t see anything on Sunday that leads me to believe that McCarthy will find any more success in New York than he did in Minnesota. Jason LaCanfora is reporting that some New York Giants executive says there is going to be a major shift in offensive philosophy for New York and to look at the 2018 Ravens with Lamar Jackson in his rookie season. Apparently, New York has been eyeing McCarthy for quite some time to bring in as their starting quarterback. I find that slightly far-fetched based on them only willing to trade a 5th-round pick to acquire him. If McCarthy finds success in New York, there will be questions about why he didn’t find success in Minnesota. Persevere Toward Excellence I know what you’re thinking: STOP TALKING ABOUT THE NEW YORK GIANTS. I am, right now. Narrative lives in a world of hypotheticals. We live in the real world. Reality cannot be denied, and the Vikings are 5-0 going into a very winnable game against the Indianapolis Colts. The Minnesota Vikings have started a season with a 6-0 record six times in the modern NFL era. Of those six seasons, they made the playoffs in all but one, which was in 2003 when they lost on the last play of the season to the Arizona Cardinals. The game that culminated in the classic Paul Allen screaming “NOOOOOOOOO.” All these narratives can be squashed if Kyler Murray goes out and performs to the level at which he is capable. The experiment of drafting a first-round quarterback is over, and we are officially under the Nolan Teasley regime. Minnesota knew what they had in McCarthy. Maybe the Giants were willing to give more in a trade, but the narrative that I am choosing to perpetuate is that the front office was simply ready to move on and was satisfied getting any value back. I wish J.J. the best, but the franchise has chosen a new path. That is what I will do here as well and move on. The Minnesota Vikings are the most enigmatic team in the NFL. Some armchair NFL analysts (people on social media who bought a microphone and know how to post on the internet) are saying that the Vikings are the third-best team in the NFC North. They’re not calling us the third-best 5-0 team; they are saying that the Bears and Packers (both of whom we beat with Carson Wentz) are better. HA! Are We Witnessing History? This defense is special. Like really special, as evidenced by how the Vikings’ current 10-game win streak has manifested itself. Over the last 10 games, the Minnesota Vikings have scored 229 points. Historically, you have to go back to 1934 to find a 10-game winning streak where the team scored fewer points (the 1934 Detroit Lions scored 215 points). That is an astonishing statistic but speaks to the dominance that we have seen from this defense. Football is about winning games. Sure, the Vikings offense has had its struggles and is still finding its footing. Is that a circumstance of poor coaching or them being a bad offense? Or is it a result of a shift in philosophy for Kevin O’Connell? From a narrative perspective, KO is rewriting the defining story of his time as the coach of the Minnesota Vikings. He recently talked about how he has shifted his mindset from being concerned with what stats look like on paper to winning football games. This team is playing complementary football at its finest. Every season has its ebbs and flows, but we also see those differences happen over the course of multiple seasons. Right now, the defense is obviously the strength of this team. When Brian Flores’ unit is fresh, they are almost unstoppable. One thing I have noticed is just how relentless the defensive front is. They just keep coming and don’t stop until after the whistle. The defense is playing with such an intensity that it simply wears down opposing offenses and beats them down into submission. Gotta Have the Ball to Score An important factor in this success is the offense’s ability to maintain drives. So far this season, the Vikings’ are averaging the second highest average time of possession in the league at 33:38 per game. They trail only the Chicago Bears in this category. I will concede that the Vikings haven’t been very efficient when it comes to scoring touchdowns, but I firmly believe that is going to change. In fantasy football, we talk about regression toward the mean. The Minnesota offense has only scored eight offensive touchdowns in 5 games played this season, which is the 2nd fewest in the league. However, this offense is better than that, and we will start to see that number look more normal going forward. Another prevailing shift in philosophy is that this now appears to be a run-first offense, as evidenced by the aforementioned time of possession statistic. This offense is about controlling the clock and taking care of the football. It’s like we are time traveling back to the Mike Zimmer era. However, this is the Teasley/O’Connell/Flores era. We are fans of one of the premier organizations in the NFL, and I think we are going to actually see success beyond the regular season. I know, as a Vikings fan, hope is a slippery slope. A slippery slope to sadness and disappointment. There Is a Long Road Ahead The game this Sunday against the Colts will set the tone for the rest of the season. I fully expect Indianapolis, with their backs to the wall, to make this game competitive for as long as they can. I can also see Daniel Jones throwing four interceptions, which would squash a different narrative that the Vikings shouldn’t have let him leave the building. I think Minnesota wins this game in dominant fashion, and we see our offense come to life. They are going to have to, because this team has a tough schedule going forward where they are going to have to put some points on the board. It’s time for this offense to get rolling and for the defense to keep doing what it does. I can’t wait for Sunday! Until Next Skol.

Questionable = the league defines a Questionable injury designation as being ‘uncertain’ of whether the player will play or not. This replaces the former definition of having a 50% chance of playing. title: Week 7 Preview (And a J.J. McCarthy Take)
summary: I’ll start with the juiciest part: J.J. McCarthy came in for the New York Giants and nearly pulled off an incredible comeback, with the Giants down 34-10 in the 4th quarter. He threw for 243 passing yards, rushed for 26 more, and threw one passing touchdown, but he also threw an interception in…drumroll…11 minutes. As […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - NOVEMBER 03: Jordan Addison #3 of the Minnesota Vikings is chased by Julian Blackmon #32 and Samuel Womack III #33 of the Indianapolis Colts during the fourth quarter at U.S. Bank Stadium on November 03, 2024 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images I’ll start with the juiciest part: J.J. McCarthy came in for the New York Giants and nearly pulled off an incredible comeback, with the Giants down 34-10 in the 4th quarter. He threw for 243 passing yards, rushed for 26 more, and threw one passing touchdown, but he also threw an interception in…drumroll…11 minutes. As a Daily Norseman contributor, I feel it necessary to discuss this. Okay, you twisted my arm… I want to discuss it. The DN game-day discussion (and Vikings-related social media) ran the gamut from calling the trade the worst thing to happen to the Vikings since the 1998 NFC Championship Game to casually dismissing it as a giant nothingburger, swiping it away like a gnat at a picnic. As I found myself during the heated Kirk Cousins debate that divided the fan base in DN daily threads and elsewhere, I believe both sides have some truth. I feel the truth fell somewhere in the middle. This time? I think there’s a better chance of a clear victor. Watching it live, McCarthy showed the same flashes of magic he did last season. The guy clearly has an intangible quality you can’t coach. I actually forgot it was a Giants game for a moment; I was rooting so hard for him to pull it off. But a few important caveats. First, the New Orleans Saints’ game plan was designed for Jameis Winston, not McCarthy. Second, up 34-10, the Saints clearly played a more prevent defense to keep the Giants’ offense off the field. That said, McCarthy did manage chunk completions. Third, the Saints’ defense is not that good. Finally, while he had an interception, McCarthy should have had a second one that could have made the rest of the excitement moot. As the episode unfolded, I kept asking myself: How could the Vikings give Christian Ponder 36 starts over four seasons and J.J. McCarthy only 10 starts in essentially one season? I simply can’t get my head around it. The Vikings ate $28.5 million in dead cap to turn the page on Cousins. Couldn’t they take a $6.95 million hit on a much higher cap to keep McCarthy around next year? You know, to ensure they at least had one QB under contract for 2027? Yeah, yeah, I know: the 5th-year option decision loomed, too. So don’t pick it up. It would still give you more time to see the finished product. If it ended up poorly, let him walk. If he looked the part and improved, resign him to something manageable. If he became the starter and had a fantastic season, tag him to buy a season and work out a larger long-term deal. Are we just going to ignore what’s going on with Bryce Young in Carolina? McCarthy will be the Giants’ starter until his play no longer warrants it. He has to. You know what Jameis Winston is like in his 12th season. He can take a team’s fan base to the highest of highs. Unfortunately, that also means there’s further to fall when the inevitable, inexplicable high-leverage interceptions start coming in bunches. John Harbaugh will need to go with McCarthy’s unknown potential and ceiling. The NFC East is theirs for the taking. The Eagles are going through a nightmarish season, and Jalen Hurts is now out for the year. The Cowboys have one of the worst defenses I’ve ever seen. And the Commanders are the definition of mediocrity. Winston is still available, worst-case scenario. But hey, this discussion could end soon. The Giants hit the road to face a Houston Texans team finally playing as it should. Their defense is among the NFL’s best. McCarthy could go down there and lay an egg, similar to the Lambeau Field game last season. Sunday could have been a mirage, a fluky performance aided by fortunate circumstances. A slight detour for a career destined to be a backup quarterback. Or…he could play well and become the quarterback I always thought he could be. I’m not going out on a limb to say the Giants would have won that game if McCarthy had started. If he strings together a series of wins over the next month, the collective agitation among Vikings fans will turn uncomfortable quickly. If he leads the Giants to the playoffs? No. No. No. No. Can’t happen. Won’t happen. Go Cowboys. Go Commanders. Heck, I’ll even root for the Eagles. Please. Someone step up. We’re on a collision course with a J.J. McCarthy-led Giants team in the playoffs, aren’t we? It would be the most Vikings outcome imaginable. I can’t talk about this anymore. WEEK 7 PREVIEW: A MUST WIN The Minnesota Vikings return home, rested and (likely) close to fully healthy, to face an Indianapolis Colts team that is an absolute train wreck right now. They’re 2-4, just lost to the winless Tennessee Titans at home, their general manager Chris Ballard was fired, coach Shane Steichen could be next, rumors are swirling that their best offensive player, Jonathan Taylor, could be moved ahead of the trade deadline, and their best player in the secondary, Sauce Gardner, will likely miss the Vikings game, too. Other than that, things are going swimmingly. VIKINGS ON OFFENSE For the third straight game, the Vikings will face a porous defense. The Colts rank 27 th in points per game, 28 th in yards per play, 26 th in sacks, and 29 th in interceptions. From what I see, they don’t crack the Top 20 in any other traditional defensive category: total yards allowed, pass yards allowed, or rush yards allowed. And this is even with holding the Tennessee Titans’ anemic unit to just 186 total yards (and somehow still losing). When they faced top-notch offenses this year, they gave up 523 total yards to the Kansas City Chiefs and 508 to the Baltimore Ravens. Meanwhile, the Vikings hope to have Christian Darrisaw, Jordan Addison, Jordan Mason, and T.J. Hockenson back for this one. Even if they can’t all play, they have no excuse not to move the ball and score at least 28 points here. With Sauce Gardner out, the Colts also appear to be without other key contributors, including DE Arden Key. If the Vikings had held onto the ball, they should have come close to or surpassed 30 points against the Saints on the road. Now they’re home, facing an equally porous defense. Get it done. VIKINGS ON DEFENSE Brian Flores has the Vikings defense rolling at a potentially historic pace heading into this one. I touched on this last week, so no need to repeat it. They now face a Colts offense led by Daniel Jones, who is struggling mightily. ESPN Colts reporter Stephen Holder has a great article on it this week. It hasn’t been pretty. Jones has been a turnover machine, and when he isn’t turning the ball over, things aren’t much better. As Holder noted, he’s hovering near the bottom in most categories, including QBR (30th), completion rate (29th), and yards per attempt (29th). Jones clearly hasn’t fully recovered from the torn Achilles tendon in his right (plant leg), which is always tricky for QBs. Dan Marino was never the same after his, and Kirk Cousins is just now beginning to resemble the guy he was for us, nearly three full years later. Either way, Brian Flores is the last guy Jones wants to see on the opposing sideline. This ain’t the 2022 season anymore, and the Vikings’ bend-and-break defense won’t magically make a comeback in Week 7 of the 2026 season. Ugh, another Giants reference. No, we aren’t going to face a J.J. McCarthy-led Giants team in the playoffs. Can’t happen. Won’t happen. Don’t even contemplate it. Anyway, what makes Jones’ struggles even more concerning is that, while not elite, the Colts WR group still has talent, even with 1,000+ yard receiver Alec Pierce out. Keenan Allen may be 34, but he’s still dangerous and leads the WR group in receptions. Josh Downs leads in receiving yards and can also stretch the defense, with a team high in 20+ receiving-yard plays. Even our…

title: Vikings vs. Colts: Can Minnesota Avoid the Ultimate Trap Game?
summary: The 5-0 Minnesota Vikings face a motivated Indianapolis Colts team coming off their bye week—and every sign points to a classic NFL trap game. In this episode of The Real Forno Show, host Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano break down why Sunday’s matchup against the Indianapolis Colts has all the makings of a trap […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 4: Kevin O'Connell head coach of the Minnesota Vikings looks on before the game against the Miami Dolphins at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 5-0 Minnesota Vikings face a motivated Indianapolis Colts team coming off their bye week—and every sign points to a classic NFL trap game. In this episode of The Real Forno Show, host Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano break down why Sunday’s matchup against the Indianapolis Colts has all the makings of a trap game—and why Minnesota must avoid complacency at all costs. Coming off a bye week with 97 of 98 analysts picking them to win, the Vikings face a Colts team that just fired general manager Chris Ballard. “This screams trap game,” Forness said. Stefano outlined the anatomy of a trap game: “A trap game is not merely a game against an inferior opponent. It’s a confluence of a record disparity, motivational symmetry, scheduling context, and cognitive load.” Forness emphasized that ball control may be the Vikings’ ticket to a Super Bowl run. “This offense’s number one job isn’t necessarily to score points, it’s to keep the defense off the field,” he explained. The Vikings have held the ball for over 79 minutes in their last two games, limiting Brian Flores’ top-ranked defense to just 84 snaps. Forness compared the approach to college football: “Ball control and time of possession. It’s ugly… But God, there’s beauty in watching Army versus Navy.” On the defensive side, Flores’ unit ranks first in the NFL in points allowed at 12.8 per game and presents a nightmare for Colts quarterback Daniel Jones, who has 15 turnover-worthy plays this season. “Eric Wilson should not be this good at football, but it’s a tribute to what Brian Flores is doing,” Forness said of the 10th-year journeyman linebacker turned Pro Bowl candidate. The Colts also feature the league’s worst run defense by EPA per rush allowed, setting up Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason for a potentially big day on the ground. Key Points: The Vikings have historically struggled coming out of the bye under Kevin O’Connell, losing to the Eagles in 2024 and the Lions in 2023. The Colts fired GM Chris Ballard mid-season, adding emotional motivation; Anthony Richardson publicly praised Ballard despite being benched. Indianapolis ranks last in the NFL in pressure percentage and EPA per rush allowed. Kyler Murray has just 18 available snaps with Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, and T.J. Hockenson all on the field together. The Colts’ offensive line features Jalen Travis starting over Bernhard Raimann at left tackle, with Tanor Bortolini vulnerable against cross-dog blitzes. Brian Flores’ simulated pressures and six-plus-man blitzes will test Daniel Jones, who remains less than a year removed from a torn Achilles. Forness predicted a 27-16 Vikings victory, calling it “ugly” but effective: “It’s okay to win ugly.” The Colts’ star tight end Tyler Warren and wide receiver Alec Pierce are trending toward not playing. Shane Steichen’s tendency to abandon the run—even when leading—could play into Flores’ hands. “As long as you win, baby,” Forness said. “All that matters is you win another game.” Listen: Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano bring the X’s and O’s, the stats, and the passion every Minnesota Vikings fan craves. So here’s a question for you: Will the Vikings come out of the bye sharp and move to 6-0, or will the motivated Colts pull off the upset nobody sees coming? full_text: CLEVELAND, OH - AUGUST 22: Cleveland Browns defensive end Benton Whitley (61) on the field prior to the National Football League preseason game between the Buffalo Bills and Cleveland Browns on August 22, 2026, at Huntington Bank Field in Cleveland, OH. (Photo by Frank Jansky/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Xavier Newman-Johnson and Benton Whitley officially reverted to the New England Patriots’ practice squad on Friday after serving as standard elevations against the Chicago Bears. The 30-24 loss at Soldier Field marked the first appearances of 2026 for the offensive lineman as well as the outside linebacker. Newman-Johnson, 27, made his Thursday night debut in protection on three extra points and one field goal. The 6-foot-2, 297-pound interior lineman provided depth behind a starting five that was missing right guard Ben Brown due to a knee injury and also lost left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker to injured reserve ahead of the 8:15 p.m. ET kickoff due to a hamstring injury . Added to New England’s practice squad in September after being hosted on a visit, Newman-Johnson now stands 26 games into his NFL career. First entering the league with head coach Mike Vrabel’s former Tennessee Titans as an undrafted free agent in 2022, the Baylor product spent parts of two seasons in the AFC South. He went on to reside on the New York Jets’ practice squad, 53-man roster and injured reserve before being released and landing in Foxborough. A five-game starter, his odometer includes 338 downs on offense and 72 downs in the kicking game. Whitley, 27, handled 13 snaps on special teams during the Midwest road trip between kickoff coverage, kickoff return and punt return. That marked 46 percent of the workload in the transitional phase. The well-traveled edge rusher signed to the Patriots’ practice squad in September. A Massachusetts native and Holy Cross alum, Whitley originally entered the NFL with the Los Angeles Rams as part of the organization’s undrafted class of 2022. He went on to make stops with the Kansas City Chiefs, Minnesota Vikings, New York Giants, Arizona Cardinals and Tampa Bay Buccaneers through 2025. And his most recent training camp was spent with the Cleveland Browns before being waived at the league’s cutdown deadline at the end of August. Seven games into his career, the 6-foot-4, 255-pound linebacker has recorded one fumble recovery and one pass defensed through 16 snaps on defense and 87 snaps on special teams. Both call-ups have two standard elevations remaining before 53-man contracts would be required to take the field. Heading into the mini bye at 4-3, the Patriots currently carry a full practice squad and an opening on the active roster.

title: Patriots running game fails to deliver against Bears
summary: Finding an opening in the Chicago Bears defense, Rhamondre Stevenson made one of the most spectacular plays of the New England Patriots season so far on Thursday night. With time winding down on the first half, he took the ball 48 yards to the house for an improbable touchdown. That, of course, was Rhamondre Stevenson, […]
full_text: Finding an opening in the Chicago Bears defense, Rhamondre Stevenson made one of the most spectacular plays of the New England Patriots season so far on Thursday night. With time winding down on the first half, he took the ball 48 yards to the house for an improbable touchdown. That, of course, was Rhamondre Stevenson, the receiver. He finished with a career-best 93 yards and a touchdown on five catches. Rhamondre Stevenson, the ball-carrier, on the other hand, didn’t enjoy the same success. He received six handoffs and turned them into only 22 rushing yards. The story of Stevenson’s day is the story of the Patriots offense as a whole on Thursday. Despite going up against a run defense ranked near the bottom of the league in multiple metrics, the unit could not generate a consistent push on the ground. Excluding scramble plays by quarterback Drake Maye, New England finished with only 44 yards on 13 carries, an average of 3.4 yards per run. This kind of production was not good enough against the Bears, as head coach Mike Vrabel pointed out after the Patriots’ 30-24 defeat . “We didn’t run the ball well enough,” Vrabel said during his postgame press conference at Soldier Field. “But, we moved it however we needed to move it and sometimes you are going to have days like that. I thought we’d be able to run it a little better. We didn’t, but then our best players were putting the ball in good spots most of the time and making good decisions. That’s how it goes, we’d have liked to run the ball a little bit better, but it didn’t happen tonight.” The Patriots gave all three of their running backs opportunities against the Bears. While Stevenson got most of the action both in terms of snaps, carries and targets, TreVeyon Henderson and Corey Kiner were also involved. Henderson played 13 snaps on the night, gaining 9 yards on three runs. Kiner fared marginally better, finishing with six snaps as well as 13 yards on four carries. The two and Stevenson all finished firmly in the red in terms of expected points added per rushing attempt, with a combined average of -0.39. Not all of that can be pinned on the running backs. The ground game is a collaborative effort and on Thursday it featured third-stringer Walter Rouse going wire-to-wire at left guard and fourth-stringer Matt Pryor doing the same on the right side. Rouse and Pryor did what they could, but for a unit built on cohesion the near-constant personnel turnover it experienced has been an issue. Ultimately, though, the Patriots remain steadfast in their determination that the run game needs to improve regardless of circumstance. “We have to find a way to run it a little better, for sure,” said Drake Maye. “But sometimes when they’re loading the box and forcing us to throw it, we’ll go out there and throw for a bunch of yards. And trusting me, and trusting me with good decisions, that’s kind of the way sometimes the ball rolls. But I think we definitely got to get the running game going, and I don’t think it’s the only thing to do. We just run it and try to be effective and knowing that we got the right guys. And I thought the guys up front that stepped in and stepped up, did a nice job.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Patriots vs. Bears: Fan observations from Week 7 loss
summary: My schedule is all kinds of out of whack right now and I don’t have as much time as I’d like to get my thoughts in order, so apologies in advance for some somewhat truncated Fan Notes this morning. I’m guessing you’re all as ready as I am to just shrug our shoulders and move […]
full_text: My schedule is all kinds of out of whack right now and I don’t have as much time as I’d like to get my thoughts in order, so apologies in advance for some somewhat truncated Fan Notes this morning. I’m guessing you’re all as ready as I am to just shrug our shoulders and move on from this game. Kudos to the Bears. I’ll start these off with my usual rant of hypocrisy and nonsense: Thursday Night Football is the worst thing to happen to the NFL since Zeke Mowatt. It’s just an awful product. Not so awful that I won’t watch it when the Patriots play, but last night represented the last TNF game I’m going to watch this year that doesn’t fall on Thanksgiving, when I’m too full and drunk to care what‘s on TV at all. Nothing about that game represents either of these teams, and I just hate it. To be fair, it wasn’t even a bad game in terms of play or content. It was actually one of the better TNF games I can remember watching. I just don’t think you get the same thing from either side if last night’s matchup got moved to Sunday when everyone had more time and rest. And even though I didn’t know what to expect and I’m not taking too much away from this game one way or another, this isn’t one of those losses that sticks with me. I was over it almost immediately after the final whistle. It more or less came down to an end zone interception and some very ticky-tack penalties on the defense to keep the Bears on the field. Considering an away game on a short week, you kind of have to take that. Before I get too deep into these Fan Notes, a quick congrats to the refs for finding an obscure footnote in the NFL rulebook that states you must call at least one holding penalty per drive. Not sure how everyone else missed that. Hindsight is always 20/20, and I guess things always look clearer in the light of day. And I appreciate the faith in the offense and the desire to be aggressive on the opening drive. But going for it on 4th-and-5 with a patchwork offensive line just a hair over midfield might not be the best call. Other than that pick, I thought that Drake Maye looked very solid. I’m sure there was something that Raridon was supposed to do there, or maybe Maye has a ton of confidence in the rookie. Because otherwise I have no idea what he saw there. But that was really the only blemish on his night, and it ended up being what decided the game. That, and the defense not being able to get off the field and seemingly forgetting how to tackle. The D looked kind of tired out there. I don’t know how many yards Bears ball carriers generated after contact, but they seemed to be dragging Patriots defenders with them like Spike on the Little Giants. Tackles that might have been made on an average Sunday weren’t made, and the score reflects that. One of the douchiest things one person can do, in my opinion, is test someone else’s fandom of a particular NFL team by asking, “So you’re a fan? Then can you name the starting offensive line?” Like who cares whether you can name the whole line or not? And maybe I’m making this note right now because I for sure wouldn’t be able to answer that question if someone asked me right now. I don’t want to blame anything on injuries. Every team is banged up. But good lord is this Patriots team struggling with depth. The line held up as well as it could, and it’s not like Maye took 10 sacks, but the early playcalling was specifically designed to get the ball out quickly, and the Bears were all over it. By halftime I had stopped hoping that someone on the Patriots would cover Luther Burden and instead started hoping I would see a Patriots player and Burden on my TV screen at the same time. I started to make a snarky comment about 70 yards rushing for the Patriots, but I’m going to gve them some slack. Ninth-string offensive linemen aren’t really known as road graders. At least A.J Brown didn’t have four drops in this game. He just had one contested catch that would have set the Patriots up with goal to go that you kind of expect him to make, even with a defender in good position. Did the better team win last night? For sure. One team made plays and limited mistakes; the other team didn’t. That’s a good recipe for victory. But these are two very strong teams that will very likely be around in January. I highly doubt that we’ll be seeing a Patriots vs. Bears rematch this season… but there could very well be one sooner than four years from now. Unless I’m mistaken, nobody else got IR’ed last night, which is all we can ask for right now. Time to enjoy a mini-bye, get healthier, and turn the page to Miami. I know the Dolphins stink, but it’s an away game, and South Florida scares me for a laundry list of reasons.

title: Patriots News: Self-inflicted wounds doom Pats vs. Bears

title: Is A.J. Brown growing frustrated by his lack of production? Patriots star says ‘No.’
summary: After every New England Patriots game, we are publishing an admittedly subjective list of “winners and losers.” A.J. Brown found himself included in each of the last two editions, and both times in the “loser” category. Why? Because the big-ticket offseason acquisition failed to live up to expectation against the New York Jets in Week […]
full_text: After every New England Patriots game, we are publishing an admittedly subjective list of “winners and losers.” A.J. Brown found himself included in each of the last two editions, and both times in the “loser” category. Why? Because the big-ticket offseason acquisition failed to live up to expectation against the New York Jets in Week 6 and again versus the Chicago Bears on Thursday night . In total, he has caught just six passes on 16 targets in those two games, gaining 75 yards in the process. His lack of production as the Patriots’ No. 1 wide receiver has been notable. Brown himself is not stressed or frustrated by it, however. “I’m a vet, I understand how the game goes,” he explained after the Patriots’ 30-24 loss in Chicago . “It’s just how the game is. I know what type of player I am and I know that that’s always the case, every time I line up I get a lot of attention. Teams try to take me away and it gives a lot of opportunities to other guys to make plays and soften that up for me. And then whenever I get my shots, I have to make them.” So far, Brown has not been able to make the shots on a regular basis. Against the Bears, he had a deep ball broken up at the catch point — a play that could have been flagged for defensive pass interference — and saw two other targets fall incomplete. He did catch passes of 18, 16 and 14 yards for his best output as a Patriot to date, but the team did not send two draft picks to the Philadelphia Eagles earlier this year for 48 yards’ worth of production. He was brought in to help lift Drake Maye and the passing offense to new heights, and so far has not delivered on that promise. Of course, the circumstances played a role in this as well. In the season opener in Seattle, Brown caught three passes in just over two quarters of play before exiting with a high ankle sprain. He missed the subsequent four games on injured reserve, and has participated in only four non-walkthrough practices since his return last week. The 29-year-old knows that he cannot force the issue, and neither can his quarterback. “Drake did a really good job just taking what they gave us. You can’t force that,” he said. “It’s tough, but you can’t get aggressive. You can’t get emotional and try to force something. I think he did a great job just taking what they gave us, and unfortunately in the first half we were just stubbing our own toe.”

title: Missed tackles tell the story of the Patriots’ loss to the Bears
summary: After missing eight tackles in a gritty win over the New York Jets last week, the New England Patriots doubled that total on Thursday night, missing 16 tackles in a 30-24 defeat to the Chicago Bears. The last time the Patriots eclipsed that total? Look no further than their 29-13 loss to the Seattle Seahawks […]
full_text: After missing eight tackles in a gritty win over the New York Jets last week, the New England Patriots doubled that total on Thursday night, missing 16 tackles in a 30-24 defeat to the Chicago Bears . The last time the Patriots eclipsed that total? Look no further than their 29-13 loss to the Seattle Seahawks in Super Bowl LX, where New England trailed 19-0 in the fourth quarter. “[Our] tackling wasn’t good enough. Not against his team,” head coach Mike Vrabel said. “We knew coming in, certainly tackling on Thursday night, but against this team, whether it’s [D’Andre] Swift, [Luther Burden III] or [Caleb Williams], it just leads to extra yards and conversions. But we fought, and I would say that we need to turn the ball over and we have to tackle better, and those are fundamental skills.” Struggling to consistently match the Bears’ physicality past the line of scrimmage, the Patriots’ defense had difficulty shedding blocks, which played a significant role in Luther Burden III’s 130 yards and one touchdown on just four catches in the first half alone. That mismatch remained in the second half. Early in the third quarter, the Chicago offense ran a naked bootleg 11 yards out from the end zone. Caleb Williams connected with his tight end, Colston Loveland, crossing over the middle of the field. Loveland, turning towards the end zone, quickly shed a Marcus Jones tackle and fought through another two New England defenders as he broke past the plane to extend the Patriots’ deficit by two scores. “I got to make the tackle when it comes down to that,” Jones said. “And then [the Bears] had certain schemes where they would line up in certain formations, run overs to where we’re away from leverage and things like that. But as the game went on, we learned and stuff, but I’m a hard critic of myself. So, I will get it corrected for sure.” On the ground, the story wasn’t much different. With Swift and a handful of Roschon Johnson carries, Chicago managed 3.1 yards after contact in the run game against New England’s defensive front. That number surpasses the Kansas City Chiefs’ league-leading average of three yards per attempt this season with Kenneth Walker. The defensive line’s shortcomings in finishing plays also extended into its pass rush. Although the Patriots sacked Williams three times, the unit generated 25 total pressures on his dropbacks and created plenty more opportunities to force Williams into inaccurate throws. Too often, however, the opposing quarterback escaped near-sacks and turned those plays into chunk gains through the air. Williams threw for 308 yards and two touchdowns on the evening, completing 22 of his 33 pass attempts. Meanwhile, New England’s defense came up short in its efforts to force a turnover. “We talked about it all week. [Williams is] very gifted with how he can run and how he can extend plays,” cornerback Christian Gonzalez said. “I talked about before the game: you got to defend the second play. There’s a play, and then there’s a second play with a quarterback like Caleb. So, it’s a challenge for the secondary. It’s about the whole team, but we look forward to it. We embrace it, and they got the best of us tonight.”
author: Andrew Guindon

title: Costly Drake Maye mistake looms large in Patriots’ loss to Bears
summary: Standing at the postgame podium, Drake Maye shook his head and looked down at ground. He let out an audible sigh of frustration. The Patriots quarterback was replaying his second-quarter interception that helped swing Thursday night’s loss to the Chicago Bears. “Huge point in the game. Gosh,” Maye said after the game. “Those plays can […]
full_text: Standing at the postgame podium, Drake Maye shook his head and looked down at ground. He let out an audible sigh of frustration. The Patriots quarterback was replaying his second-quarter interception that helped swing Thursday night’s loss to the Chicago Bears . “Huge point in the game. Gosh,” Maye said after the game. “Those plays can swing the game, can impact the game, and that was definitely one of them right there. I wish I definitely had that one back.” After a slow offensive start Thursday night while dealing with Chicago’s pressure packages, New England’s offense found its footing with a pair of strong drives to open the second quarter. Maye finished the first with a rushing touchdown, then led the Patriots back into the red zone with a chance to take the lead. Instead, his pass up the seam to rookie tight end Eli Raridon sailed short and was intercepted. “We hit the same thing, the same exact play later in the game,” Maye said, recalling his 30-yard touchdown pass to Raridon in third quarter quarter. “I like my chances in there. It’s frustrating … I let my team down.” The interception cost the Patriots a chance to add seven points, a missed opportunity that loomed large in their 30-24 to the Bears. Trailing 27-21 in the fourth quarter, New England had two possessions to take the lead but managed just one first down between them. The Bears then drained more than 11 minutes of clock across their following two possessions. Those missed opportunities weighed on Maye as much as the interception. “That’s probably what I’ll be thinking about most over the weekend, having two chances with the ball down 27-21,” Maye said. “We got a good chance to go score and trust our defense … We just fell short tonight.” Despite the costly turnover, Maye kept New England within striking distance against Caleb Williams and Chicago’s high-powered offense. With little help from the running game, he completed a season-high 77.4% of his passes and was nearly perfect against pressure, completing 11 of 12 attempts for 151 yards and a touchdown. “He gave us a chance. He competed,” head coach Mike Vrabel said. “I know he’d like to have that one back. He’ll learn from it like he always does. I’m glad he’s ours.”

title: Key matchups: Saints vs. Steelers
summary: The New Orleans Saints are coming off a must-win game against the New York Giants. Coming off their big win, the Saints are now enjoying their time in Paris ahead of another probable must-win game against the Pittsburgh Steelers. Gayle Benson and the Saints organization have put a lot of resources into being the ambassadors […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 18: Alvin Kamara #41 of the New Orleans Saints runs against Jason Pinnock #25 of the New York Giants during their game at MetLife Stadium on October 18, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints are coming off a must-win game against the New York Giants. Coming off their big win, the Saints are now enjoying their time in Paris ahead of another probable must-win game against the Pittsburgh Steelers. Gayle Benson and the Saints organization have put a lot of resources into being the ambassadors of the NFL in Paris, and a win will certainly help. But if the Black and Gold want to go into the bye with a win, they’ll have to utilize these key matchups. Saints pass protection vs. Steelers’ star pass rushers The Saints have surprisingly held their own against some of the league’s top pass rushers through their first six games of the season. Abdul Carter, Maxx Crosby, Aiden Hutchinson, and Trey Hendrickson have combined for one sack against the Saints’ pass protection. Despite their success, they haven’t faced a group as talented as the Steelers pass rushers, highlighted by T.J. Watt. The former Defensive Player of the Year has 4.5 sacks so far this season and remains in contention for the prestigious award this season. The Saints’ pass protection has struggled this season, mostly due to blitz packages, and is facing a Steelers team that blitzes just 26% of the time. Pittsburgh is confident in their pass rushers to win one-on-one with Watt, Nate Herbig, and Alex Highsmith therefore don’t send in extra pass rushers. The key to winning the game is keeping Tyler Shough upright, and the Saints are certain to be tested in pass protection. Saints run game vs. Steelers run defense Unfortunately for the Saints offense, they’re facing a defense that’s good against the pass and against the run. While their run defense isn’t as good as their top-10 pass defense, it’s still above average, ranked 14th in the NFL. But a 14th-place ranking doesn’t tell the whole story. Pittsburgh held Tampa Bay Buccaneers running back Bucky Irving to 2.3 yards per carry on 19 carries, Jonathan Taylor to 3.0 yards per carry, and Quinshon Judkins to 3.1 yards per carry. The Steelers’ run defense is performing exceptionally against running backs and will be facing a Saints team coming off their best rushing performance of the season. The Saints rushed for 175 yards against the Giants, highlighted by Kendre Miller, who rushed for 70 yards on 3.5 a carry. Alvin Kamara and C.J. Donaldson, however, were more efficient with their touches, rushing for 4.9 and 6.5 yards per carry, respectively. The Saints are dealing with injuries to their offensive line, with rookie Jeremiah Wright taking over for Cessar Ruiz. Wright was impressive in his NFL debut and played a big role in the Black and Gold’s rushing success. If New Orleans wants to find their third win of the season, it will have to come with more success running the ball. Saints’ pass defense vs. QB Aaron Rodgers The Saints’ secondary had their best three quarters of the season, then followed it up with an unbelievably bad fourth quarter. After intercepting Jameis Winston twice and J.J. McCarthy once, the Saints defense allowed 243 passing yards to McCarthy in their fourth-quarter meltdown, and will now face a veteran in Aaron Rodgers, who is playing good football. Rodgers has thrown for 3+ touchdowns in four of his last five games. While he has made mistakes, throwing four interceptions in that span, the veteran is playing his best since leaving the Green Bay Packers. Pittsburgh is a solid rushing team, but they rely on Rodgers to win them games. Stop Rodgers, and you have a good chance to come out of Paris with a win.

full_text: DALLAS, TX - OCTOBER 10: Texas Longhorns wide receiver Cam Coleman (8) catches a touchdown pass during the Allstate Red River Rivalry between the Texas Longhorns and Oklahoma Sooners on October 10, 2026, at Cotton Bowl Stadium in Dallas, TX. (Photo by Brian Rothmuller/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images While the New Orleans Saints are preparing to take on the Steelers in Paris tomorrow morning, there are some intriguing college players to watch on Saturday who could potentially become additions to the Saints’ roster in 2027. Here are three college players to watch this Saturday. Cam Coleman, WR, Texas Yes, a wide receiver. The likelihood of this happening is very low, but Coleman is still an exciting player to watch. He will be matching up against a very talented Ole Miss team tonight at 6:30 PM on ABC. Coleman and quarterback Arch Manning are still looking to make the Texas offense more explosive, but Coleman’s combination of size, speed, athleticism, and ability to make contested catches makes him one of the best receivers in the class. Suntarine Perkins, EDGE/OLB, Ole Miss Perkins will be on the field at the same time as Cam Coleman, and if the Texas offense is sputtering, there’s a good chance it will be because of the impact Perkins is having on Arch Manning and the rest of the Longhorn offense. Perkins possesses the ability to rush the passer and play off-ball linebacker. His versatility would be a welcome addition to a Saints defense looking for a consistent complement to Chase Young, as well as a player who can operate off the ball and make plays in space. Justin Scott, DT, Miami The No. 1 team in the nation will take on Pitt at 11 AM on ESPN, and in the middle of Miami’s defense will be Justin Scott. Scott is a powerful interior defensive tackle who can play well against the run and affect the quarterback from the interior. This has been a major issue for the Saints’ defensive front this season. Not having a consistent presence in the heart of the defensive line has negatively affected the Saints’ run defense while also allowing opposing quarterbacks more time to step up in the pocket and find open receivers downfield. The Saints have a lot of issues, so adding talent at almost any position this offseason would be a breath of fresh air. Are there any players you’re excited to watch today?
