title: Our Defense vs. Their Offense: Pittsburgh Steelers
summary: This game between the Steelers and the Saints will be determined when the Saints’ defense is on the field. The Steelers’ offense will feature Aaron Rodgers in his second season as their quarterback, and his primary target will be DK Metcalf. Metcalf is a physical freak and a matchup nightmare because of his combination of […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Carl Granderson #96 and Chase Young #99 of the New Orleans Saints stand on the sidelines during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images This game between the Steelers and the Saints will be determined when the Saints’ defense is on the field. The Steelers’ offense will feature Aaron Rodgers in his second season as their quarterback, and his primary target will be DK Metcalf. Metcalf is a physical freak and a matchup nightmare because of his combination of size and speed. However, the Steelers have not been explosive offensively so far this season. They are averaging only 320 yards per game, with 221 passing yards and 99 rushing yards per game. Jaylen Warren is a very physical running back who is difficult to take down. The Saints will have to make sure they are ready to hit and wrap him up. He will run through arm tackles and rarely go down on first contact. The Steelers are also averaging 22.8 points per game, so this offense is very steady as it goes. The biggest issue the Steelers have on offense is their inability to protect the quarterback. So far, they have surrendered 19 sacks in six games. This is where Chase Young, who is currently tied for third in the NFL with 5.5 sacks, should get very excited. The issue here, though, is the matchup. As average as the Steelers’ offense is, the Saints’ defense has just been bad. The Steelers rank 20th in rushing yards and 18th in passing yards per game. Defensively, the Saints rank 30th in rushing yards allowed per game, surrendering 138 yards per contest, and 20th in passing yards allowed per game at 239.7. The Saints’ defense has an opportunity to get right against this opponent. The issues that the Saints have on defense are the same issues the Steelers have on offense, but the same can be said in reverse. If the Saints’ defense allows the Steelers’ offense to find a rhythm by establishing a running game and fails to put Rodgers into obvious passing situations, this game could get out of hand. The Steelers’ defense is already a challenge in itself for the Saints’ offense, but the Saints do not want Pittsburgh to play complementary football in Paris. If anything, this defense should come out aggressively, look to get in Aaron Rodgers’ face, and hit him early and often. This is a great opportunity for defensive coordinator Brandon Staley to turn this defense around.

summary: The New Orleans Saints are overseas this week for a historic matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday, October 25, at Stade de France in Paris. full_text: The New Orleans Saints are overseas this week for a historic matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday, October 25, at Stade de France in Paris. The Week 7 game marks the NFL’s first regular-season game in France, giving both franchises an opportunity to make history on an international stage. However, for the Saints, the trip represents something more important: a chance to build momentum and potentially turn their season around. New Orleans enters Sunday’s matchup at 2-4 after a much-needed 34-27 victory over the New York Giants, which snapped their three-game losing streak. Meanwhile, Aaron Rogers and the 4-2 Steelers arrive in Paris riding the momentum of a 26-19 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. With their bye week approaching, the Saints have an opportunity to string together consecutive victories for the first time this season and return home with renewed confidence. However, Tyler Shough and the offense will face a challenging Pittsburgh defense that ranks 9th in total defense, allowing just 307.5 yards per game. The Steelers have also been effective against the pass, surrendering an average of 204.3 passing yards per contest. PREDICTION: Saints 31 – Steelers 27 Yes, the Saints have an opportunity to make history in Paris, but the bigger question is whether they can turn one encouraging victory into sustained success. Following last week’s comments from team owner Gayle Benson, the pressure is mounting on both players and coaches to deliver results. Add in the spotlight of an international stage and Sunday’s matchup against the Steelers becomes even more significant. I believe the Saints will win this game but more importantly, Sunday will provide a clearer picture of whether the Saints are finally finding their footing after a slow start to the season or if the team still has more questions than answers. title: NFL Week 7 betting advice: Giants-Texans picks and props
summary: Welcome to the New York Giants betting angle, Week 7 edition! Each week, I’m giving you my three favorite wagers for that week’s New York Giants game. My one rule: I won’t ever give you wagers that are less than -120. No gimmes! For the third straight week, the Giants are underdogs to a team with a […]
full_text: J.J. gets his shot | Getty Images Welcome to the New York Giants betting angle, Week 7 edition! Each week, I’m giving you my three favorite wagers for that week’s New York Giants game. My one rule: I won’t ever give you wagers that are less than -120. No gimmes! For the third straight week, the Giants are underdogs to a team with a record that’s worse than theirs. Not only that, they’re big underdogs this time around. The 2-4 Houston Texans are laying a whole bunch of lumber — 10.5 points to be exact — to the 3-2-1 Giants. It’s the biggest line on the board in Week 7. When the Giants announced earlier in the week that J.J. McCarthy would be getting the start at Houston, the line moved by about three points. Clearly, the betting public thinks it’s more likely that we’ll get the 2025 version of J.J. than the one that provided about 250 yards of offense in less than a quarter of mop-up duty against New Orleans last Sunday. The Texans started out 0-4, but have won two straight since. Their fearsome defense hasn’t lived up to the hype, but quarterback C.J. Stroud, who completely melted down in the 2025 playoffs, has turned it around and is playing even better than he did in his excellent rookie season. As for the Giants, it’s been an adventure. They’re 0-1-1 in their last two games, both of which were very winnable. This one might not be, as the line suggests. Big Blue is banged up at a number of spots, and the Week 8 Bye looms as a time to recover. In an odd twist, the Giants will remain in first place in the NFC East through Week 7 regardless of the outcome of this game. After going 8-1 from Weeks 3-5, I went 1-2 last week. My picks are 11-7 on the season – not bad! I’m looking to get back in the win column this week. Let’s get to this week’s picks. All lines and odds are from Fanduel and are as of Friday, October 23. The line for the game is Texans -10.5, with a game total of 43.5. The line and total are both stay-aways for me, as are most Giants’ props. With the Giants changing quarterbacks for the second time this season, there are a lot of unknowns. Texans 1 st half total points OVER 13.5 (-115). I’m nervous that this game will get away from the Giants in a hurry, with Houston’s defense finally playing to its potential, J.J. McCarthy struggling in his first start, and the banged-up Giants just trying to get out alive. I can see Houston having a pretty big first half, and then going conservative in the second half with a lead. Marvin Harrison, Jr. OVER 2.5 receptions (-118). Harrison caught three balls on four targets in his Texans’ debut last Sunday in London, despite playing just 12 snaps (19% of the total). The game was also highly competitive, and Houston threw a lot. I think Harrison should be on the field a lot more this week, and while they’ve got plenty of other options in the passing game, they don’t run the ball well and there should be enough to go around. C.J. Stroud and Harrison are quite familiar from their time at Ohio State, and that’s a plus. I also think there will again be a concerted effort to get their new toy involved. Take the over. J.J. McCarthy UNDER 200.5 passing yards (-114). I know, I know. McCarthy eclipsed this total in less than a quarter last week. That gives me some pause, but that was in garbage time, against a bad defense that had pulled some of its starters. In ten starts for Minnesota last season, McCarthy only topped 200 yards twice. Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely have been beasts, and they give McCarthy a chance to exploit a Texans’ secondary that’s been a major disappointment. I don’t think that’s going to happen with any kind of consistency. The Giants’ O-line is banged up, and I expect McCarthy to be under duress from Houston’s outstanding edge rushers. I foresee a lot of bad throws when he isn’t taking off on a run or getting sacked. Those are the picks for Week 7. Good luck with your wagers! And if you play fantasy football, be sure to check out my Week 7 fantasy preview, with start/sit advice and more, right here .

title: New York Giants mailbag: J.J. McCarthy, Jon Runyan, Cam Skattebo, more
summary: Alan Backman asks: I know everyone (including me) may be over-reacting to J.J. McCarthy having 2 great quarters. But let’s take the upside for a minute. 1. Contract – How does that work? Did Giants acquire the rights to that 4 year locked deal from the Vikings? My understanding is that this contract is guaranteed. So who absorbs the guarantee […]
full_text: Alan Backman asks: I know everyone (including me) may be over-reacting to J.J. McCarthy having 2 great quarters. But let’s take the upside for a minute. 1. Contract – How does that work? Did Giants acquire the rights to that 4 year locked deal from the Vikings? My understanding is that this contract is guaranteed. So who absorbs the guarantee cost – Giants or Vikes? 2. If McCarthy continues to do well, what do you think Giants should do when Dart recovers? I assume that no matter how well McCarthy plays, Dart gets the job back. But then what ? Winston just signed a new deal. Do the Giants keep 3 QB’s going forward? Don’t get me wrong. This would be a good problem to have. If not 3 QBs, do you think the Giants would consider trading McCarthy or Winston for draft picks? Or just keep all the QBs? Ed says: Alan, McCarthy had one great quarter. Actually, he had a great nine minutes. The Giants pick up McCarthy’s rookie contract. They are responsible for the pro-rated portion of his $1.075 million base salary this season. Next season, they are respnsible for $3.775 million — $1.19 million in base salary and the rest is a $2.585 million roster bonus. They also get the fifth-year option, should they want to exercise it. Next year? Jaxson Dart is the Giants’ quarterback. They did not acquire McCarthy to compete with Dart, and I have serious doubts he can do anything to change that. They acquired McCarthy to help them try to navigate a season without Dart. Maybe, just maybe, if McCarthy plays well enough that someone out there thinks he can be a starter the Giants can flip him and get the fifth-round pick they used to get him — or better — back in a deal. To me, Winston is a great locker room presence, a leader and a big help to Dart. He is fine for a couple of games. No team, though, wants to try and get through 15 games with backup quarterbacks — which is what the Giants are trying to do. Spencer Gross asks: What do we do about our offensive line and why in God’s name did we extend Runyan? Is there an out for the contract or did we just give him some money for the sake of it? Ed says: Spencer, what would you like the Giants to do about their offensive line? Look around the NFL, there are a lot of teams with offensive lines far worse than the Giants. As it happens, the Giants happen to have one of the league’s best pass-blocking lines. Pro Football Focus ranks the Giants No. 4 in the league in pass-blocking, and fourth-worst in run-blocking. ESPN’s ‘win rate’ statistic has the Giants 16th in the league in pass-block win rate and 14th in run block win rate — basically in the middle of the league. Sharp Football Analysis says the Giants have given up pressure on 31.8% of pass plays, seventh-best in the NFL. Conversely, Sharp has the Giants at 0.8 yards rushing before contact, fifth-worst in the NFL. They are, overall, a middle of the pack line. Really good in pass protection. Not good in run blocking. Can the run-blocking get better? Sure. Sisi Mauigoa is struggling, but has played only six games. Andrew Thomas has not been healthy. Jermaine Eluemunor just missed a game. Bryan Hudson has had two good games and one bad one since becoming the starting center. Runyan? The Giants knew what he was when they gave him that extension. He’s an adequate starter, far better at pass protection than run blocking. They had to do something to get under the salary cap, and extending his contract is one of the choices they made. A closer examination of his two-year, $22 million extension shows that it isn’t as bad as it might seem. Yes, he has $19.25 million in guaranteed. The full guarantee consists of a $9 million signing bonus and his 2026 and 2027 base salaries. There is no guaranteed money for Runyan in 2028, effectively making the extension a one-year deal through 2027. The Giants can get out of that deal in 2028 with a $3 million dead cap charge and $11 million in cap savings. Matthew Mosley asks: Curious of your thoughts on JMS & Adebo? Do they possess any trade value this year, whether it be player for player swap or draft capital? JMS seems to have lost his job and it’s clear with the practice squad additions, that the Giants have zero intent on playing him. Regarding Adebo, his return could be great depth for a run in the second half of the season. However, he’s looked fairly pitiful in the action we’ve seen this year. Giants have an opportunity to win this division, but there are glaring holes that need to be filled in order to do so. Do these players present any value to the current roster or potentially another team looking for added depth? Ed says: Matthew, I think it might be possible that the Giants could move John Michael Schmitz to a center-needy team, perhaps one that has an injury at the position and needs an adequate short-term fix. I doubt he would bring more than a seventh-round pick, maybe even a conditional seventh based on playing time. I doubt that Paulson Adebo has much trade value, given his contract, injury history, and performance since he has been a Giant. An acquiring team would take on whatever pro-rated portion of his $17.25 million base salary for the rest of this season is. That’s a lot to swallow for a player who has been available for just 20 of the last 40 regular-season games, and has not played well since signing with the Giants last season. I don’t know why anyone would do it. Caleb Hoke asks: Why is everyone so up in arms about Skattebo not getting many touches? I understand the love from the fans, I like the way he runs hard. (He could, maybe, not look for contact every play.) But, as a coach, myself, there goes more into playing time than just what fans see on Sundays. While I only coach middle school and high school and it is VASTLY different from coaching the NFL (I coach kids and not adults), but the basis is, there are practices throughout the week. Film, practice, walkthroughs, etc. Could it be that Skattebo is missing something in practices that led to the “benching”? Could it be that he has missed other assignments? Could it be more than just he fumbled in key moments of games? I just think that we, as fans, get into seeing what happens on Sundays and thinking that is all there is to it. We aren’t at practices and meetings. We aren’t on the sidelines on Sundays either. We don’t know all that goes into decisions. Ed says: Caleb, since when does not knowing everything — or anything about what goes on inside a team — prevent fans from having, and loudly sharing, opinions? That’s just the nature of fandom. Skattebo’s popularity/appeal outweigh his talent/production. Fans don’t want to hear that, but it’s the truth. He is an important player for the Giants the way they are constructed, but his lack of speed and size make him a limited one. There is a reason the Giants were interested in Kenneth Walker in free agency, Jeremiyah Love in the draft, and why there is so much speculation about trying to trade for Jonathan Taylor of the Colts. Skattebo is not the equal of players like Taylor, Derrick Henry, Saquon Barkley, Walker, Christian McCaffrey, James Cook, Jahmyr Gibbs, and Bijan Robinson. Skattebo’s lack of opportunity against the New Orleans Saints was not related to anything more than his issues with ball security. The message, though, had to be sent. And, it was. Ronald Buchheim asks: After Tracy failed to block a runner and then fumbled, Harbaugh said the back would be judged by his entire body of work rather than a few recent mistakes. Then he was immediately dropped on the depth chart before being banished from the rotation almost entirely. Next he answered your question regarding Harris’s frustration about getting few touches by saying that he understands and respects the runner’s feeling but touches obviously have to be earned. Then Harris is immediately cut. Harbaugh seems quite genial, but what do you make of these falsehoods? Ed says: Ronald, in my view John Harbaugh has actually been quite good with the media. He…

title: NY Giants news: Tremaine Edmunds reportedly headed to IR, special teams issues, more
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants get set to battle the Houston Texans this Sunday. Struggles in all three phases leave Giants feeling heat heading into matchup at Texans | The Athletic The New York Giants’ coaching staff turned up the heat this week. […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants get set to battle the Houston Texans this Sunday. Struggles in all three phases leave Giants feeling heat heading into matchup at Texans | The Athletic The New York Giants’ coaching staff turned up the heat this week. It started after Sunday’s 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints when coach John Harbaugh challenged someone from a disappointing backfield to step up and seize the top running back job. Offensive coordinator Matt Nagy noted that the coaches need to look inward as the team searches for solutions to their weaknesses. One area that falls under the coaches’ purview is penalties. The Giants have been flagged for the 13th-most penalties in the league. They have the most pre-snap offensive penalties, lowlighted by consecutive false starts on running back Tyrone Tracy and left tackle Andrew Thomas to turn a third-and-8 into a third-and-18 in the third quarter against the Saints. Giants’ Matt Nagy ready to open up playbook for J.J. McCarthy’s first start | New York Post “Maybe now 20 percent of that 30 that was gone is back,” Nagy said. “For us, what does he do well? You’ve seen some of the packages he’s done, but that can become predictable. We don’t want to be predictable. Now that he’s the starter, it probably benefits us some that he’s just not always coming in to do predictable QB-driven runs.” “Just the confidence of him being able to, in practice, talk to us about the scheme, where his eyes are going in the pass game, where he’s snapping the ball with a motion or a shift,” Nagy said. “If there was a shoestring with Jameis or he got hurt, he could go in and function. Whereas the first two weeks, I had a highlighted [play] call sheet that, if something happened and he was in, these were the plays. It was probably 50 percent. Last week, it was probably 90 percent. Now this week, it’s going to be 100 percent.” Harbs Weekly: A chance to take control of the division before the bye week | Giants.com Q: A lot of times we see quarterback changes made at the bye week, which is coming up. But if something is inevitable, is it best to do it as soon as possible because now you get this week too? Harbaugh: I just never thought of it that way. I never considered whether the bye week is coming up and that’d be a better time. To be honest with you, it never even crossed my mind. I’m just thinking about what was the best thing for the next game and was he ready. It really wasn’t all that. I mean, it’s good to think about. Now that people have brought it up, I’m like, I didn’t really care about that. Harbaugh on the release of Najee Harris John Harbaugh explains why the Giants cut Najee Harris: "It was more about, 'Alright, we're going to set a course.' It's hard to carry four backs. I just felt like, in this situation…nothing against what he did." https://t.co/8CPrezderd pic.twitter.com/HWW5OMtF4B — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) October 23, 2026 Cam Skattebo set to return to Giants RB mix after being ‘ taught a lesson’ | ESPN.com “It’s been good, you know. I think I got taught a lesson,” Skattebo said. “I don’t know if that’s from them or from myself, but I kind of had to step back and look at it and figure out why I was doing the things I was doing, what was happening. Came to practice, corrected those things, worked on them. Ready to go back out there and play ball.” The second-year running back knows he still has to prove it on the field. “I didn’t do anything yet,” Skattebo said. “I took care of the ball during practice, and whatever my role is on Sunday is going to be my role and I’m going to give it everything I’ve got.” Colts’ Jonathan Taylor to Giants? Why Cam Skattebo knows he shouldn’t rule it out | NJ.com Giants coach John Harbaugh wants a dominant, single-back running game, as he chases an unlikely NFC East title this season. Really, that also is Harbaugh’s broader vision for his offense in East Rutherford. So Cam Skattebo — who entered his second year as the Giants’ much-hyped but largely unproven No. 1 back — knows he can’t and shouldn’t rule out Harbaugh trading for the Colts’ Jonathan Taylor (a New Jersey native) prior to the Nov. 10 deadline. New York Giants’ skill players call for improved run-game execution | USAToday.com Nabers said the offense must do a better job establishing the run so defenses cannot simply play the pass on every down. “Yeah, I mean, we’ve got to do a better job on offense of getting the ball — I mean, making sure we want to run the ball well, finding good runs for the running back that just hearing their thoughts on what runs that they like, too,” Nabers told reporters on Thursday. “Trying to do a better job of asking them, asking the O-line of what specific runs that they like, where they feel like we can gain a lot of yards off of to just help the whole offense.” Interesting stats since the change at center Giants center comparison after 3 starts each: ⚫️Giants RBs averaged more yards per carry (3.69) behind John Michael Schmitz in Weeks 1-3 than they did in Weeks 4-6 behind Bryan Hudson (3.1) (my data) ⚫️Schmitz's QB pressure percentage (6.2%) is lower than Hudson's (7.1%), too,… — Pat Leonard (@PLeonardNYDN) October 22, 2026 The 10 best NFL player matchups to watch in Week 7 | PFF New York Giants WR Malik Nabers vs. Houston Texans CB Derek Stingley Jr. Nabers hasn’t taken long to already look as sharp as ever after tearing his ACL. His 81.7 overall PFF grade is the 10th-best among qualified wideouts, and his 23 first downs secured are tied for sixth. The third-year pro has also produced 2.88-plus yards per route run in three games, including in Week 6 against the Saints. The 2026 season has not been a lockdown one yet for Stingley. The All-Pro has permitted a 101.8 passer rating into his coverage — the 15th-worst among qualified cornerbacks — allowing 40 or more yards in three of his six outings. On top of that, Stingley’s 16.1 yards per reception given up are the fourth-highest at his position. The Texans have primarily played zone coverage in 2026, which may lend the upper hand to Nabers. His 78.3 PFF receiving grade against such softer looks is the sixth-best among receivers with 12 or more targets in zone. Meanwhile, Stingley ranks as the 26th-graded corner in zone with a 66.1 PFF coverage grade. title: Giants-Texans final injury report: Tremaine Edmunds out, Micah McFadden in
summary: The New York Giants will be without starting inside linebacker Tremaine Edmunds this Sunday against the Houston Texans. Edmunds has a torn chest muscle and that injury that will reportedly end his season. The good news for the Giants is that starting offensive tackles Andrew Thomas (groin) and Jermaine Eluemunor (calf), and backup tackle Marcus […]
full_text: Tremaine Edmunds | Getty Images The New York Giants will be without starting inside linebacker Tremaine Edmunds this Sunday against the Houston Texans. Edmunds has a torn chest muscle and that injury that will reportedly end his season . The good news for the Giants is that starting offensive tackles Andrew Thomas (groin) and Jermaine Eluemunor (calf), and backup tackle Marcus Mbow (knee) are all expected to play. McFadden ready for opportunity With Edmunds out, fifth-year linebacker and former starter Micah McFadden will get the starting nod. “If I get to go out there and play and start and do what I’ve gotten to do before, I’m excited,” McFadden told Big Blue View earlier this week. McFadden was a full-time starter for the Giants in 2023 and 2024. In Game 1 last season, McFadden suffered a foot injury that kept him out for the remainder of the season. He admitted that “without a doubt” it isn’t easy to no longer have a starting role. “Whenever you’re used to something, you’ve had a taste of the pie, I guess, and then you don’t get to go out there and eat with your boys anymore, it’s tough, but I think it’s just about staying present,” McFadden said. “This game is a week-to-week basis, and obviously I had a pretty upsetting first week last year, and I learned a lot through that process, though. A lot of gratitude to be healthy and just to be able to play again, and I think that’s what I found most throughout these past six weeks is just, just finding gratitude in whatever situation I’m in.” At least for this week, McFadden will be starting again. Could he also be wearing the green dot, relaying defensive calls from coordinator Dennard Wilson? “I’ve done it before, and I think Dennard knows that there’s a handful of guys that could all do this on our defense,” McFadden said. “Whether I am that guy or not I’ll be prepared for it. I’m glad that I have had experience doing it in the past just to, you know, so this wouldn’t be my first time. “Obviously if that opportunity presents itself, it’s something I would take pride in and make sure I’m communicating with everybody.” Adebo appears set to return The Giants designated cornerback Paulson Adebo to return this week, and it looks like he could be activated before Sunday’s game. “He’s ready to go,” Harbaugh said. “He’s a legit corner. He’s a cover corner, he tackles. He’s been a high-end corner in this league. I think he’s really determined to play that way. I think he’s finally probably healthy and ready to go. I can’t wait to see it … it looks like it’s going to be Sunday.” With starting cornerback Greg Newsome II still in concussion protocol and ruled out, there could be immediate snaps for Adebo vs. the Texans. Texans injuries Houston will be without safety Reed Blankenship (concussion/hand), offensive tackle Blake Fisher (thumb), running back David Montgomery (groin), and safety Jalen Pitre (shoulder). title: NY Giants have sprung some leaks on special teams the past 2 weeks
summary: Through the first four games of the season, the New York Giants special teams were rock solid. That has not been the case the past two weeks as the Giants have tied the Washington Commanders and lost to the New Orleans Saints. Sunday in the loss to the Saints, there were a number of special […]
full_text: Charlie Jones | Getty Images Through the first four games of the season, the New York Giants special teams were rock solid. That has not been the case the past two weeks as the Giants have tied the Washington Commanders and lost to the New Orleans Saints. Sunday in the loss to the Saints, there were a number of special teams errors: Charlie Jones fumbled a kickoff return with less two minutes remaining in the first half, setting up the Saints in position to tie the game before halftime. Placekicker Dominic Zvada couldn’t send a kickoff out the back of the end zone with 2:08 remaining, That allowed New Orleans to run the ball out, using precious time the Giants needed in their comeback bid, and costing them a timeout. They could have used that timeout rather than spiking the ball on third-and-1 with :12 to play. The Giants had three penalties on kickoff or punt returns in the second half, negating returns by Jones of 32, 33, and 9 yards. The Giants gave up punt returns of 23 and 21 yards. For at least the second time this season, the Giants only had 10 players on the field for a special teams play. The Giants have been good on special teams this season, but there have been cracks over the past couple of games. View Link Special teams coordinator Chris Horton said his units need to get back to “playing winning football.” What happened on the Jones fumble? “Just got to take care of the football, right?,” Horton said. “We’re in traffic. Protecting the ball. Two hands on the football. Guys came free. Again, we’ve got to block. We’ve got to make sure no one’s in his way. But at the end of the day, we’ve got to take care of the football.” Horton said “communication” was behind not getting enough players on the field. “That thing starts with me. It’s making sure that I’m communicating to the guys,” Horton said. “Then it’s also the players understanding, being in the flow of the game, being in the moment. We’ve got to get out there, we’ve got to make calls, and we’ve got to have everybody up. We’ve got to put an end to that. I can assure you that, man. “Quite frankly, it’s embarrassing that that is continuing to happen. I want to make sure that we get a handle on that and we’re able to put an end to it.” The penalties? “They came at opportune times, situations where we could have definitely flipped the field,” Horton said. “When you get in situations and you’re talking about losing yards because of blocks in the back, those are decision-making things. “Those are things that happen within the game, and we can coach against those things because we offer a lot of tools in those toolboxes so you don’t block a guy in the back. Balls being returned, for an example, if I’m running behind the guy, if I’m in chase mode, we call it chase mode, just turn and climb. Put your foot in the ground, go climb and go block somebody else. Returners are good enough to make guys miss at the point of attack. Secondly, if I’m in a situation where I feel like I’m going to block a guy in the back, maybe I run in between my man and the ball, and then I shield that guy off. There’s opportunities to make sure that those things don’t happen. And, again, it comes back to playing winning football and pure execution of the plays.” The Saints’ 41-yard kickoff return on Sunday was the longest return the Giants have allowed this season. “Before I talked about just pure execution on where we need to be. We didn’t have an edge. Every kickoff cover team needs an edge. And we had two guys that we didn’t have an edge,” Horton said. “It just comes back to just executing the plays at hand, the plays that we get. That’s all it comes down to. It wasn’t a big fire. We go in there, we watch the tape, we knew exactly what happened. We need our edge players up on the edge. The ball doesn’t get outside.” The kickoff that didn’t get out of the end zone? “We firmly believe that we could have kicked that ball out the back of the end zone,” Horton said. “We’ve got a guy that we believe in and feel like we can go out there and we can save those five yards and we can get that done, but we didn’t get it done. So, again, that comes back down to the things that I talked about, just playing winning football and doing the things that we know we’re very capable of doing.” The Giants are a flawed team that needs to win games around the margins, with special teams often providing — or not providing — those margins. Getting the special teams back to the way it was performing over the season’s first four weeks would be a massive boost as the Giants try to get back in the win column this week.
author: Ed Valentine

title: Giants at Texans matchup: J.J. McCarthy vs. talented Houston defense
summary: The 3-2-1 New York Giants travel to Houston to face the 2-4 Houston Texans on Sunday. Houston has won its last two matchups against the Jaguars (34-31) and the Tennessee Titans (26-3). The Texans faced Jacksonville last week in London; Texans’ kicker Ka’imi Fairbairn nailed a 49-yard field goal with zero on the clock to […]
full_text: J.J. McCarthy signing his jersey after last Sunday’s game. | Getty Images The 3-2-1 New York Giants travel to Houston to face the 2-4 Houston Texans on Sunday. Houston has won its last two matchups against the Jaguars (34-31) and the Tennessee Titans (26-3). The Texans faced Jacksonville last week in London; Texans’ kicker Ka’imi Fairbairn nailed a 49-yard field goal with zero on the clock to give Demeco Ryans’ team their second win in as many weeks. The Giants named J.J. McCarthy the starting quarterback for Week 7. McCarthy gives the Giants a mobile quarterback who better fits an offense designed for Jaxson Dart. Still, communication in a loud environment for a young quarterback with less than a month in Giants blue could be an issue for New York. Whatever happens — I’m excited to watch! Houston’s defense finished second in scoring last year, allowing just 17.4 points per game, and it allowed the fewest yards per game (277.2 yards) while forcing the third-most takeaways (29). The defense isn’t as stout through six games in 2026. Texans defensive statistics The Texans rank 20th in points allowed per game (23.8) and 15th in yards allowed per game (329). The Texans rank 27th in passing yards allowed per game (246) while ranking third-best in run defense (83 yards rushing per game). The Texans have 18 sacks through six games, tying for third-most in the NFL. Houston doesn’t blitz much — the Texans rely on their personnel. They blitz at a 20.7% rate, 29th in the league. Houston is middle of the pack in pressure percentage at 22.7%. The Texans rank 19th in red zone touchdown percentage (62.5%), and the defense ranks 18th in third-down conversion rate (40.78%). The defense is 14th in EPA per play allowed ( – 0.02), fourth in defensive success rate allowed (39.8%), with just five total takeaways (23rd in the league). Matt Burke is the coordinator under defensive head coach Demeco Ryans. Texans’ personnel The Texans defense aligns in a traditional 4-3. They’re a gap-sound defense with a strong nickel package that has underperformed this season. Star nickel/safety Jalen Pitre missed Week 6 with a sprained AC joint; he’s questionable. Houston’s front seven is among the best in the league. Edge defender Will Anderson Jr. is a phenomenal player for Demeco Ryans. He has 28 tackles, 7.5 sacks, and 18 pressures. He leads the league in sacks; Danielle Hunter plays opposite Anderson, and Hunter has three sacks with 14 pressures. Jadeveon Clowney and Dominique Robinson rotate into the lineup for Anderson and Hunter. Sheldon Rankins and Tommy Togiai are the defensive linemen; Rankins has two sacks and five pressures this season. Rookie Kayden McDonald and Logan Hall rotate into the lineup. Linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair is a fast and physical linebacker who has 49 tackles this season. Henry To’oTo’o plays alongside Al-Shaair. Houston has one of the best secondaries, but it is underperforming and beaten up. Pitre missed last game, and Reed Blankenship — who has struggled this season — was concussed in Week 6. They have two star cornerbacks: Derek Stingley Jr. and Kamari Lassiter, with the latter struggling more in 2026—he’s allowed a 66.7% catch rate on 28 receptions. Stingley, however, has just allowed a 48.5% catch rate. Callen Bullock and veteran M.J. Stewart could be the starting safeties, with Blankenship dealing with a concussion. The matchup The Giants believe McCarthy gives them a better chance against Houston, in part because of his ability to escape and evade from within the pocket. Jameis Winston was sacked 15 times this season, and the offense — which lacks a run game — relied so heavily on Winston’s arm that is historically known for its inconsistency and borderline reckless play. McCarthy’s mobility will help the Giants’ offense in multiple phases: designed quarterback runs, read plays (zone-read, RPO, etc.), and pocket escapability, while also providing the offense with better overall arm talent. Expect the Giants to lean on read plays when in shotgun, while trying to establish the run with heavier personnel packages. The play-action passing attack will likely have a few bootlegs and move the pocket plays that utilize McCarthy’s ability to operate on the move. New York should not be shy to take shots when pre-snap coverage is confirmed in one-on-one scenarios to receivers who aren’t Malik Nabers or Isaiah Likely — who will still be the focal points of the offense. McCarthy can let the ball fly, and Malachi Fields and Darnell Mooney have created adequate separation this season, especially the latter of the two. The Giants should keep up the high motion rate if McCarthy is up to speed on running the offense effectively with pre-snap movement. The Giants should run a similar offense that we saw in Week 1 with Jaxson Dart at quarterback, while calling more plays that get McCarthy moving. Hopefully, McCarthy’s ability to run will lighten boxes for the Giants’ struggling rushing attack, specifically on zone reads. Zone-read plays with either Tyrone Tracy Jr. or Cam Skattebo should be used by the Giants’ staff. Tracy Jr. can still operate as the third-down back, but a return of involvement for Skattebo, who received zero touches last week, should happen, especially with Najee Harris released. Devin Singletary should also receive his touches. The health of Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemunor is crucial, especially against strong power rushers like Hunter and Anderson, who would both be incredibly difficult matchups for Marcus Mbow. Houston doesn’t need to blitz — and they don’t do it much — but they may look to send the pressure and spy on McCarthy until the young quarterback proves he can defeat the blitz; it will also be a loud environment, so exotic pressure looks could confuse not only McCarthy but the protection with possible young starting tackles. Final thoughts The Giants are heavy underdogs heading into Houston with a new starting quarterback. Their offense has struggled to run the football, and McCarthy can hopefully help to spark something for the rushing attack. Still, this is a tough environment, and communication will be key to keeping pre-snap penalties to a minimum, but it could be hard to achieve on the road, given the circumstances. Even if the Giants lose, though, they will have a full week during the bye to assess the situation and improve on their struggles with a new signal caller.

title: Giants at Texans matchup: Houston’s passing offense will test New York defense
summary: The New York Giants will travel to take on the Houston Texans in Week 7 as the G-Men look to bounce back from last week’s implosion against the New Orleans Saints.The Giants are 3-2-1 following their loss to the Saints, but still lead the NFC East. The Texans, meanwhile, are 2-4 and second in the […]
full_text: QB C.J. Stroud and WR Nico Collins | Getty Images The New York Giants will travel to take on the Houston Texans in Week 7 as the G-Men look to bounce back from last week’s implosion against the New Orleans Saints. The Giants are 3-2-1 following their loss to the Saints, but still lead the NFC East. The Texans, meanwhile, are 2-4 and second in the AFC South. The story of the game will be J.J. McCarthy’s first start as the Giants’ quarterback following his 243-yard fourth quarter last week. However, there are plenty of things to pay attention to on the defensive side of the ball as the Giants seek to slow down C.J. Stroud and the Texans offense. Stats that matter Giants Defense Texans Offense Total Yards 1,954 (17th) 2,130 (13th) Yards Per Attempt 6.2 yards allowed (5th) 7.8 yards per attempt (8th) Yards Per Carry 5.0 yards allowed (30th) 3.6 yards per attempt (28th) Total EPA 0.025 (22nd) 0.045 per play (10th) Pass Rush Win Rate 59% (4th) 49% block win (18th) Run Stop Win Rate 28% (23rd) 72% block win (22nd) Health in the secondary The Giants have transformed their defense over the last three weeks. They’ve gone from a fairly standard “Baltimore 2.0” defense using simulated pressures and coverage rotations out of the middle of a Match Quarters shell to confuse protections and quarterbacks to one of the NFL’s most aggressive defenses. The Giants are blitzing at one of the highest rates in the NFL, and winning their rushes at one of the league’s highest rates. But unlike the Minnesota Vikings, the Giants are calling their hyper-aggressive blitz schemes out of man coverage, and calling Cover-0 at the highest rate in the NFL and Cover-1 at one of the highest rates as well. Between that and still using a high rate of Match Quarters, the Giants have one of the highest rates of man coverage in the NFL. Each team's coverage mix through Week 6 pic.twitter.com/TjyCabytWh — SūmerSports (@SumerSports) October 20, 2026 A key aspect of man coverage, and press-man in particular, is that it requires a specific skill set. One question that isn’t being discussed widely is whether the Giants will be healthy enough on Sunday to call those aggressive schemes. Paulson Adebo is, as of this writing, still on the injured reserve, Colton Hood has yet to clear the concussion protocol, and Greg Newsome II and Jevon Holland left Sunday’s loss with concussions of their own. While Deonte Banks is playing very well, there was a real drop-off from Newsome II to Colton Hood before his injury, and the Saints targeted reserve corner Nic Jones to good effect. The effectiveness of the Giants’ blitzing defense could come down to whether they get healthier during the week. Perhaps due (in part) to the injuries at the second level, the Giants incorporated more simulated pressures against the Saints. There were multiple plays where the Giants had defenders showing blitz in the A-gap only to drop into coverage. That, however, created rushing lanes that quarterback Tyler Shough exploited. The good news is that C.J. Stroud isn’t the same type of athlete as Shough and isn’t nearly as effective a runner. However, Stroud is a very effective passer who is playing some of his best football this year, and the Texans have a full complement of receiving weapons. Slowing down C.J. Stroud The Giants have one of the best passing defenses in the NFL this year, but that might have as much to do with the caliber of offenses (and the weather) they’ve faced over the last month as their own defense. This week they’ll face a stiff test in the aforementioned Stroud. While the results haven’t been there, Stroud has been playing some of the best football of his career and is the reigning AFC offensive player of the week. He completed 24 of 34 attempts (70.6%), for 312 yards (9.2 per attempt), and 3 touchdowns to just two interceptions in a thrilling 34-31 win over the Jaguars. He’s operating quickly, seeing defenses well, placing the ball with precision, and attacking down the field. Stroud will also have a deep receiving corps with Nico Collins, the newly-acquired Marvin Harrison Jr., a returning Tank Dell, and 2025 third-round pick Jaylin Noel. Collins is among the best X receivers in the NFL and the Texans offense — and Stroud himself — is simply different with Collins on the field. And while Marvin Harrison Jr. flopped as a WR1 with the Arizona Cardinals, he has a pre-existing relationship with Stroud from their time together at Ohio State. Likewise, Harrison Jr. might fit better as a WR1b or WR2 with another receiver drawing most of the attention. Noel had a breakout game against the Jaguars with 107 yards on 4 catches. He only has 17 catches on the season, but that’s on just 21 targets (80% catch rate), and he’s third in the NFL averaging 19.6 yards per catch. He’s proving to be both reliable and a real big play threat. And speaking of explosive big play threats, the Texans are getting Dell, an undersized, spark plug, back from injury. Dell hasn’t played since a gruesome knee injury ended his season back in 2024, and it’s unknown whether he’ll have the game-changing ability he showed before the injury. However, the Giants can’t afford to overlook his potential for explosive plays. The injuries to the Giants’ secondary might make matching up with the Texans’ receiving corps difficult, so the answer could be attacking Stroud. That, of course, circles back to the Giants’ blitz schemes and whether the Giants can effectively blitz Stroud without being picked apart if Stroud is able to decipher the Giants’ rushes. Can the Giants stop the run? This is turning into an evergreen question for the Giants. New York’s run defense has been wildly inconsistent, alternating between stout and incredibly porous. The Giants have given up the second most rushing yards, the most runs of 20+ yards, and the second-most runs of 40+ yards in the NFL. However, the Giants defense’s Run Stop Win Rate is an “okay” 23rd, while they’re 20th in rushing EPA per play allowed and 16th in rushing success rate allowed. As John Harbaugh has said, the issue seems to be a tendency to give up those big plays. When the Giants’ run defense breaks, it tends to break badly, with poor angles and missed tackles allowing decent runs to turn into explosive runs. The good news this week is that the Texans simply aren’t good at running the ball. Their carries are split between 2025 fourth-rounder Woody Marks and veteran Davind Montgomery, but neither has been particularly effective. Marks is averaging 3.5 yards per carry on 58 rushes, Montgomery is averaging just 2.7 per carry on 52 carries this year, and each back has two touchdowns. Likewise, the Texans’ run blocking is merely “OK”, coming in at 22nd in the NFL. On paper, this looks like a meeting between a resistible force (the Texans’ run game) and a movable object (the Giants’ run defense). It’s possible that this could be a “get right” game for one of these two struggling units, though it’s not clear which one that would be. If (and that’s a load-bearing “if”) the Giants are able to contain Montgomery and Marks, their best bet for slowing Houston’s offense would be to force the ball out of Stroud’s hands. The Giants likely don’t want to find themselves in a shootout in J.J. McCarthy’s first start, so they may actually prefer Houston to run the ball. That could mean bringing enough pressure to disrupt Stroud and discourage the pass, or it could mean playing more light boxes to encourage the run. Either strategy comes with a risk — the former requires an injured secondary to contain a potent passing attack, while the latter demands the Giants be stout and tackle securely with reduced personnel. Either way, the Giants could be in for a tough test on defense.

title: Previewing the Jets’ opposition: Miami Dolphins
summary: The Miami Dolphins has won six out of the last seven, 10 of the last 12 and 14 of the last 17 against the New York Jets. However, they enter Sunday’s clash at MetLife Stadium as a winless underdog. Let’s break down the Dolphins’ roster going position by position: Quarterbacks The Dolphins had a strange […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - DECEMBER 07: Jordyn Brooks #20 of the Miami Dolphins in action during the NFL 2025 game against the New York Jets at MetLife Stadium on December 07, 2025 in East Rutherford, New Jersey."" (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Miami Dolphins has won six out of the last seven, 10 of the last 12 and 14 of the last 17 against the New York Jets. However, they enter Sunday’s clash at MetLife Stadium as a winless underdog. Let’s break down the Dolphins’ roster going position by position: Quarterbacks The Dolphins had a strange approach to the offseason, primarily heading into a rebuild as they traded guys away and looked to shed salary. This is a team that had six pro bowlers in 2023, but now all six are off the team. However, they coupled that approach with the signing of the biggest prize in this year’s free agent quarterback market when they signed Malik Willis to a three-year deal. Willis is getting a chance to be a full-time starter for the first time and he’s had mixed results due to the lack of a supporting cast around him. So far, he’s completed just 56 percent of his passes with two passing touchdowns, two rushing touchdowns and four interceptions. The backup to Willis is Kyle McCord, who has never thrown an NFL pass. Offensive Line Despite making so many other changes, Miami retained most of their offensive line and built on the foundation already in place by drafting Kadyn Proctor in the first round and putting him into the starting line-up at left guard. The rest of their starters were all also starting for them last year, although former first round right tackle Austin Jackson only started the first game and the last five due to injuries. The other three starters are center Aaron Brewer, left tackle Patrick Paul and right guard Jonah Savaiinaea. Savaiinaea struggled badly as a second round rookie last season and he was knocked out of the last game due to injury with Jarrett Kingston filling in for him the rest of the way. Miami’s starting tackles have given up five sacks and eight penalties between them so far this season. The other backups include Andrew Meyer – who started a game at center last year – and sixth round rookie DJ Campbell. Chukwuebuka Godrick and Caedan Wallace round out this group. Running Backs Miami’s plans for the year further shifted towards rebuild mode when they lost their star running back De’Von Achane to a torn ACL early in the season. The starter is now Ollie Gordon II, who – to his credit – is averaging five yards per carry with three rushing touchdowns. Jaylen Wright is the main backup, but Miami also has rookie Kaytron Allen as the number three. Allen was drafted in the sixth round by the Commanders but did not make their roster. Another rookie, the undrafted DJ Herman, is also on the roster as a fullback. Pass catchers With Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle now gone, Miami is hoping that Malik Washington can develop into a true number one receiver. He has 29 touches in the first five games, but less than 300 yards and no touchdowns. Tight end Greg Dulcich is the only other Dolphins player with double digits in catches. In order to find Willis some passing game weapons, Miami went pass catcher heavy in the middle rounds of the draft. Receivers Chris Bell and Caleb Douglas were selected along with tight end Will Kacmarek in the third round and then another receiver, Kevin Coleman, and another tight end, Seydou Traore, were picked in the fifth. Out of all of these, the Jets may view Bell as the biggest threat as they had Malik McClain operating as him during the week on the scout team, presumably in an effort to try and replicate his combination of size and athleticism. Bell had a nice game against the Chiefs with four catches but otherwise only has two other touches all year. Those two touches gained 25 and 26 yards though, so he may be a chunk play threat. Douglas is also a threat. He caught five passes for 94 yards in his NFL debut in the opener, but then got hurt in week two and hasn’t played since. He’ll make his return on Sunday. Further depth comes from receivers Jalen Tolbert and Jared Wayne, and from tight end Justin Joly. Defensive Line Miami’s defense got a boost in the game before the bye week with the return of last year’s first round pick Kenneth Grant at defensive tackle. Grant had been dealing with a toe issue but should now see his playing time increase alongside Zach Sieler. Sieler has been a thorn in the side of the Jets for several years with eight sacks in his past six games against them. Miami has won 10 of 12 games over the Jets with Sieler in the line-up. With Grant out, Jordan Phillips and Zeek Biggers had been sharing the workload alongside Sieler, who has a team-high two sacks. Miami’s best edge rusher is Chop Robinson, but the former first rounder’s production has been inconsistent. He had three sacks in four games towards the end of last year but only has one in five since then. The other starter on the edge is Josh Uche with Malik Herring as the main backup. Robert Beal Jr. and undrafted rookie Rodney McGraw are also on the roster, but Beal has been listed as doubtful with a hamstring issue. Linebackers At linebacker, Miami is getting excellent production from their second round pick, Jacob Rodriguez, who has 57 tackles and an interception in his first five NFL games. Rodriguez starts alongside last year’s leading tackler, Jordyn Brooks, with Willie Gay also getting plenty of reps. Gay is questionable with an illness, but did return to practice on Friday. Shaka Heyward and Jackson Woodard are the other backups with fourth round pick Trey Moore on injured reserve. Defensive Backs Miami’s depth is slightly compromised in the secondary, as fourth round safety Kyle Louis and veteran safety Ronnie Harrison are both on injured reserve. In addition, cornerback Darrell Baker remains on the PUP list. Louis did return to practice this week so could be activated for Sunday. He’s officially questionable. The starters right now at safety are Dante Trader Jr. and fifth round rookie Michael Taaffe. Trader leads the team with three pass breakups but the rookies Taaffe and Rodriguez have been inconsistent tacklers, combing for 14 missed tackles in the first five games. At cornerback, the top three are JuJu Brents, Jason Marshall Jr. and Chris Johnson. The first round rookie Johnson has been the primary slot corner. Brents leads the team with four defensive penalties. Further depth comes from safeties Zayne Anderson and Julius Wood, and cornerbacks Marcellas Dial and Reese Taylor, although Taylor has been ruled out due to injury. Miami also has former Jet Jaylin Simpson, who can play safety or corner. Special Teams The Dolphins just made a change at placekicker with another ex-Jet, Riley Patterson, having been released earlier this week after missing three kicks in five games. Zane Gonzalez was added to the practice squad to take over from Patterson. The veteran Bradley Pinion is the Dolphins’ punter, but his net average is below 40 yards per punt so far this year. In the return game, Washington is dangerous but hasn’t done much this year as his focus has shifted more onto the offense. Wright, who is listed as the backup kickoff returner, had a 79-yard return earlier this season. Coleman is listed as the backup punt returner. The Dolphins also recently released wide receiver Ryan Miller, who had been a primary gunner. Simpson and Dial would be options to handle this role on Sunday. So far this year Woodard and Simpson have been productive in coverage.

title: Eagles Film Preview: Cowboys offense surprisingly difficult to project
summary: Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite. I also record a video version for Patreon, where I break down […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 05: CeeDee Lamb #88 of the Dallas Cowboys drops a pass as Quinyon Mitchell #27 of the Philadelphia Eagles defends during the second half of an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 5, 2025 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite . I also record a video version for Patreon , where I break down the plays in greater detail and where you can further support my work. The Cowboys were a surprisingly difficult offense to break down this week. I watched the Texans game and saw an offense that could protect its quarterback and find plenty of ways to get the ball to its best players. Then I watched the Packers game and wondered where all of that had gone. This is still a talented offense, and I can’t shake the feeling that it will come together at some point. However, I thought the Cowboys were more creative last year, and their coaching staff isn’t getting enough from this group right now. With everything going on with the Eagles’ offense, the defense needs to play well if this team has any chance. There are opportunities to disrupt the Cowboys, but there is also enough talent here to make this a very uncomfortable matchup. Pass Game Everything starts with CeeDee Lamb. He remains an outstanding receiver, and the Cowboys are using him outside more frequently this season. He has aligned outside on approximately 61% of passing snaps, but that doesn’t mean he stays in one spot or runs a limited selection of routes. Against the Texans, Lamb caught 17 of his 21 targets (!) for 189 yards and a touchdown, with 72 yards coming after the catch. His targeted routes included outs, hitches, screens, crossers, a corner, a post, and several other concepts. They found him underneath, across the field, and at intermediate depth. That version of this offense is difficult to defend because Lamb can win in so many different ways. The Eagles cannot treat him as the responsibility of one cornerback. Some snaps will have him outside against an Eagles corner, while others will have him move inside and test the communication between the nickel, linebackers, and safeties. After some of the communication problems we have seen from the Eagles recently, that worries me. Lamb is too good at finding space to give him free releases into areas nobody has properly accounted for. Cowboys’ Offense All22 Thread. 1) They have been disappointing by their standards, but I still think they have the talent to be very good. CeeDee Lamb plays outside a lot this year (highest rate of his career), and he is as good as ever. Dak hasn't played well the past 2 weeks,… pic.twitter.com/H64VwO6BVU — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 23, 2026 The Cowboys are a true 11-personnel shotgun offense. In some ways, watching them feels like going back five years, before seemingly every offense started building around condensed formations, constant motion, and an extensive under-center package. They use 11 personnel on 73.3% of their snaps, the third-highest rate in the league, and they want to spread the defense out and let Dak Prescott distribute the football. Their pass rate over expectation leads the league, and they throw on approximately 68% of first-and-10 situations. This passing game is the foundation of the offense. Their route combinations have a strong vertical element, even though much of Prescott’s production comes on shorter throws. They want receivers to push defenders downfield, create space underneath, and force the secondary to communicate. Lamb’s presence can also open opportunities for others. In the example below, the attention he receives helps Jake Ferguson escape downfield on a wheel route. Ferguson hasn’t produced much yardage this season, but the Eagles still need to account for him when their attention shifts toward the receivers. 2) This is a true 11-personnel shotgun offense. It feels like a throwback to what every offense ran 5 years ago. You can see the attention that Lamb draws here, and Ferguson sneaks out on the wheel route downfield. They want to spread the defense out, throw on 1st down, and… pic.twitter.com/x7S9GexETf — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 23, 2026 Prescott hasn’t played particularly well over the past two weeks, but I still think he is a very good quarterback. His understanding of the position shows up in the small details. He can identify favorable matchups before the snap, manipulate underneath defenders, and create throwing windows with his eyes and body position. If the Eagles show him exactly what they intend to play, he is capable of picking them apart. The empty formation example below is excellent. Prescott shapes his body as though he is throwing the short route to the flat, draws the cornerback forward, and then hits the corner route behind him. George Pickens finishes the play by showing his ability to elevate and attack the football. Pickens hasn’t been at his very best this season, but he is an outstanding second receiver who can win vertically even when the coverage is competitive. He has aligned outside on approximately 93% of passing snaps, and in the film I watched, he usually lined up to the left. The Eagles have to respect his ability to finish at the catch point when deciding how much coverage to send toward Lamb. 3) Dak is still a high-level pre-snap QB, and if you don't confuse your coverages, he can throw it all over the place. Here they are in empty, so the defense expects the short route to the flat, but Dak uses his body position to fake the short throw, drawing up the flat… pic.twitter.com/DU6j7ADh5c — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 23, 2026 How aggressively should Vic Fangio pressure Prescott? This is where the contrast between the games becomes fascinating. The Packers had considerable success attacking the Cowboys’ protections, but their season-long numbers still suggest caution. The Cowboys rank eighth in EPA against the blitz at +0.13 per play. Prescott usually understands where his answers are and gets the football out quickly enough to punish defenses for removing players from coverage. Personally, I would be selective. If Fangio brings pressure, the disguise needs to be convincing, and the rush needs to arrive quickly. I wouldn’t want linebackers starting from depth and announcing a delayed pressure that Prescott has time to recognize. The Eagles need to threaten the protection, make him uncertain about who is coming, and close off the immediate answer. Simply sending an extra defender and hoping for the best could leave Lamb or Pickens with a very favorable opportunity. 4) It's hard to know how to play the Cowboys' offense because the Packers had a lot of success blitzing Dak. However, historically (and for most of this season), I would be very cautious about blitzing Dak a lot. As I said above, Dak is a veteran QB who is excellent at getting… pic.twitter.com/chs8EIhIKG — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 23, 2026 The Packers showed that Prescott can still be caught out by coverage rotation. Jonathan Gannon, of all people, did an excellent job disguising the picture and getting Prescott to throw into coverage he hadn’t properly confirmed. On the interception below, the weak safety drops into the throwing window, but Prescott commits to the post without accounting for him. It is a good defensive disguise and a poor decision by the quarterback. That is the balance with Prescott. He is experienced and technically excellent, but he will still attempt difficult throws over the middle and give defenders opportunities to make plays. His completion percentage falls from 75% when kept clean to 47.4% under pressure, while his yards per attempt drops from 7.6 to 4.6.…

summary: Given the Eagles’ current disposition, it feels like we might already be looking ahead to the offseason. With the NFL Draft being a never-ending source of hope for the future, there is good reason to watch college football every weekend for the rest of the season. Here are some players I’m keeping a close eye […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA OCTOBER 17: Darian Mensah #10 of the Miami Hurricanes celebrates with fans after teammate Malachi Toney scores a touchdown against the Florida State Seminoles at Hard Rock Stadium on October 17, 2026, in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Michael Pimentel/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images) | ISI Photos via Getty Images Given the Eagles’ current disposition, it feels like we might already be looking ahead to the offseason. With the NFL Draft being a never-ending source of hope for the future, there is good reason to watch college football every weekend for the rest of the season. Here are some players I’m keeping a close eye on this week. All listed times Eastern . Darian Mensah, Quarterback, Miami v. Pittsburgh (12 PM on ESPN): It is highly possible, if not likely, that the Eagles will be in the quarterback market this spring. If they are, this is a great class to need a quarterback in. For my money, Darian Mensah has emerged as the QB1 in this group midway through this season. Mensah, on his third team in three years, has gotten better every season as a quarterback. He is decisive with a strong arm and great accuracy. Last week was the first time he and Miami faced any adversity all season and Mensah responded by delivering in the clutch to keep the Canes unbeaten. Pittsburgh is a feisty squad that has a great habit of pulling off upsets. Mensah will need to stay locked in to keep his Heisman campaign afloat and Miami unbeaten. Kingston Lopa, Safety, Cal v. SMU (12 PM on CW): If the East Coast could stay up a bit later, Kingston Lopa would be a household name. He has linebacker build at 6’5” and 210 pounds but he moves and covers like a safety. With five interceptions midway through the season, Lopa is one of the best playmaking defenders in the country. SMU’s offense has big play potential on any snap, meaning Lopa will need to be at his best against the pass and the run. KJ Duff, Wide Receiver, Rutgers v. Northwestern (12 PM on Peacock): The best receiver in the country not named Jeremiah or Malachi might be in New Brunswick, New Jersey. KJ Duff is massive at 6’6” and 225 pounds. His size allows him to dominate above the rim, but he is a great athlete that can separate downfield. If he played in a more stable offense, Duff would be a household name outside of the Northeast. Duff is coming off a dominant game where nine catches and two scores helped Rutgers beat Maryland in a rivalry game. Now he faces a much tougher test in Northwestern. Can he stay hot and show everyone he can ball out on a bigger stage? Greg Johnson, Guard, Minnesota v. Iowa (3:30 PM on FS1): Let’s talk big boys. The Eagles need ‘em and college football has ‘em. Greg Johnson is a massive, mauling guard for a scrappy Minnesota offense this year. Now the Golden Gophers have a shot at taking down a ranked Iowa squad. Johnson will have his hands full with a physical Iowa defensive line, but he can further prove himself as one of the best linemen in the country. Wayshawn Parker, Running Back, Utah v. Houston (10:15 PM on ESPN): Another Eagles need is getting younger and more explosive in their backfield. While Howie Roseman has never valued running backs enough to draft them higher than the second round, Wayshawn Parker strikes me as a Day Two player who could come in and contribute immediately. Parker has a strong blend of toughness, vision, and explosiveness. He was underutilized in the Utah passing game through his first two years, but has really shown out as a true three down back in his junior season. He’s a do-it-all player who will get to show out against a tough Houston team this weekend.

full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Dontayvion Wicks #13 celebrates with his teammate DeVonta Smith #6 of the Philadelphia Eagles after scoring a touchdown against the Washington Commanders during an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles issued their second injury report of the week on Friday in advance of their Week 7 Monday Night Football game against the Dallas Cowboys. The Eagles listed six players under DID NOT PARTICIPATE: DeVonta Smith, Dontayvion Wicks, Dallas Goedert, Nolan Smith, Jonathan Greenard, and Michael Carter II. Smith, Wicks, Goedert, Smith, and Carter II missed practice for the second day in a row. Two straight missed practices to begin the week typically does not portend well for a player’s chances of playing in the upcoming game. The Inquirer’s Jeff McLane reports that Smith and Wicks are indeed tracking to miss Monday night … but there’s “optimism” that Goedert might be able to suit up. If neither Smith nor Wicks play, the Eagles will be down to these receivers: Makai Lemon, Darius Cooper, Elijah Moore, Hollywood Brown, and Britain Covey. Electric. Greenard was downgraded from limited on Thursday to DNP on Friday. Not ideal. With Greenard and Smith on track to miss this game, the Eagles are looking thin at edge rusher. The Eagles listed eight players under LIMITED PARTICIPATION: Saquon Barkley, Landon Dickerson, Jalyx Hunt, Tyler Steen, Moro Ojomo, A.J. Epenesa, Willie Lampkin, and Fred Johnson . Barkley is expected to play on Monday night. Not ideal that he hasn’t been able to fully participate in practice yet but guessing the Eagles are managing his workload to help get him to the game. There seems to be a sense that Dickerson might play on Monday … but I’m not buying it until we see him practice in full at least one time before the game. Maybe that happens on Saturday? We’ll see. Hunt was limited for the second day in a row. He might be able to suit up against the Cowboys. With Philly being so light at edge rusher, the team really needs Hunt to play. Steen, Ojomo, and Epenesa were also limited for the second day in a row. Guessing Steen and Ojomo will play. We’ll see about Epenesa. Lampkin was upgraded from DNP on Thursday to limited on Friday due to illness. Johnson was added to the report with an illness. He’ll probably be able to suit up on Monday. The Eagles listed 11 players under FULL PARTICIPATION: Drew Kendall, Zack Baun, Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, Arnold Ebiketie, Jihaad Campbell, Britain Covey, Grant Calcaterra, Eli Stowers, Jakorian Bennett, and Hollywood Brown. Kendall was upgraded from being limited on Thursday to full go on Friday. Looks like he’ll be able to return to the starting lineup at center. If that’s the case, who plays left guard? It’ll be Dickerson if they activate him from IR prior to 4:00 PM Eastern on Monday. If not, maybe it’s Lampkin once again. Or might they move Jake Majors from center to guard? We’ll see. Baun, Carter, Davis, Ebiketie, Campbell, Covey, Calcaterra, Stowers, Bennett, and Brown were all full participants for the second day in a row. They should be healthy enough to suit up. But it remains to be seen if the Eagles will activate Calcaterra and/or Stowers and/or Bennett from injured reserve. Dallas Cowboys (2-4) at Philadelphia Eagles (2-4), 8:20 p.m. Monday The Line: Cowboys minus-3.5/Total: 44.5 What is the line telling you: The bad news heading into Monday night is that the Eagles’ offense is the most banged up in the entire league. The good news is they are going up against a Dallas Cowboys defense that is ranked in the basement of the NFL in every metric that counts, and the Cowboys’ pass defense is extremely banged up as well. Bottom line: Ultimately, the only way I could bet this game is to buy the half-point on the Cowboys down to -3 . I also don’t expect many points to be scored, so taking the Cowboys on a 7-point teaser up to +3.5 and teasing the under up to 51.5 probably cashes you a ticket as well.
