title: Eagles Film Preview: If the offense can’t take advantage of this Cowboys defense …
summary: Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite. I also record a video version for Patreon, where I break down […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 4: Saquon Barkley #26 of the Philadelphia Eagles runs the ball into the end zone for a touchdown during the second quarter of an NFL game against the Dallas Cowboys at Lincoln Financial Field on September 4, 2025 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images Each week, I’ll publish two film-room previews: one focusing on the offense and one on the defense. These are primarily film-based, focusing on the schemes, tendencies, and matchups that could shape Sunday’s game, with all statistics coming from the Fantasy Points Data Suite . I also record a video version for Patreon , where I break down the plays in greater detail and where you can further support my work. I was frustrated enough last week to call for changes to the Eagles’ offense, and watching the Cowboys’ defense hasn’t changed my mind. It has, however, made this week feel like a pretty significant test. The Cowboys have been terrible defensively. They improved against the Packers, but they still have a long way to go before I’d call it average. With Saquon Barkley returning and Landon Dickerson (?) potentially back too, the Eagles need to get something going. Sean Mannion, in particular, seems to believe execution is the main problem with the offense. Well, this is the week to prove it. There are weaknesses everywhere to attack, and another performance where the offense cannot function would leave me with very little hope. Pass Defense The first thing that stands out is the communication. Or, more accurately, the lack of it. Since the beginning of the season, the Cowboys have repeatedly allowed receivers to run into completely vacant areas of the field. These aren’t always difficult throws into tight windows. Sometimes, two defenders cover the same route while another receiver runs free. In the example below, both defenders take the flat, leaving nobody responsible for the corner route. The Cowboys rank last in EPA per dropback allowed, and the coverage busts help explain why. This is a defense that plays a lot of zone and asks defenders to communicate and exchange routes as receivers move through their areas. Even the Eagles, with Vic Fangio himself, have struggled with communication at times because of new players in the secondary. So, imagine Christian Parker teaching this system for the very first time. Those rules take time to learn, and I wouldn’t expect the same volume of mistakes to continue forever. However, the Eagles have to make the Cowboys demonstrate that they have fixed them. They cannot line up, run the same static combinations repeatedly, and make the secondary’s job easy. Cowboys' Defense All22 Thread. 1) This has not been a very good defense, and that's probably an understatement. Since the start of the season, they have had a ton of coverage busts in the secondary. You can see here: two defenders take the flat, and no one is covering the corner… pic.twitter.com/fKxs8ggTOZ — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 23, 2026 Christian Parker’s defense has played zone on approximately 70% of its charted dropbacks, with Cover 3 its most frequent coverage at 38%. The defense also uses Cover 1 substantially, along with Cover 4 and Cover 6. It’s similar to the Eagles’ defense in many ways. The Eagles should have opportunities to test how the Cowboys handle combinations that put multiple receivers into the same area. Motion, switch releases, crossing routes, posts and corners should all feature in the plan. I want to see the Eagles force defenders to make decisions and communicate after the snap. Flood concepts are an obvious option. Send routes through one side of the field at different depths and make the defenders establish who is taking each receiver. Motion can change formation strength before the snap, while a switch release can change which receiver attacks which space afterward. None of this guarantees a coverage bust, but the Cowboys have provided plenty of evidence that those exchanges can cause problems. I will be disappointed if the Eagles don’t repeatedly test them. There should also be opportunities to build a rhythm without needing every completion to be explosive. This is supposed to be a bend-but-don’t-break style defense. Opponents have completed 83.6% of targeted throws traveling 10 yards or fewer against the Cowboys. Their linebackers and underneath defenders have allowed too many easy catches, and intermediate throws have been particularly damaging. Dallas Goedert and the Eagles’ receivers should have chances to find space if the concepts give them sensible spacing and the quarterback has a clear progression. This defense leaves a lot of open field to attack. 2) The Eagles simply have to test the communication of this defense downfield. If they don't use motion, switch releases, posts, crossing, and corner routes, etc., I will be pretty disappointed. The Cowboys may not have as many busts as they did early on in the season, but the… pic.twitter.com/jWwR8SCAPt — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 23, 2026 Even if the communication improves, the Cowboys have an individual problem at cornerback. DaRon Bland has been struggling badly. The Eagles need to identify who Bland is covering and make that matchup a regular part of the offense. Last week, I wanted them to target Akayleb Evans because the Panthers’ film showed clear opportunities against him. They didn’t do it enough. I don’t want to spend another week watching an opposing cornerback struggle against everyone else while the Eagles barely make him work. DeVonta Smith can win against Bland, but the Eagles should challenge him with their other receivers too. 3) However, even if the secondary gets better, they have a huge problem at CB2. DaRon Bland has been nothing short of a disaster. He is struggling hugely out there. The Eagles need to target him repeatedly, no matter who he is covering. I called last week for the Eagles to… pic.twitter.com/kpwGty3wRf — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 23, 2026 The next example initially looks like another communication error because the receiver ends up so open. On closer inspection, Bland loses the matchup. He jumps inside, loses his footing and cannot recover when the receiver breaks outside. There is a balance here. I want the Eagles to challenge the Cowboys’ communication with combinations, but I also want them to exploit a straightforward individual advantage when it presents itself. Too often this season, it has felt as though the Eagles are determined to run their offense regardless of who is standing opposite them. This week should be about making the Cowboys defend the things they have shown they struggle to handle. 4) I thought this was another coverage bust watching live, but it was just DaRon Bland in coverage again. He loses his footing as he jumps inside and can't cope when the wide receiver breaks outside. He's just really struggling out there. pic.twitter.com/VGuvJXrVOv — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 23, 2026 I’m not treating this as an automatic offensive breakout because of the Cowboys’ defensive line and how they looked against the Packers (which, to be fair, does have a dreadful offensive line). The Cowboys have a credible pass rush, and the Eagles’ protection has been bad enough that any credible rush is a concern. Their overall pressure rate ranks 14th at 36.5%, which is a much healthier number than their coverage results. Rashan Gary is a dangerous edge rusher, Quinnen Williams remains excellent, and Kenny Clark produced an impressive sack against the Packers to show that he can still play, conveniently against his former team! The Cowboys aren’t constantly blitzing to manufacture everything, either. Their blitz rate is approximately league average, and they primarily rely on four rushers. They need those individual players to win quickly enough to give the coverage a chance. I thought the Packers game was their best defensive performance of the season, with the rush arriving…

title: Eagles opposing player to stop, Week 7 edition
summary: The Eagles and Cowboys will be embarking on something Monday night we could call “The Dismal Bowl.” The Cowboys have the 30th rated defense in the NFL, giving up an average of 382.5 yards a game under Dallas’ first-year defensive coordinator and once-prized former Eagles’ assistant coach Christian Parker. The Eagles are not much better, […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - NOVEMBER 23: Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott (4) gets hit by Philadelphia Eagles linebacker Zack Baun (53) during the game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Philadelphia Eagles on November 23, 2025 at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Matthew Pearce/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Eagles and Cowboys will be embarking on something Monday night we could call “The Dismal Bowl.” The Cowboys have the 30th rated defense in the NFL, giving up an average of 382.5 yards a game under Dallas’ first-year defensive coordinator and once-prized former Eagles’ assistant coach Christian Parker. The Eagles are not much better, with the 27th-rated defense giving up 363.8 yards a game. The one glaring difference between these 2-4 teams that will be playing for their seasons on Monday Night Football is Dallas moves the ball. The Eagles don’t. The Cowboys are 13th in the NFL in offense, averaging 343.2 yards a game while the Eagles are 30th, averaging 255.5 yards a game. Dallas is 12th in the league in scoring, averaging 25.2 points a game while the Eagles are tied for 29th, averaging 17.7 points a game this season. The only real weapon on either team is Cowboys’ quarterback Dak Prescott, who remains one of the best in the league. Through six games this season, Prescott is No. 5 in the NFL in passing, throwing for 1,639 yards. He is No. 2 in the NFL in completions (163), only one behind the NFL leader, the Los Angeles Rams’ Matt Stafford (164). Although, Dallas has lost three of its last four games, averaging 23.5 points a game, and failing to reach 20 points in its las two defeats. The Cowboys, fortunately, will be playing an Eagles’ team that has not scored over 24 points in a game this season, is riding a four-game losing streak in which they are averaging an anemic 14.5 points a game. “I see a well-balanced, talented offense,” said Eagles’ defensive coordinator Vic Fangio when asked this week what he saw in the Cowboys’ offense. “They’ve got great receivers, as everybody knows. Their tight end group is really, really good. They’ve got a good offensive line. [Dallas Cowboys QB] Dak [Prescott] is one of the top quarterbacks in the league, and [Dallas Cowboys RB] Javonte [Williams] is a good runner. I had him in Denver, so I know what he’s all about, and he’s really good. They got behind the other night, and it became a passing fest for them, but they’d really like to be more balanced, and I expect them to try and be that.” The Eagles have failed to get to the quarterback this season and been forced to rely on special team players like linebackers Arnold Ebiketie and rookie Keyshawn James-Newby to be edge rushers. Fangio thinks the pair did a good job when they were pushed to play far more than expected in the 25-14 loss to Carolina last week. “I think, for the circumstances, they did a good job,” Fangio said. “AK [Arnold Ebiketie], I think, played in the 70s of snaps, and Keyshawn played close to 50, I think. We were planning on playing Keyshawn a little bit in the game, but then when [OLB] Nolan [Smith] went down and [OLB Jonathan Greenard] JG’s ankle started bothering him, he went from a handful to close to 50.” The NFC East is a collective train wreck this season. The division is a combined 0-6-2 over the last two weeks. The division is there for the taking, although that may apply more to the Cowboys than the moribund Eagles, who are on the brink of losing five-straight games for the first time since 2012, when the Eagles lost eight-straight games in Andy Reid’s last season as head coach. With Jalen Hurts done for the season, with the skittish Tanner McKee now at quarterback, and a tired defense that is missing tackles, not getting any push up front, and breaking apart, the Eagles are flailing downward with nothing to grasp but the tank tonic. Howie Roseman may be on an SEC tour, seen more at Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Ole Miss and Tennessee games than he is at Lincoln Financial Field in the coming months. It looks like the Eagles are entering another white-helmet era (look it up), when the Eagles went 20-45-5 from 1969 to 1973 wearing white helmets and green wings. It was a nice clean look for very bad teams.

title: Steelers keys to victory vs. Saints: Get Jaylen Warren the ball
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers will be looking to get to 5-2 on the season when they face the New Orleans in Paris on Sunday. That 5-2 number is a huge one, as 80 percent of teams that start 5-2 have made the playoffs since the league expanded the playoff field to 14 teams, per Zach Smith. […]
full_text: (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers will be looking to get to 5-2 on the season when they face the New Orleans in Paris on Sunday. That 5-2 number is a huge one, as 80 percent of teams that start 5-2 have made the playoffs since the league expanded the playoff field to 14 teams, per Zach Smith . That number drops to 57 percent for teams that are 4-3. A Steelers win would also put them in prime position to head into their Week 9 bye week atop the AFC North, as they will face the Cleveland Browns in Pittsburgh in Week 8. But first, they have to take care of business in France against the 2-4 Saints. Here are the keys to victory for Week 7. Run the ball a ton The Steelers are good at running the ball. Since Week 3, they are fourth in the league in EPA per rush, per Sumer Sports . However, despite being so good when they run, they are only running on 32.8 percent of snaps, which is second to last in the league. They throw the ball on just over 67 percent of snaps – the second most in the league. The Saints’ defense is the worst unit in the NFL in EPA per rush, and they are allowing the third-most rushing yards per game. Don’t make this a game where you spread the ball out – pound the ball with Jaylen Warren and control the clock. Find a way to succeed vs. single-high coverage No quarterback in the NFL has faced more single-high looks than Aaron Rodgers, and no one has a lower EPA per play when facing single-high coverage than Aaron Rodgers (min. 25 dropbacks). The Saints show single-high at the second-highest rate in the NFL, behind only the Browns. Plays over the middle will be open, the Steelers just need to be able to make them. Win the battle on third down In many metrics, the Steelers are the NFL’s worst team on third down. They rank last in EPA and success rate, and are 28th in third-down conversions. And it’s not as if they are at the bottom of the league in terms of how long their average third down is. Per Sumer Sports, their average third down distance is 6.96 yards, which is 13th in the NFL. For comparison, the Philadelphia Eagles average third-down is a league-high 8.37 yards. The Saints’ defense ranks 24th in success rate on third down, so if there was a week to get their third-down woes turned around, it’s this week. Let us know what you think in the comments . title: Germie Bernard’s production is here to stay for the Steelers
summary: When the Pittsburgh Steelers traded up to select Alabama wide receiver Germie Bernard 47th overall in the second round of the 2026 NFL Draft, the image of the Steelers on the phone with USC wide receiver Makai Lemon before the Philadelphia Eagles jumped the Steelers to select the receiver just the night before was still […]
full_text: (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images When the Pittsburgh Steelers traded up to select Alabama wide receiver Germie Bernard 47th overall in the second round of the 2026 NFL Draft, the image of the Steelers on the phone with USC wide receiver Makai Lemon before the Philadelphia Eagles jumped the Steelers to select the receiver just the night before was still fresh on everyone’s minds. Fast forward to Week 7, and Bernard has captured the attention of the NFL world. Pittsburgh made it a point to add to their receiver room this past offseason, as they traded for Michael Pittman Jr. from the Indianapolis Colts back in March. Despite the high draft capital investment the team made in him, Bernard found himself buried as the WR4 on the Steelers depth chart to start the season. After injuries to both Pittman and Roman Wilson, though, Bernard has had to step up in their absence and has exceeded all expectations. Bernard is second among all rookies in catches through six weeks with 24. He is just five receptions behind number four overall pick Carnell Tate for the most among all rookies. What sticks out the most is the fact that Bernard has 17 of his 24 catches over the last two weeks. With Pittman and Wilson both on injured reserve for an undetermined amount of time, Bernard is already making the most of his role. Quarterback Aaron Rodgers praised the rookie for his confidence that has clearly grown over the past several weeks after his breakout 11 reception 87 yard performance against Tampa Bay in which the rookie receiver scored the game-winning touchdown in overtime. “There comes a time when the confidence starts to match the potential, and I think we’re reaching that time with Germie,” Rodgers said. “Very proud of him.” Aaron Rodgers on Germie Bernard: "There comes a time when the confidence starts to match the potential, and I think we're reaching that time with Germie. Very proud of him." — Mike DeFabo (@MikeDeFabo) October 18, 2026 For someone who has the reputation of not trusting his rookie receivers enough, Rodgers has certainly shown a good bit of confidence in Bernard over the last few weeks as he continues to pepper him with targets. Not only does Rodgers seem to be trusting Bernard more and more, but the passing volume of the Steelers offense also bodes well for Bernard’s role the rest of the season. Rodgers’ 233 passing attempts through six weeks is the fifth most by any quarterback in the league. The veteran quarterback’s ADOT currently ranks 22nd in the league with a 7.3 mark . Bernard excelled in those short and intermediate areas of the field and after the catch in college. His play style translated seamlessly int the Steelers offense, coupled with the sheer amount of opportunities he could see, should have all Steelers fans excited. So much to get excited about with Germie Bernard's game. Dude is already a smooth and savvy football player who knows how to set up his defenders at the top of his routes. #Steelers pic.twitter.com/WdgKOClcbZ — Tommy Jaggi (@TommyJaggi) October 22, 2026 We have only seen Bernard in this expanded role for a few weeks, but it’s hard to see this as a flash in the pan instead of a real rookie breakout. In a year in which nobody is running away with the Offensive Rookie of the Year award, Bernard could very well put his name in the running in the coming weeks. Bernard’s breakout makes it that much more unlikely that the Steelers trade for a big-name receiver at the deadline, even with all of the injuries to their receiver room. It would be silly for them to consider trading for someone who would take snaps away from the rookie that they have invested serious capital into and that their quarterback continues to trust. “The Infection” is here to stay as one of the most important and dynamic pieces on the Steelers offense. Even when Pittman and Wilson eventually return from injury, it would be shocking to see Bernard go back to being the fourth receiver in the offense, especially if he keeps playing this way. title: Steelers-Saints preview: What to expect from New Orleans’ offense, defense in Week 7
summary: The 4-2 Steelers and 2-4 Saints will clash in Paris early Sunday morning in Week 7. Currently second in a tight and highly competitive AFC North, Pittsburgh is hoping to stay in the mix and add to a current two-game winning streak following an overtime win against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers last week. Meanwhile, the […]
full_text: Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images | Getty Images The 4-2 Steelers and 2-4 Saints will clash in Paris early Sunday morning in Week 7. Currently second in a tight and highly competitive AFC North, Pittsburgh is hoping to stay in the mix and add to a current two-game winning streak following an overtime win against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers last week. Meanwhile, the Saints are third in a weak NFC South after the first third of the season — and after New Orleans was a popular pick for the league’s breakout team in 2026. Under second-year head coach (and former Cowboys offensive coordinator under Mike McCarthy) Kellen Moore, New Orleans will be hoping to establish its first winning streak of the season after a high-scoring win over the Giants last week. What can Steelers fans expect from the Saints across the pond? What to expect from the Saints’ offense Rushing YPG: 97.3 (21st) Passing YPG: 224.2 (17th) PPG: 25.3 (10th) RP: The first thing you’ll notice about the Saints offense is that while they have a dismal rushing attack and middling overall passing numbers, they also are somehow a top-10 scoring offense. Don’t be too alarmed, though. While there are some talented playmakers, and Kellen Moore is an offensive mind I view favorably, a slightly deeper examination of the Saints reveals they are more of a paper tiger. For starters, the Saints have not faced many difficult defenses at this point in the season. Consider the points allowed per game rankings of five of their six opponents: Detroit (29.6 / 30th) Las Vegas (27.0 /26th) Atlanta (25.5 / 23rd) New York Giants (23.3 / 19th) Baltimore (22.0 / 15th) Not exactly a murderers’ row of defenses. When the Saints did face a strong defense — the Vikings, who allow the fewest points per game (12.8) — they predictably folded, losing 23-13. I suppose some props should be awarded for clearing the Vikings’ season average. Also consider that the Saints offense has often been late to the party. New Orleans is averaging just 7.2 points in the first half of games this season. All told, they have run 215 plays while trailing against just 26 plays while holding a lead. A big factor in this is their ineffective running game. Some of this is due to losing starting tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. early in the season, which has forced 2023 fifth-round pick Asim Richards into a starting role. Richards has the 10th-worst run-blocking grade from Pro Football Focus among tackles with at least 100 run-blocking snaps this season. Some of the Saints’ struggles are also due to losing prized free agent signing Travis Ettiene Jr. to injury in Week 3, though he had struggled prior to injury, failing to top 57 yards in a game. In his absence, that has left a rotating trio of Kendre Miller, a past-his-prime Alvin Kamar, and CJ Donaldson. None of them have found consistent success. It's been tough sledding for the Saints' running game pic.twitter.com/k9zok0qpDY — Ryan Parish (@ArmchairScout21) October 23, 2026 The Steelers should be prepared to see a lot of inside zone against the Saints. So far this season, they’ve called 88 zone running plays compared to 31 gap runs, and their rate of inside run calls (64.3%) is second highest in the league. Regardless of what they call, the underlying metrics spell out how ineffective they’ve been. New Orleans averages just 3.8 yards per carry (T-19th), with an average of just 0.97 yards before contact (21st), and 2.84 average yards after contact (16th). They’ve been stuffed at the 14th-highest rate (16.9%), have a 39.6% success rate (T-17th) when running, and are failing to create explosive runs with just 12 runs of 10-or-more yards (T-20th). They are also averaging a half-yard less rushing yards than expected per rush, the fourth-worst mark in the league. Because the Saints struggle to run the ball and are always trailing, a lot of strain is then put on the shoulders of second-year quarterback Tyler Shough. A former second-round pick who had a longer-than-usual college career due to injuries, Shough is in many ways a cool story for the Saints. Right now, he’s tied for the second-most passing touchdowns in the NFL. In fact, he has the same number of touchdowns (12) and interceptions (5) as Aaron Rodgers this year. Shough also has the 10th-lowest sack rate (5.2%), and he’s been making quick decisions with the eighth-quickest average time to throw (2.73 seconds). But much like the rest of the Saints’ offense, the underlying metrics paint a more complicated picture for Shough. One reason he might be getting the ball out so quickly is because the Saints give up the seventh-quickest average time until pressure at 2.55 seconds. While they rank 20th in pressure rate (37.6%), the sheer volume of plays New Orleans runs has also allowed them to give up the second-most pressures (97) this year. The Saints don’t run much play-action either, with their 11.9% play-action rate ranked the second-lowest in the NFL. Like most quarterbacks, Shough’s effectiveness takes a hit under pressure compared to when he’s kept clean. When facing no pressure, Shough completes 72.8% of his passes, racking up 1,012 yards, nine touchdowns, just two picks, and he averages 6.4 yards per attempt at an average depth of target of 6.5 yards. Under pressure, though, Shough’s completion percentage plummets to 49.4% and he’s thrown three interceptions against three touchdowns. His YPA drops to 5.6 while pressured, but oddly enough his ADoT spikes to 12.1, which seems to indicate he throws the ball away or forces attempts downfield when he gets a defender in his face. So it would seem the simple answer for the Steelers defense is to get pressure on Shough and watch him crack. However, don’t think it will be as easy as dialing up the blitzes. Shough has seen a lot of football for just a second-year player thanks to his prolonged college career. And while his numbers dip when pressure gets home, he has a decent enough head for the game that he’s able to adjust when he knows where the blitz will be coming from. Despite opponents blitzing the Saints at the 10th-highest rate in the league (35.1%), Shough’s completion percentage actually improves when he’s blitzed (66.3%) compared to when he isn’t (64.1%). He’s thrown six touchdowns and three interceptions when blitzed, compared to six touchdowns and two interceptions without a blitz. And with an ADoT of 7.3 yards against the blitz, he isn’t just checking it down to his running back either. It ends up with a drop, but Tyler Shough showing one of the ways to handle a 4 weak pressure. Watch him keep the OL's slide to the right and point at the Safety, signaling to Chris Olave that if #25 blitzes that he is to run a sight adjust slant route. pic.twitter.com/Vp0bWVSsmX — Nate Tice (@Nate_Tice) October 20, 2026 If there’s one secret to stopping Shough beyond getting pressure home, it’s his struggles against zone. Shough’s numbers against man coverage are some of the best in the league, but his efficiency takes a dip when he faces zone. Tyler Shough Total EPA (Rank) EPA/Play (Rank) Success rate (Rank) Comp % (Rank) TD (Rank) INT (Rank) Time To Throw (Rank) ADoT (Rank) YPA (Rank) vs. Zone (minimum 100 dropbacks) -11.94 (23rd) -0.06 (20th) 43.3% (18th) 65.7% (18th) 3 (T-12) 5 (T-2nd most) 2.70s (T-10th) 7.49 (15th) 6.3 (22nd) vs. Man (minimum 50 dropbacks) 6.12 (5th) 0.08 (5th) 48.6% (3rd) 67.2% (1st) 8 (1st) 0 (1st) 2.24s (1st) 8.5 (8th) 6.1 (6th) Perhaps Shough’s struggles with zone coverages might explain why he avoids throwing to the middle intermediate (10+ yards) and deep (20+ yards) parts of the field. Oddly enough, he’s been effective when he attacks the middle intermediate area, going 14-for-15 for 197 yards and two touchdowns, but that’s at an average of less than three attempts a game. And that effectiveness isn’t exactly a fluke, as he went 25-for-31, 383 yards and a touchdown in 10 games in 2025. Again, though, that was at roughly a rate of three attempts per game. title: Why the Seahawks may not trade for Jonathan Taylor
summary: It’s no secret that the Seattle Seahawks want to be a running team but have been unable to jumpstart their offense with the ground game. Could a team that just fired its general manager, and may be holding a fire sale, be the answer to helping the Hawks solve this issue? Principal owner of the […]
full_text: It’s no secret that the Seattle Seahawks want to be a running team but have been unable to jumpstart their offense with the ground game. Could a team that just fired its general manager, and may be holding a fire sale, be the answer to helping the Hawks solve this issue? Principal owner of the Indianapolis Colts, Carlie Irsay-Gordon made the decision to relieve Chris Ballard of his post as GM this past week. This comes after Indy looked like a surprising contender early last season with Daniel Jones at the helm, then went all-in with blockbuster trade for CB, Sauce Gardner. Unfortunately for them, Jones was lost for the season shortly after. This year’s Colts team hasn’t looked the same and has sputtered to a 2-4 start. Pushing the chips to the middle ended in disaster, and it could ultimately cause the team in Indiana to clean house and sell off assets in order to enter a rebuild. One of the most prominent players involved in trade speculation is a running back who is tied for 7th league-wide in rushing yardage per game (82) and is in a 6-way tie for tops in rushing touchdowns (7) among RB’s: Jonathan Taylor. View Link Taylor is a great back. Thoughts of J.T. rampaging through defenses to keep Sam Darnold ahead of the sticks and in advantageous situations is undoubtedly a really fun idea that would give fans immediate confidence. But do they need to? I don’t think it’ll happen, for a few reasons. I get it. Taylor is a ready-made superstar at the position. One who is fast, powerful and durable. BUT when I see 12’s suggesting we send Jadarian Price and future picks for a soon-to-be 28-year-old… I just don’t think that’s how Schneider operates. Especially not at the halfback position. This team has championship repeat aspirations, but Seattle is not going to sell the farm to make it happen. Price has a future here as a playmaker. Caveat : I don’t have any personal connection to or 100% accurate bead on GM, John Schneider. He is unafraid of taking big swings when he deems it warranted. Schneider has repeatedly mentioned how he likes to save some gun powder to make improvements in-season. He has shocked us before… but we can surmise some things when looking at the way he operates. Schneider stated back in March that the running back is “a position that… you can find guys.” They could’ve paid Ken Walker. Actually, bump that: they could’ve at least made an offer to K9 . A working theory is that the writing was really already on the wall for both sides, any way you want to slice it. Walker was unhappy in not having his talents maximized and may currently feel slightly justified about that, as he tears up the league for the Kansas City Chiefs. From the Seahawks’ perspective, Walker priced himself into holding the leverage for a possible once-in-a-lifetime type of running back contract after a magical postseason run on the way to a Super Bowl trophy and Super Bowl MVP award. There’s also the fact that Taylor signed a 3-year contract this past offseason and averages a cap hit of ~$20M over the life of that deal. If the team were to cut him next year, they could but would incur a $10M dead cap hit. That’s more than Walker III is getting paid! Ever since Marshawn Lynch left, the Seahawks shifted to more of a running-back-by-committee approach, rather than the bell cow model. In the four seasons where Marshawn Lynch played in more than 12 games for the Seattle Seahawks, he averaged over 295 carries per year. Chris Carson has been the only one since to clock more than 230 carries in a season, with 247 and 278 in back-to-back years (both over 1.1K rushing yards). Ken Walker was the next closest thing, taking 228 attempts in his rookie season and 221 in his final year in Seattle. Other than those standout seasons, the Seahawks have platooned players like Christine Michael, C.J. Prosise, Thomas Rawls, Rashaad Penny, Zach Charbonnet, Carson, Walker and others. The Seattle Seahawks under Mike Macdonald have committed to a Shanahan-style run game. That is an offensive system that attacks with outside zone run concepts, play-action and (more recently) quarterback pocket movement. It’s not named after Kyle, although the younger Shanahan deserves credit for innovating the system forward. His father, Mike Shanahan, was a pioneer in this aspect, and weaponized a wide array of seemingly anonymous backs to great effect. Terrell Davis was a sixth-round pick and is now a Hall-of-Famer. Olandis Gary was a fourth-Rounder who popped out to be a 1,100-yard rusher. Mike Anderson was taken in the sixth, yet went on to win OROY with over 1,400 on the ground and 15 TD’s. Reuben Droughns was a converted fullback! Denver went with him, feeling good enough about it to trade the great Clinton Portis for Champ Bailey. Remember Tatum Bell? The Shanahan offensive scheme de-prioritizes running back financial commitments in favor of emphasizing the line and other aspects of the offense/defense. This could explain the mentality in letting Kenneth Walker leave without even an offer. The Seattle Seahawks are leaning into what they believe is an advantage of this offensive structure and team approach to the running game. Having that been said, the Seahawks do have multiple players returning soon, and one is a recent 1st-round pick. Seahawks team reporter, John Boyle iterated reasoning for no panic very succinctly: “how it will shake out with Zach Charbonnet expected back soon, possibly this week, and with first-round pick Jadarian Price not far behind. The Seahawks will always look at every option, but that position won’t seem like as much of a need in the next couple of weeks as it might at this very moment.” Wilson seems to be a fine third back; a back who can be a bruiser, a closer and a change-of-pace runner. He has, at least, given this team a chance during his run as starter. Working behind Charbonnet and Price (who could be the future tandem, if Charbs comes back on a favorable deal) might form a much stronger rushing attack than when Seattle was feeding former Bears WR, Velus Jones Jr. rushing attempts. Funny thing is that Seahawks backs are forcing missed tackles at a strong rate… but gaining yards before being contacted at a lower rate than the rest of the league. RB Yards Before Contact & Missed Tackles Forced pic.twitter.com/DQVHChRyKb — Jrfortgang (@throwthedamball) October 21, 2026 That makes one think… maybe a different position should be on the docket. 🤔

title: Seahawks-Chiefs injury designations: Zach Charbonnet out, Nick Emmanwori questionable
summary: Coming off back-to-back losses against the San Francisco 49ers and Denver Broncos, the Seattle Seahawks are in desperate need of a win but it won’t get any easier in Week 7 as they’re set to remain without their starting running back and possibly a star second year safety—against the undefeated Kansas City Chiefs. Seahawks injury […]
full_text: Coming off back-to-back losses against the San Francisco 49ers and Denver Broncos, the Seattle Seahawks are in desperate need of a win but it won’t get any easier in Week 7 as they’re set to remain without their starting running back and possibly a star second year safety—against the undefeated Kansas City Chiefs. Seahawks injury desingations Out : RB Zach Charbonnet (knee) LB Drake Thomas (ankle) LB Chazz Surratt (calf) Questionable: S Nick Emmanwori (hip) LB Uchenna Nowsu (hip) De Demarcus Lawrence (knee) QB Drew Lock (right elbow) LB Connor O’Toole (hamstring) The Friday injury report. Read more » https://t.co/0rmTlN4D2H pic.twitter.com/uIB8ySlEmE — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) October 23, 2026 While the continued absence of linebackers Drake Thomas and Chazz Surratt certainly impacts Seattle’s defense, Charbonnet not being able to take the field is especially troubling. The fourth year ball carrier was activated off the physically unable to perform (PUP) list on Thursday and practiced in a full capacity all week, which seemingly boded well for his return. Although he won’t suit up, head coach Mike Macdonald said he didn’t suffer a setback. With Charbonnet sidelined, Emanuel Wilson and George Holani appear poised to continue to split carries and while both have shown flashes of potential—neither has made a consistent impact and both have struggled with ball security. As a result, Seattle’s backfield has lacked the burst that departed in free agency in the offseason as the team prepares to face off against Kenneth Walker III, who leads the league with 665 rushing yards and six touchdowns in spite of the Chiefs already enjoying their bye week. Without their starting running back, Seattle ranks 18th in rushing yards per game and leads the league in fumbles, with six. After missing practice for a second consecutive week, Thomas’ absence should come as no surprise and Tyrice Knight—who played well in the team’s Week 6 loss, is in line to fill in once again. With fellow linebackers Uchenna Nwosu and Connor O’Toole’s status’ also in doubt, the Seahawks may be forced to turn to the practice squad once again where they’ll have Jimmy Ciarlo, Aidan Hubbard as well as the recently signed Josh Ross to choose from. Following injuries to their secondary across the first four weeks, it appeared Seattle was finally in the clear but Nick Emmanwori’s status is certainly alarming and could also require the team to activate a safety from the practice squad tomorrow. Macdonald said the second year safety experienced an issue with his hip during Friday’s practice, but wouldn’t describe it as an “injury,” and Saturday’s elevations will likely provide an indication on whether or not he’ll play. Regarding defensive end Demarcus Lawrence, the veteran was awarded a rest day on Wednesday, but remained on the practice report with a knee issue that forced him to practice in a limited capacity on Thursday as well as today. Macdonald did not provide an update as to which side of questionable he was trending on. The same goes for quarterback Drew Lock, who’s practiced in a limited capacity for the past two weeks as he navigates through an ongoing injury to his throwing elbow. While concerning, especially considering Sam Darnold’s recent turnovers, it’s worth noting he was active for last week’s game against the Broncos. As for Kansas City, wide receiver Rashee Rice (hamstring), offensive tackle Jaylon Moore (concussion) and running back Brashard Smith (hamstring) were ruled out, leaving Xavier Worthy as Kansas City’s clear cut number one wide receiver against one of the best secondaries in the NFL. Cornerback L’Jarius Sneed (hamstring) and linebacker Cooper McDonald (knee) are listed as questionable. Both teams will release their official inactives 3:50 pm P.T. on Sunday.

title: Seahawks vs. Chiefs game preview: How can Seattle turn its season around?
summary: The Seahawks are heading back to primetime for another difficult test, this time against the Kansas City Chiefs at Lumen Field. After facing the San Francisco 49ers, Seattle gets another opportunity to prove it can compete with one of the NFL’s best teams. The difference is that the Seahawks cannot afford another performance filled with […]
full_text: The Seahawks are heading back to primetime for another difficult test, this time against the Kansas City Chiefs at Lumen Field. After facing the San Francisco 49ers, Seattle gets another opportunity to prove it can compete with one of the NFL’s best teams. The difference is that the Seahawks cannot afford another performance filled with defensive lapses and missed opportunities. At 3–3, Seattle has already made its path forward more complicated with losses to the Washington Commanders and Denver Broncos. Beating Kansas City would not solve every problem, but it could restore confidence and give the Seahawks some much-needed momentum before the next stretch of a challenging schedule. There is also an intriguing storyline on the other sideline: former Seahawks running back Kenneth Walker III, who has become one of the Chiefs’ most productive offensive weapons. The biggest test for Seattle’s run defense Seattle’s defense has gone 35 consecutive games without allowing an opposing running back to rush for 100 yards. That streak is now facing one of its toughest challenges yet. Walker has rushed for 665 yards and six touchdowns through five games, averaging 133 yards per game and 6.3 yards per carry. He has surpassed 100 rushing yards in four of his five appearances, with his lowest total being 70 yards against Miami. He has also added 95 receiving yards and two receiving touchdowns. The numbers tell the story, but Walker’s explosiveness is what makes this matchup particularly dangerous. He can turn a routine run into a game-changing play with one missed tackle. A defender who fails to finish the play could be the difference between a one-yard loss and a 30-yard gain. Seattle knows Walker well, and that familiarity could help. But it also means the Seahawks understand exactly how quickly he can punish a defensive mistake. The potential return of Zach Charbonnet adds another layer to the storyline. If he is able to play, Seattle would get a boost to its depleted backfield while facing the running back who once shared the workload with him. Still, Charbonnet’s availability must be confirmed before Sunday. Defensive discipline will be essential Seattle has continued to defend the run well, allowing approximately 96 rushing yards per game this season. The unit has not been quite as dominant as it was last year, however, and the Denver game exposed how costly lapses can become. The Seahawks managed to limit Denver’s passing production in the second half, but that does not necessarily translate into success against Kansas City. Patrick Mahomes presents a different level of challenge, and the Chiefs have more ways to punish a defense that loses its discipline. Seattle cannot afford to switch off for two drives and expect to recover without consequences. Against Mahomes, even a short stretch of poor execution can swing a game. The first priority is controlling Walker. That means maintaining gap integrity, tackling consistently and preventing explosive runs. Seattle must also be prepared for the possibility that Walker becomes a receiving threat, particularly on quick passes designed to get the ball into his hands in space. Stopping the Chiefs passing game Stopping Walker would be a significant step, but it would not solve the entire problem. Kansas City’s ground game helps sustain drives and keeps the offense in manageable situations, creating opportunities for Mahomes to attack through the air. Travis Kelce has recorded 299 receiving yards and two touchdowns through five games. Xavier Worthy has added 206 yards and a touchdown, while Tyquan Thornton has produced 219 yards and two scores. Those numbers illustrate that Kansas City can distribute the ball to multiple targets. Thornton will be out due to injury, as will Rashee Rice, so this is a banged up group. Kelce is particularly important because of the problems he can create for linebackers. Seattle has had moments of misalignment between its linebackers and defensive front, while coverage against tight ends has occasionally left room for opposing offenses to exploit. Ernest Jones, Tyrice Knight (assuming Drake Thomas doesn’t play), and Nick Emmanwori will be important pieces in keeping those responsibilities organized. Seattle must recognize when to prioritize Walker in the backfield and when to account for Kelce working underneath. The Chiefs do not need to rely exclusively on explosive downfield throws. If Seattle overcommits to stopping the run, Mahomes can take the easier completions underneath and allow his receivers to gain yards after the catch. A familiar face, a different challenge Seattle has seen Walker’s explosiveness firsthand, but this is a different challenge from the one the Seahawks faced when he wore their uniform. Now he is operating in an offense led by Mahomes, and the combination makes every defensive mistake more dangerous. There is also a historical reminder of how strange these reunions can be for Seattle. Former Seahawks tight end Jimmy Graham once scored against his old team while playing for Chicago. That is a fun footnote, but Walker is a far more central concern heading into this matchup. The last meeting between Seattle and Kansas City came in November 2022, when the Chiefs won 24–10 with Geno Smith at quarterback for the Seahawks. Seattle’s more memorable recent win came in December 2018, when Russell Wilson and the Seahawks defeated Mahomes and Kansas City 38–31. The 2018 game offers a reminder that Seattle can compete with an elite Kansas City offense. But this year’s matchup will require a complete performance rather than relying on history. Final Thoughts This is a difficult matchup for Seattle, but it is also an opportunity to change the narrative surrounding its season. The losses to Washington and Denver have created legitimate questions about the Seahawks’ consistency, and another defeat could make the road ahead even more difficult. A primetime win over Kansas City, however, would give the team a significant confidence boost and put it back in the conversation as a contender. The Seahawks do not need to play a perfect game, but they must avoid the extended lapses that have hurt them recently. Containing Walker, tackling well and staying disciplined against Mahomes and Kelce will be essential. Seattle has the home crowd and the defensive track record to make this competitive. Now it needs to turn those advantages into four quarters of consistent football.
author: Alexandre Castro

title: Inside the Seahawks: The Athletic’s Andrew Destin assesses Seattle’s sputtering offense
summary: The Seattle Seahawks are six games into defending their Super Bowl title, and the biggest question isn’t whether this roster has talent. It’s whether a talented team can stop beating itself long enough to get back on track. On the latest episode of The Hawks Eye, I welcomed Andrew Destin, the newest Seahawks beat reporter […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks are six games into defending their Super Bowl title, and the biggest question isn’t whether this roster has talent. It’s whether a talented team can stop beating itself long enough to get back on track. On the latest episode of The Hawks Eye, I welcomed Andrew Destin, the newest Seahawks beat reporter for The Athletic , to examine Seattle’s uneven opening stretch and preview Sunday’s matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs. At 3–3, Seattle remains firmly in the playoff race, but the path forward is uncertain. Turnovers have piled up. Sam Darnold has struggled to find consistency behind an offensive line dealing with protection problems, while an unreliable running game has made life harder for the entire passing attack. These issues are connected. When Seattle cannot stay ahead of the chains, defenses can dictate terms. When protection breaks down, the quarterback’s decision-making window shrinks. When possessions end in giveaways, even an excellent defense has only so many answers, and no team has allowed more points off turnovers than Seattle. That’s why the spotlight extends beyond Darnold. How much responsibility belongs to new offensive coordinator Brian Fleury? What adjustments can Mike Macdonald demand from his staff? And how quickly can the offense rebuild the complementary identity that made last season’s Seahawks so difficult to beat? Andrew’s perspective is valuable because he covers this team up close. The goal of our conversation was to dig past box scores and examine the people, decisions and bigger questions shaping Seattle’s season. Here’s a sampling of what Andrew said regarding potential changes on offense, whether at quarterback or offensive coordinator, as well as trade deadline possibilities. If the Seahawks make a change, is it firing Brian Fleury or benching Sam Darnold? “I’ve said this on the record a few times […] If the Seahawks are going to make a change it’s going to be at offensive coordinator before they do so at quarterback, just going by dollars and cents. Sam Darnold is being paid $30+ million to be the guy. Drew Lock sure showed himself to be a more than capable backup, but there’s a reason the sentiment around the team is we are so lucky to have who we think is the best backup in the NFL. Nobody in the building right now is looking to it as, ‘Sam Darnold is the issue, he must be benched.’” I mean, there was a story I put out last week coming off the Broncos game where Mike Macdonald basically said, “Yeah, he’s got our full faith. We fully believe in Sam Darnold.” “I think right now it really is a matter of if Brian Fleury isn’t the guy, then that would be who they move off quicker than Darnold. Because let’s remind ourselves, history is a precedent. Darnold’s coming off the two best seasons of his career. He’s coming off of a glute injury. We’re talking about four games and change. That’s such a small sample size. I also don’t think the offensive issues necessarily are—I don’t know that it’s schematic. I don’t want to put blame on the players and absolve Brian Fleury of blame, but so much of this comes down to execution. So much of this comes down to players who just haven’t been hanging on to the dang football or have been throwing away the football. I’m not expecting a change at either spot, but if one is to come before the other, I think it would be Brian Fleury before Sam Darnold.” If the Seahawks replace Brian Fleury midseason, who could be the new OC? “My expectation would be that it would be [quarterbacks coach] Jake Peetz just because he’s somebody who works so closely with the quarterbacks and is so in line and in tune with what Sam Darnold wants to do offensively and what the Seahawks want to do offensively. “I really do think that it would be Peetz. Unfortunately, it’s not really my expectation at this point for the Seahawks to move off of [Fleury], but if they were to do so, educated guess would be Jake Peetz just given his background at the quarterback spot, his play calling [at LSU], all those sorts of things. But first and foremost, I think it’s going to be Brian Fleury [remaining offensive coordinator]. If they’re to move off though, perhaps by committee, and if not, then it would be Peetz.” Will the Seahawks do anything at the trade deadline? “I think they are more than likely to make a deal and we’ve seen that over the last few trade deadlines, right, of getting guys like Rashid Shaheed, Ernest Jones, Leonard Williams all come to mind. I think the precedent is there and especially with where the Seahawks are at salary cap wise that they absolutely would add. They have the flexibility to do so because you didn’t re-sign Kenneth Walker, because you didn’t re-sign Boy Mafe because you didn’t re-sign Coby Bryant.And you gave extensions but that’s neither here nor there; you’ve got the space and you’ve got the flexibility to do so. “I think they would add and if they were to add it would be at a skill position, whether that’s tight end, whether that’s another number two receiver. Perhaps that would be some kind of swap where to acquire a more veteran receiver and let Rashid Shaheed go in that trade to make it salary cap negligible. I think offensively speaking, you’ve got to add another weapon. The Seahawks are sorely lacking a true number two guy alongside Jaxon Smith-Njigba. Kupp isn’t that guy at this point in his career. Shaheed hasn’t been. That’s where I am kind of looking.” We also turned toward Sunday’s prime-time showdown at Lumen Field. Patrick Mahomes leads an undefeated Chiefs team into Seattle, while former Seahawk Kenneth Walker III returns in Kansas City colors as the league’s leader in rushing yards, in stark contrast to Seattle’s lackluster running game. It’s a matchup that will test Seattle’s defensive discipline and its offense’s ability to avoid self-inflicted damage. Whether you’re looking for a closer look at the coaching staff, the quarterback, the locker room or the challenge ahead, this episode offers plenty to consider. And let us know: Is Seattle’s slow start fixable, or are the problems deeper than six games suggest? Video (interview starts at 11:09 and runs 20 minutes) Join the conversation! title: NFL predictions: 4 game picks for pivotal Chiefs-Seahawks matchup
summary: Sunday Night Football brings the Kansas City Chiefs to Seattle for a Week 7 matchup, also unofficially known as the “Kenneth Walker III Bowl.” If you’re looking for player props and game-day value, check out the latest lines at FanDuel Sportsbook before kickoff.  The Seattle Seahawks are coming off of two straight losses and are […]
full_text: Sunday Night Football brings the Kansas City Chiefs to Seattle for a Week 7 matchup, also unofficially known as the “Kenneth Walker III Bowl.” If you’re looking for player props and game-day value, check out the latest lines at FanDuel Sportsbook before kickoff. The Seattle Seahawks are coming off of two straight losses and are staring a sub .500 record straight in the eyes. The Chiefs meanwhile are undefeated and are currently elated with their recent running back signing (and Offensive Player of the Year candidate) Kenneth Walker III. Let’s look at some game picks ahead of this matchup Sunday Night. Kenneth Walker III over 84.5 rushing yards (-114) I know Walker III is not a Seahawk anymore. However, considering his dominance this season, and the Seahawks lack of dominant running game, this is surely the game pick on the top of everyone’s mind. Walker III is averaging 133 yards per game this season . Meanwhile the Seahawks defense has not allowed a 100 yard rusher in a franchise record, 35 games – not since October 27, 2024. One of these juggernauts will have to break in this matchup. The betting line being at 84.5 seems to be lower than many expected, or at least lower than I expected. Walker III is on a career heater right now. His ability to flip the field at any moment and break any run into a house call is very rare. Even if the Seahawks defense holds Walker III in check, it only takes one explosive run to get close to this 84.5 line. On top of this, Walker III already gets a large share of carries, and is now facing a revenge game. I would expect Walker III to get a ton of carries in this game, which means tons of opportunities to hit this line. All of this considered, it is tough to see Walker III not being able to hit at least 85 yards rushing. That doesn’t mean that he will break 100 yards – the Seahawks could still very easily extend their streak to 36 games. However, this will be their hardest challenge yet. The pick: Kenneth Walker III over 84.5 rushing yards . Over 42.5 points (-112) The line for this game is 42.5, also a little lower. The Seahawks have scored at least 29 points four times this season. Their only two games where they scored less was in Week 1 with Drew Lock coming in with no first team reps, and in Week 6 with a short week Thursday Night Football game. Add to this, the fact that the Seahawks are playing the red hot Kenneth Walker III and the Chiefs. There is a good chance that the Seahawks offense will need to keep up with Kansas City and their elite running game. That will surely be easier to do with Anthony Bradford and Zach Charbonnet likely returning for this game. Expect a high scoring affair in the battle of former AFC West foes. The pick: Over 42.5 total points (-112) . Jaxon Smith-Njigba over 92.5 receiving yards (-114). Leading the NFL in receptions (49), receiving yards (717), and receiving touchdowns (7) , JSN is once again on a heater. JSN has only missed the receiving yards line once this season – week 4 against the Los Angeles Chargers where he put up only 76 yards (18.5 yards shy of the line). With the Seahawks run game struggling, and Sam Darnold looking less confident week in and week out, expect the safety blanket, JSN to have another big game this week against the Chiefs. Despite averaging 143.4 yards per game, the lines still remain fairly low. With it this low, the smartest move would be to bet the over. The pick: Jaxon Smith-Njigba over 92.5 receiving yards . Zach Charbonnet to score 2+ touchdowns (+750) The first three picks may not be too risky. However, this last pick is very risky. Trying to correctly guess who will score two or more touchdowns is a Hail Mary of sorts, but why not live on the edge? Charbonnet, who was just activated off of the PUP list , is expected to make his season debut against the Chiefs. This season, the Seahawks have struggled in short yardage situations. That is exactly where Charbonnet’s return is huge. When on the field, Charbonnet tends to find the end zone. Last season, Charbonnet led the Seahawks with 12 touchdowns. The year prior, Charbonnet had 8 touchdowns . Although this will be his first game back since tearing his ACL in the 2025 playoffs, look to see Charbonnet get these opportunities once again. It isn’t just the short yardage situations however. Charbonnet is also a strong pass catcher and gives the Seahawks an opportunity to score as a receiver as well. Despite only having one career receiving touchdown, Charbonnet still has 95 receptions for 693 yards in his young three year career. The other elephant in the room with Charbonnet’s return is Kenneth Walker III’s absence. Throughout his career Charbonnet has always split the backfield with Walker III. However, this season Charbonnet has an opportunity to prove he is the clear number one running back. With Jadarian Price still on injured reserve, and the other running backs on the roster proving lackluster, this week will be a perfect opportunity for Charbonnet to prove he can lead this backfield. The pick: Zach Charbonnet to score 2+ touchdowns .

title: 49ers injury updates: Nick Bosa dealt with soreness recently in a workout
summary: The San Francisco 49ers continued their weekly roster gymnastics. For the second consecutive week, the team released Ogbo Okoronkwo. He played 17 snaps on Monday night. Nick Bosa didn’t practice all week. Head coach Kyle Shanahan ruled Bosa out. That means the 49ers will be down an edge rusher. The team will likely re-sign Okoronkwo […]
full_text: (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers continued their weekly roster gymnastics. For the second consecutive week, the team released Ogbo Okoronkwo. He played 17 snaps on Monday night. Nick Bosa didn’t practice all week. Head coach Kyle Shanahan ruled Bosa out. That means the 49ers will be down an edge rusher. The team will likely re-sign Okoronkwo to the practice squad on Saturday and elevate him to the active roster to play against the Falcons. Shanahan said Bosa was “a little too optimistic” when he said a couple of weeks ago that he would definitely play in Week 7. Shanahan added that Bosa was “a little sore” in his first workout after telling the media he’d play, which “surprised all of us.” Shanahan said that wasn’t a great sign with a turf game coming up, then circled back to Bosa being overly optimistic about returning. Mike Evans also missed Friday’s session. Shanahan ruled out Evans. The 49ers will play their first game of the season without their star wide receiver. Evans has missed time in a couple of games and remains the team leader in several categories. Offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak said the ball will find Jordan Watkins . For Watkins and Jacob Cowing, Atlanta could be their last chance to impress the coaching staff in a live setting. The 49ers have a bye week in Week 8. Heading into Week 9, veterans Demarcus Robinson and Deebo Samuel could return to the lineup. We’re headed for Christian Kirk’s debut. Because the team released Okonkwo, they don’t need to create another roster spot for Kirk, who practiced all week. Here’s the injury report: OUT: WR Deebo Samuel LB Garret Wallow EDGE Nick Bosa S Marques Sigle WR Mike Evans LB Luke Gifford Questionable: S Siran Neal CB Upton Stout WR Christian Kirk Shanahan confirmed that listing Kirk on the injury report is a procedural move. The 49ers will enter this game with fewer than the usual 48 players. Shanahan said players like Kurtis Rourke and maybe Enrique Cruz would be active on Sunday. He joked that those two would be the emergency receivers. This will be the first game Shanahan has played with fewer than the maximum number of players. “I don’t think so. I don’t think here. I don’t think ever in my career. It’s a unique situation.” Shanahan explained how you’re always a few injuries away from those types of situations. Still, the odds of having emergency players needing to fill in in spots they wouldn’t normally play go up with all of the injuries on the roster.

title: One player to steal from the Falcons for the 49ers
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are hobbling into Atlanta with an uncertain receiver group. Mike Evans hasn’t been ruled out, but I still believe he won’t be available on Sunday. Today is the day to find out, once the final injury report is released. Christian Kirk is trending toward playing, but the top four receivers on […]
full_text: Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers are hobbling into Atlanta with an uncertain receiver group. Mike Evans hasn’t been ruled out, but I still believe he won’t be available on Sunday. Today is the day to find out, once the final injury report is released. Christian Kirk is trending toward playing, but the top four receivers on Sunday could be Kirk, Brandin Cooks, Jordan Watkins, and Jacob Cowing. Not exactly striking fear in opposing defenses’ hearts. Each week, we ask which players the 49ers could use on offense and defense from their opponents. It’s the Falcons’ turn. Offense: WR Drake London Bijan Robinson is the belle of the ball. The 49ers have Christian McCaffrey, so adding Robinson doesn’t advance the roster. Kyle Pitts is up and down, but a pairing with George Kittle could be intriguing. Still, the answer is Drake London. Adding another big X receiver to pair with Mike Evans is game over for any defense. Of course, this move is impossible, but we are running a hypothetical exercise here. London and Evans as a duo is as good as it gets in the NFL: two receivers with a huge catch radius. Just think of the possibilities for Brock Purdy with both receivers. Game over. A guy can dream. Defense: DT Gervon Dexter Sr. If you asked this question during the offseason, the answer would have been safety Jessie Bates. Now, the 49ers’ safety situation is so solid, there’s no need for Bates. Maybe you’d say, AJ Terrell? Unfortunately, he is injured, and the cornerback duo of Deommodore Lenoir and Renardo Green is solid enough. The 49ers defensive tackle situation has completely flipped from last season. Gracen Halton, Osa Odighizuwa, and Sebastian Valdez have been a vast improvement over the group from 2025. Adding Dexter Sr. would give the 49ers a fierce rotation at defensive tackle. The former Chicago Bear is second in the NFL for interior defensive linemen with a 13.1% pressure rate. Through six games, the defensive tackle is well on his way to shattering his career-high pressure total of 43. Which two players would you choose from Atlanta? Did I get it right or wrong? Let us know in the comments.

title: NFL predictions: The 49ers will rely on Brock Purdy to beat the Falcons
summary: Fresh off a 23-17 win over the Washington Commanders, the San Francisco 49ers have one more game ahead of a much-needed bye week: a road contest against the Atlanta Falcons in Week 7. FanDuel Sportsbook expects a close game, given the 3-point spread. San Francisco stands at 6-0 after another close win, as they nearly […]
full_text: (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) | Getty Images Fresh off a 23-17 win over the Washington Commanders, the San Francisco 49ers have one more game ahead of a much-needed bye week: a road contest against the Atlanta Falcons in Week 7. FanDuel Sportsbook expects a close game, given the 3-point spread. San Francisco stands at 6-0 after another close win, as they nearly blew a 20-point lead against the Commanders but stopped them on their final defensive drive to seal the deal. It didn’t come easy, though, as the efficient 49ers offense went three-and-out on its final three drives of the game. Additionally, San Francisco could be without Mike Evans this week after he dealt with Achilles soreness and missed the second half of Monday’s game. So there are a lot of factors to deal with for the 49ers heading into what might be their toughest challenge of the season, given the circumstances. San Francisco entered the week as 4.5-point favorites, but that has come down to 2.5 as we inch closer to Sunday morning. Can the 49ers find another way to win and remain undefeated? Here are our three predictions for San Francisco’s Week 7 bout with the Falcons. Last Week First, let’s take a look at how last week’s predictions fared. Last Week Brock Purdy pads his MVP case Niners hit the 30-point mark again The Niners make Washington one-dimensional With Washington being quite solid against the run, but very susceptible to the pass, it felt like a favorable matchup for Brock Purdy and the Niners offense with Mike Evans healthy. We saw that play out in the first half, where the 49ers scored three touchdowns on five drives, while Purdy was clicking with Evans, George Kittle, and Christian McCaffrey. However, it wasn’t the same story offensively in the second half. The 49ers did get a good first drive, which ended in a field goal, but had three three-and-outs to end the game, with two being derailed by sacks. So, after 20 points in the first half, San Francisco also did not reach the 30-point mark for the game. They did make Washington one-dimensional, though. Washington’s running backs had just 13 carries, while Jayden Daniels had 40 pass attempts. As a whole, the Commanders rushed for just 53 yards on 3.1 yards per carry. It just was overshadowed by some high-quality play from Daniels in the second half, as the quarterback’s 300 passing yards nearly engineered the comeback. Now, let’s move on to this week’s game. Raheem Morris is going to blitz Michael Penix The Falcons offense has been a completely different story with Michael Penix at the helm. They’re fourth in EPA per play since Week 3. A big part of that has been their run game, which has been easily the most efficient in the league during that timeframe. But Atlanta’s needed at least an average passing attack to complement Bijan Robinson, and it’s done that with Penix, who specializes in getting the ball out quickly, averaging a 2.57-second time to throw. When looking at the trends this season, it feels like a game where the 49ers are going to blitz Penix a good amount. Penix has been blitzed on 47.2 percent of his dropbacks, and has actually done quite well against it, completing 62.3 percent of his passes with four touchdowns, no interceptions, and 9.3 yards per attempt. But that’s also in part because Penix has done a great job getting the ball out while getting played, averaging just a 2.35-second time to throw on those 58 dropbacks. Where Penix has really struggled this year is when he’s under pressure. He’s completed just 10 passes on 42 dropbacks, as he’s gone 10-for-32 passing while taking nine sacks. San Francisco will need to take advantage of Penix’s desire to get the ball out quickly, and with their defensive line, I think Morris will find a way to blitz Penix. Looking at past weeks, the 49ers blitzed Bo Nix around 40 percent of the time, Sam Darnold around 27 percent of the time, and Jayden Daniels around 36 percent of the time. I’d think the blitz rate hovers around a similar range here in Week 7. Niners will swarm to the ball, and it could make or break them San Francisco’s defense has always looked to swarm to the ball, which is why they can be as physical and violent as they are. I’d expect no less against an offense looking to run the ball a ton and get the ball out quickly in the passing game. However, against this specific opponent, that philosophy could make or break them, and that’s because of Bijan Robinson. Arguably the best back in the league, Robinson is averaging a whopping 4.72 yards after contact per carry. He’s broken off 15 runs of 10+ yards, and he’s also very dynamic in the passing game. The star is averaging 5.8 yards per carry, and is one of the best in the NFL at breaking tackles. There will be screens and a ton of runs in this one, and the 49ers will be tasked with tackling well. If they swarm to the ball, but cannot wrap up, it could be a rough day on the ground. The 49ers will have to rely on their passing game again This is admittedly a very tough matchup for the 49ers. I’ve written how the 49ers have been able to establish the run well enough over the past two weeks behind quality blocking, but the Falcons have been one of the NFL’s best run defenses throughout the year. They even held a strong Chicago Bears rushing attack to just 3.0 yards per carry last weekend, despite losing 31-23 in that game. Atlanta is also good against the pass, ranking ninth in EPA per play there, so this will be a tough spot for the 49ers to generate offense. Instantly, it feels like a bigger game plan for second-year wide receiver Jordan Watkins. Watkins saw a huge boost in routes and snaps last week, leading the receivers in snaps with 47 after being behind Brandin Cooks and Jacob Cowing the week before. It also comes with a tough matchup, but this also feels like a game where Brock Purdy might have to make some magic happen with extending plays. The Niners aren’t expected to be with Mike Evans, increasing the responsibilities for George Kittle and Christian McCaffrey. But the 49ers will have to set up their passing game if they want to win on Sunday.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: 3 areas where the 49ers must capitalize against the Falcons
summary: The 6-0 San Francisco 49ers must take on what could be their trickiest test yet this season before heading into a well-earned bye week.  The 49ers put their undefeated record on the line against the volatile Atlanta Falcons in a morning tilt between the former NFC West rivals in Atlanta. Atlanta looked like one of […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 6-0 San Francisco 49ers must take on what could be their trickiest test yet this season before heading into a well-earned bye week. The 49ers put their undefeated record on the line against the volatile Atlanta Falcons in a morning tilt between the former NFC West rivals in Atlanta. Atlanta looked like one of the worst teams in the league after the first two weeks of the season, but suddenly morphed into a competent team with the return of Michael Penix, winning their next two games to move to 2-2. But the Falcons are on another two-game skid and now 2-4 as the 49ers head to town. As the 49ers look to extend their win streak to seven and Atlanta looks to get back on track, these are the three numbers to know for the Week 7 meeting: 2.0 Turnovers per game. The Falcons offense averages two turnovers per game, the fifth-highest average in the league. Four of Atlanta’s 12 turnovers this season were interceptions thrown by Cooper Rush, now a free agent, and five of the 12 came in the Falcons’ Week 2 loss to Carolina. But even under Michael Penix, Atlanta has been turnover-prone, turning the ball over four times in the last two games. The first of those four was Tua Tagovailoa’s overtime interception in the loss to the Ravens, but that was Atlanta’s only turnover against Baltimore. Three came last week in Atlanta’s loss to Chicago, with Penix fumbling twice and losing one and Zachariah Branch losing both of his fumbles. Regardless of who the quarterback is, turnovers have snakebitten Atlanta’s offense. Because of Atlanta’s inability to hold on to the ball, it’s one of five teams in the league that average at least two turnovers per game, and San Francisco has already faced one of those five teams. The Seattle Seahawks have turned the ball over 12 times this season, like the Falcons, and four of those 12 came at the hands of the 49ers. That’s not to say the 49ers are going to force four turnovers against Atlanta, but the small sample size shows that the San Francisco defense can take advantage of teams who aren’t careful with the ball. 29.5 Rush attempts per game. Atlanta averages 29.5 rushes per game, the fifth-highest average in the league. One way Atlanta tries to avoid the turnovers is by feeding Bijan Robinson as much as they can, and can you blame them? Entering Week 7, Robinson ranks top-five at running back in: Rushing yards (2nd – 641) Rushing first downs (4th – 30) Yards per attempt (2nd – 5.8) Attempts (4th – 11) But it’s not just Bijan Robinson, as former 49er Brian Robinson has made himself comfortable as Bijan’s spell back. Brian Robinson has averaged 35.2 yards on about eight carries per game (about three-and-a-half more carries per game than he averaged with San Francisco in 2025), matching Bijan’s four rushing touchdowns. With Robinson and Robinson, Atlanta’s offense ranks fourth in rushing yards (897) and has the third-highest yards per rush attempt (5.1). San Francisco’s defense has proven to be ready to handle the run through the early part of the season. The 49ers are one of 10 defenses to allow fewer than 100 rushing yards per game, allowing 90.2 per game, seventh-best in the league. Only twice has San Francisco allowed more than 100 rushing yards in a game (Weeks 1 and 2), while Atlanta has rushed for fewer than 100 yards just once (Week 6). The 49ers haven’t yet faced a team in the top-ten of rush attempts (the closest being Week 6 against Washington, who ranks), so Atlanta will be a stress test for a 49ers run defense that’s been in good form. 7.2 Percent. Atlanta’s defense has forced a turnover on 7.2 percent of drives, the fourth-lowest rate in the league. If the 49ers defense can take advantage of Atlanta’s turnover-prone offense, then the 49ers offense should be able to handle an Atlanta defense that hasn’t forced too many mistakes this season. As its offense is one of five to average two or more turnovers per game, the defense is also on the wrong side of the leaderboard defensively, one of six defenses to force fewer than a turnover per game. But Atlanta’s only turnover-per-game is because it couldn’t force a turnover in Week 2. Outside of that, the Falcons have forced a turnover in five of their six games. But San Francisco’s offense hasn’t been known to turn the ball over too much. Its 6.7 turnover rate is the eighth-best in the league, but three of the 49ers’ six turnovers came in one game. Outside of the Seattle game, San Francisco has turned the ball over three times in five games. Maybe Atlanta gets one by chance against the 49ers’ offense on Sunday, but their season track record shows one is the most the Falcons should get against Purdy and the 49ers’ offense.
