title: NFL Week 7 betting guide: the value bets to make on lines, props and anytime TDs
summary: Our experts dive into the odds and player props for Week 7 and offer their betting tips and favorite plays.
full_text:
Value is value, no matter where -- or how -- you find it. And that's what we'll aim to do each week in this space: find betting value.

 Ben Solak, Seth Walder and Matt Bowen bring different perspectives into how they approach sports betting. Solak leans on his expertise in player evaluation and the X's and O's to find edges, while Walder relies on statistical models to pick out plus-expected value bets, focusing mainly on defense. Bowen, a former NFL safety, predicts positive matchups and game winners from tape study and his understanding of the league. Also included are fantasy projection creator Mike Clay's top predicted anytime TD scorers for Week 7.

 From spreads and money lines to totals and defensive player props, a good price might be found anywhere. Results will be tracked throughout the season, with flat one-unit wagers for each listed bet. Let's get into it.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 Jump to: 
 Bowen's favorite bets 
 Solak's plays  | Walder's props 
 Clay's TD projections 

 

 

 Bowen's favorite bets 
 Heading into Week 7 of the NFL Sunday slate, I'm going to try some different things in this space. Yes, I'll still have some game picks in here that we need to hit on, but I'll also move around the league a little more. Spreads, totals, props, etc. -- with the same analysis based on the numbers and the game tape. Plus, I'll have more bets to play.

 We'll start in Detroit, where I see two offenses with explosive-play ability -- playing indoors and on a really fast track -- pushing past the total.

 Green Bay Packers at Detroit Lions 
4:25 p.m. ET on Fox, Ford Field, Detroit

 

 Total points OVER 53.5 (-110) 

 Let's see if the Lions made some defensive adjustments over the bye week (such as playing less man coverage). This unit has given up 29.6 points per game, and the Packers will have matchup advantages with Christian Watson and Matthew Golden . Plus, Josh Jacobs returns to the Green Bay backfield. While I do think the Packers defense has played really good football over the past three weeks (11.5 PPG), limiting Jared Goff , Amon-Ra St. Brown and  Jahmyr Gibbs  is a different test. The Lions are scoring 32.8 PPG for a reason. This has the makeup of a shootout in the controlled environment of Ford Field.

 More bets to consider 

 Two-team, 6-point teaser: Vikings -0.5 vs. Colts , Broncos - Cardinals UNDER 49.5 (-143) 

 Getting the Vikings down to basically a moneyline play is a win. Brian Flores' defense is the story here, too. The Vikings lead the NFL in blitz rate (67.6%), and they are allowing a league-low 12.8 points per game. That's trouble for a Colts offense lacking a vertical element in the pass game. And with Daniel Jones ' reduced mobility due to his Achilles injury in 2025, Flores can heat up the pocket.

 Pushing the Denver-Arizona number up to 49.5 feels like a smart play here to get the Vikings number we want, as a straight moneyline bet on Minnesota would cost -278. Both teams rank in the bottom 10 in offensive scoring. The Cards aren't a vertical offense with Jacoby Brissett at quarterback, and Bo Nix is playing subpar football. This feels like a low-scoring game to start with, and we're pushing the number up by 6

 Atlanta Falcons +3 vs. San Francisco 49ers 

 The 49ers travel cross country for this one -- after playing the Monday night game -- and Mike Evans could be down due to Achilles tendinitis. Atlanta also features a defense that is top five against the run, has produced four sacks in back-to-back games and has taken the ball away in four straight. Let's take the Falcons as a home underdog to cover.

 Bijan Robinson rushing + receiving yards OVER 112.5 (-112) 

 Robinson has posted at least 118 total yards in four of six games played this season, and the 49ers are allowing an average of 46 receiving yards to opposing running backs (second most). Trust the volume and the big-play ability with Robinson as an elite dual-threat back.

 Kaelon Black rushing yards OVER 28.5 (-115) 

 The 49ers want to reduce to the total volume for Christian McCaffrey , which would create more opportunities for Black in Kyle Shanahan's run game. Black, who rushed for 34 yards on eight carries in the Monday night win over the Washington Commanders , should hit the over versus the Falcons.

 Tyler Higbee anytime TD (+280) 

 With Davante Adams out, there are open red zone opportunities in L.A., and the Rams can go heavy on tight end personnel in scoring position. Higbee has only one touchdown catch on the season, but he has averaged 37 routes run over his past four games. Keep an eye on boot concepts with Matthew Stafford in the low red zone.

 J.J. McCarthy  rushing yards OVER 23.5 (-115) 

 McCarthy rushed for 26 yards on two carries in the fourth quarter versus the New Orleans Saints last week and averages 17.4 yards per game as a pro. McCarthy has the traits to run the ball on designed carries, and he will be forced to eject from the pocket (as a runner) versus the Texans' pass rush.

 

 

 
 Solak's plays 
 

 New York Jets -4.5 (-115) vs Miami Dolphins 

 I've been looking for a spot to bet the Jets as they return to offensive health, and it seems like that day is here. The Dolphins are coming off their bye and are potentially frisky for a divisional win as a so-far winless team, but the Jets saw both receiver Adonai Mitchell (finger) and guard Dylan Parham (knee) return to practice in a limited capacity this week, just after first-round receiver Omar Cooper Jr . splashed into the starting lineup off IR with a six-catch, 103-yard outing. There's even a chance Breece Hall  will be back for this game!

 

 The Dolphins have a bottom-10 passing offense by pretty much every metric we've got, but they have been able to run fairly well (fourth in explosive rush rate, 10th in EPA per designed rush). But the Jets' defense is strong on the ground, ranking seventh in EPA per designed rush allowed and 11th in explosive rush rate. If the Dolphins can't find chunk plays on the ground, they can't move the football -- and that's where the Jets' bread is best buttered.

 Offensively, I've enjoyed the Geno Smith 's renaissance and expect him to have his best cadre of available receivers -- Cooper, Mitchell, star Garrett Wilson , and tight ends Mason Taylor and Kenyon Sadiq -- of the season. The Jets are a rising team, and I want to be ahead of them on the market, especially against the least talented roster in football.

 Kyler Murray passing yards OVER 204.5 (-113) 

 The Colts' passing defense is a disaster. Indianapolis is allowing 7.6 yards per passing attempt -- the eighth-worst mark -- despite surrendering a completion percentage of 61.4%, the eighth-best mark. That's because they don't tackle well at all in space (6.5 yards after the catch per reception, the highest figure in the league) and can't pressure the quarterback. Their 24.4% pressure rate on the season is the worst figure in the league by over 5 percentage points. Even when they do get pressure, they're allowing an astonishing 9.7 yards per pass attempt -- more than second place by more than a yard.

 All of this to say I love the potential for Murray to accumulate passing production in this one. Off of Minnesota's bye week, Murray will get his first game with a healthy set of pass catchers. Justin Jefferson got hurt in Week 3, and then T.J. Hockenson and Jordan Addison  missed Week 5. Star left tackle Christian Darrisaw is also back, and while the return of RB Jordan Mason might impact the Vikings' overall pass rate some, the potential for big plays is just too high here.

 

 Tanner McKee completions OVER 20.5 (-115) 

 We were on McKee over 18.5 completions against the Panthers last week, and in another great spot against an even weaker pass defense in Dallas, we'll take the completions again. McKee didn't even have a high completion percentage and still ended with 26 completions. The Eagles have a high pass rate when McKee is in, and he…

title: Kenneth Walker III is thriving with Chiefs. Why did the Seahawks let him go?
summary: While the Seahawks' run game is struggling, the Super Bowl MVP is on a historic pace for the Chiefs this season.
full_text:
Moments after Kansas City Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III ripped off a 33-yard touchdown run Sunday inside Arrowhead Stadium, the CBS broadcast showed a sign of the rough times in the Seattle Seahawks ' backfield. It was an actual sign, too, held by a fan wearing a royal blue Seahawks jersey amid a sea of Chiefs red.

 The sign read: "COME BACK HOME K9!! PLZ!!!"

 After the 22-6 Chiefs win over the Los Angeles Chargers , Walker sat inside the locker room and scrolled through several text messages on his phone. Many of those messages, from family and friends, included a screenshot of that same Seahawks fan and his sign.

 "That was crazy," Walker said of the fan's sign. "I've never seen something like that before."

 Minutes later, Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes had an even bigger reaction, his eyes and mouth widening when he was shown the image for the first time.

 "That's hilarious," Mahomes said. "He's a game changer."

 

 In five games, Walker has been just that for the Chiefs, demonstrating how much of a dynamic playmaker he can be performing alongside Mahomes. The Chiefs' leading rushing last season was former running back Kareem Hunt , who had 611 rushing yards in 17 games. Walker has already surpassed that mark, producing a league-leading 665 rushing yards, 152 scrimmage yards per game and eight total touchdowns. He joined Hall of Famer Jim Brown in becoming just the NFL second player to record at least 600 rushing yards, at least six rushing scores and have multiple receiving touchdowns through the first five games.

 This week, Walker will return to Seattle, just not in the manner that the Seahawks fan at Arrowhead -- and many like him around the country -- dreamed. Instead, the early-season betting favorite for AP Offensive Player of the Year will lead the 5-0 Chiefs into Lumen Field for a Sunday primetime game against his former team.

 The matchup invites a closer look at why the Seahawks let Walker leave in free agency one month after he was named MVP of their Super Bowl LX victory -- a decision that has been second-guessed amid their 3-3 start -- and how the fifth-year veteran has taken his game to another level in Chiefs coach Andy Reid's offense.

 "He's a stud," Reid said Sunday of Walker.

 Walker's historic start has led to many analysts suggesting he was the best veteran acquisition in the league this offseason after joining the Chiefs on a three-year, $43.05 million deal in March , including $28.7 million fully guaranteed.

 

 Meanwhile, without Walker, the Seahawks rank 18th in rushing yards per game, having struggled to find consistent production with their top two options -- rookie first-round pick Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet -- sidelined with injuries. It's one of several issues that have held their offense back under first-year coordinator Brian Fleury.

 Stopping Walker on Sunday night will be a challenge. And seeing him in a Chiefs uniform, having put together a historic start to the season in Kansas City, might be difficult for the Seahawks and their fans.

 "I'll just say, I love Ken," Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald said Wednesday when asked if he has any second thoughts about Seattle letting Walker leave. "I thoroughly enjoyed him being on our football team. We've had some great one-on-one conversations. I thought we had a great relationship. I respect the heck out of him. ... But I think there's mixed emotions in terms of, you're happy for him, but also, we're trying to figure out ways to stop this guy, too, because he's playing at a really high level."

 

 'We have to move forward now': Why didn't the Seahawks re-sign Walker? 
 As the Seahawks prepare to see Walker, are his former teammates wondering why he's no longer in Seattle?

 "It's crazy when you look at the tape and see, man, this guy is incredible," safety Julian Love said Wednesday when asked. "We knew he was incredible. But that's people above us."

 Walker's game-breaking talent was never a question with the Seahawks, who made him the second running back drafted in 2022 when they chose him 41st. But the team's decision-makers had reservations about his availability dating to his rookie season, according to sources familiar with the team's thinking.

 That helped explain why general manager John Schneider spent another second-round pick on Charbonnet in 2023, and why he didn't attempt to lock up Walker with an extension after 2024, by which point the running back had missed 10 games over his first three seasons. It also helped explain why the Seahawks had Walker split snaps with Charbonnet in 2025, and why -- according to multiple sources familiar with the team's plans -- they were only willing to go as high as roughly $10 million per season to re-sign him in March.

 

 At the time Walker agreed to his deal with Kansas City, its $14.35 million average ranked fourth among running backs (it has since fallen to ninth). The Seahawks did not want to pay that kind of money to a back who they would have preferred to again use in a timeshare.

 Even if the Seahawks were willing to match Kansas City's contract, the Chiefs were offering something Seattle hadn't -- a chance to be featured.

 Over his first three seasons, Walker totaled 3,251 scrimmage yards and 26 touchdowns while averaging roughly 17 touches per game. During the 2025 regular season, that dropped to roughly 15 touches compared to 13 for Charbonnet, who averaged two more snaps per game than Walker -- 31 to 29.

 Walker set career highs with 1,309 scrimmage yards and 4.6 yards per carry in 2025. He scored five touchdowns while regularly ceding opportunities to Charbonnet at the goal line. When Charbonnet tore an ACL in the divisional round, Walker delivered. In three playoff games, he totaled 417 scrimmage yards and four touchdowns, averaging roughly 25 touches and 41 snaps. His 161-yard performance in the Super Bowl LX win over the New England Patriots earned him MVP honors.

 It was the culmination of Walker's first healthy season in the NFL.

 

 Over his first three seasons, he missed games due to a hernia, separate ankle injuries, separate oblique injuries and a calf injury. He also missed chunks of spring and summer 2025 with soreness in a foot and ankle. Then he played in all 20 games, did not miss a single practice during the season and was a full participant in all but five. He appeared on the injury report in only three out of 21 weeks the team released one.

 Was that a sign that, with offseason changes to his diet and sleeping habits, Walker was now durable enough to carry a full load? The Seahawks could have bought a year to help determine the answer via the franchise tag, but the $14.3 million cost was clearly prohibitive in their eyes.

 Instead, they added veteran Emanuel Wilson on a one-year, $1.6 million deal and spent the 32nd pick on Price with a plan to use those two as well as George Holani until Charbonnet returned. Charbonnet could return as early as Sunday , while Price (chest) has to spend at least one more game on injured reserve .

 Before landing on IR, Price averaged 4.3 yards on 28 carries with zero touchdowns over the first three games. Wilson (3.5 yards per carry) has been effective in spurts, but neither he nor Holani (3.1 YPC) have much explosiveness, something Seattle's backfield has missed with Walker gone. Then again, the Seahawks have been contacted in the backfield on 22% of their rushing attempts this season -- the fifth-highest rate in the NFL, per ESPN Research -- which is indicative of blocking struggles that most running backs would find difficult to overcome.

 

 A final judgement on the Seahawks' decision to let Walker leave should not be rendered until Price and Charbonnet have a chance to show whether they can lead an effective run game. Time will also tell whether Walker can hold up physically in a featured role.

title: Fernando Mendoza is embracing being Raiders' latest Hispanic QB
summary: The rookie's next chapter is inspired by the legacies of a Hispanic coach, QB and a Raiders' fan base embracing the culture.
full_text:
IN HIGH SCHOOL in 2021, Fernando Mendoza watched former Texas A&M quarterback Zach Calzada, a Cuban American like himself, and wondered about other Cubans and Hispanic quarterbacks who played at the next level. More importantly, he wanted to know how many of them had success in the NFL, even winning Super Bowls --- a dream of his.

 A Google search opened Mendoza's eyes. He researched Tom Flores and Jim Plunkett, who are considered trailblazers for Latinos in the sport. Flores (Mexican American) was the first Hispanic quarterback in the NFL in 1960 when he debuted for the Oakland Raiders -- who are now based in Las Vegas. Plunkett, also Mexican American, was a college standout at Stanford, winning the Heisman Trophy in 1970 before being drafted by the New England Patriots with the first overall pick in 1971.

 Plunkett is the first Hispanic American player to win the Heisman Trophy and be drafted No. 1.

 

 Flores and Plunkett simultaneously became the first Hispanic coach and first Hispanic quarterback to win a Super Bowl. The duo helped the Raiders defeat the Philadelphia Eagles in Super Bowl XV in 1981 -- the first of two Super Bowls that they won together. Plunkett was named the game's Most Valuable Player.

 "To see that example [and] to know whatever I am doing, it is possible, meant a great deal to me," Mendoza told ESPN.

 As the Raiders' No. 1 pick in April's draft, Mendoza is now doing more than just viewing Flores and Plunkett as inspirational figures. Mendoza is continuing their legacy. Should Mendoza start for the Raiders, he'll join another No. 1 pick in Carolina Panthers QB Bryce Young as the only starting quarterbacks of Hispanic descent in the NFL this season.

 Regardless of whether he wants to be, he is a beacon of hope for the Raiders, with a fairly large Hispanic fan base. Flores and Plunkett symbolize the franchise's glory days, and they believe Mendoza can help bring the team back to relevance. Mendoza understands the role bestowed upon him can be pressure and a privilege. At the same time, it's added motivation for him to have a career that can be an inspiration for others who look like him.

 "It's a great sense of pride knowing that it's been done before and it can be done; winning a championship [while] being Hispanic as the focal point," Mendoza said. "However, it's also a great deal of pressure, and that's something I take upon myself whenever I make decisions."

 
 

 WHEN MENDOZA ARRIVED in Las Vegas after April's 2026 NFL draft , the magnitude of his presence was evident. The Raiders have not been to the postseason since 2021, which was the last year they finished with a winning record. The organization hasn't been to the Super Bowl since 2002 and hasn't hoisted the Vince Lombardi Trophy since Plunkett and Flores led the Raiders to a victory over the Washington Commanders in Super Bowl XVIII in 1984.

 On top of that, Las Vegas has also swung and missed at finding a long-term answer at quarterback in recent years. Even now, with 38-year-old Kirk Cousins leading the offense, he is still a short-term solution. Mendoza, on the other hand, is looked upon as someone who can provide stability for years to come.

 Fernando Paredes, a 45-year-old Mexican and founder/president of Raiders Laguna, a fan club for those living in the Comarca Lagunera region of Mexico, said it's a "dream" for Mendoza to be a part of the organization.

 Paredes became a Raiders fan at age 9. No one in Paredes' family watched football. However, his dad gifted him a Raiders bomber jacket, leading Paredes to watch Raiders games and ultimately fall in love with the organization.

 

 Paredes' excitement for Mendoza stems from Latinos such as Flores and Plunkett leading the team to championships.

 "That is the hope that Raiders Nation has with Fernando Mendoza," Paredes said. "All of Raider Nation in Mexico ... we hope."

 Flores played six seasons (1960-61, 1963-66) with the Raiders. In 84 games (64 starts) with the Raiders, Flores threw for 11,635 yards, 92 touchdowns and 83 interceptions. Flores was hired by late owner Al Davis to be the head coach in 1979, becoming the second Hispanic coach in NFL history. Tom Fears was the first when the New Orleans Saints hired him in 1967.

 Mendoza is the fifth quarterback of Hispanic descent to play for the Raiders, joining Flores, Plunkett, Chon Gallegos (Mexican American) and EJ Manuel (Afro-Latin American). Gallegos was a backup for six games in 1962, while Manuel made one start in two games with the Raiders in 2017.

 "We've accomplished a lot of good things, and I'm looking forward to watching [Mendoza] progress and help the Raiders get back to the Super Bowl," Plunkett, who played eight seasons with the Raiders (1978-86), told ESPN.

 The Raiders are believed to have one of the league's largest Hispanic fan bases, welded in part by Plunkett and Flores. At the same time, the team's previous homes, Los Angeles and Oakland, and even their current one, Las Vegas, have substantial Hispanic populations.

 Hispanics represent 34.7% of Las Vegas' population, according to the latest U.S. Census . They make up 47.2% of the population in Los Angeles and 28.7% in Oakland.

 

 Mexico has one of the Raiders' largest international fan bases. In 2021, the Raiders were awarded marketing rights in Mexico through the league's Global Markets Program . They also have various fan clubs based in Mexico such as Raiders Laguna and Raiders Nation MX, which occasionally host watch parties and events.

 Raiders Spanish play-by-play commentator Harry Ruiz, a Mexican American from Los Angeles, said Mendoza playing quarterback for the Raiders is significant for their Hispanic fans because they have a quarterback who looks like them.

 "When it comes to Latinos, especially in a space like football in the United States, you support each other," continued Ruiz, who is in his seventh year as an announcer for the Silver & Black. "He might not be our [same country of origin], but we embrace him because his family went through the fight that my parents went through -- fighting for the American dream -- and now he's living the dream at the highest level in the NFL as the quarterback."

 Former Carolina Panthers and Washington Commanders coach Ron Rivera, a former NFL linebacker and the third Hispanic coach in league history, expressed a similar sentiment.

 " The Black Hole [a well-known Raiders fan club] is a mixture of all the fan bases that are out there celebrating the Raiders," Rivera said. "To know that Fernando represents one of them is a big deal."

 When former punter Leo Araguz, a Mexican American, was with the Raiders, he remembered the strength of the team's Latin fan base and the love they showed him. The Raiders provided Araguz with his first shot at the NFL after he played college football at Stephen F. Austin State University.

 He had brief stints with the Miami Dolphins and San Diego Chargers, but the Raiders gave Araguz a chance to play when they signed him in 1996. Araguz went on to play four seasons (51 games) with the Raiders and holds the NFL record for most punts in a game (16).

 "Al Davis took a chance on us," Araguz told ESPN. "The Latin community is always going to be cheering for the Raiders because I think it comes from the fact that Al Davis did have that Hispanic connection to his players."

 Davis was a champion of diversity. In 1989, 10 years after Flores became the Raiders' head coach, Davis hired Pro Football Hall of Fame offensive tackle Art Shell to be the NFL's first African American head coach. In 1968, the Raiders drafted Eldridge Dickey with the 25th overall pick, making him the first African American quarterback selected in the first round.

 Araguz said the stars aligned perfectly for the Raiders when they drafted Mendoza. Araguz looks forward to seeing the community standing behind Mendoza and watching kids wear the former Indiana star's jersey to games.

 "We are excited for all of it," Araguz…

title: Jay-Z's greatest sports lyrics, ranked ahead of his SoFi Stadium show
summary: Jay-Z's catalog is packed with sports references -- here are the ones that top our list.
full_text:
One of the greatest rappers of all time -- or the greatest in many eyes -- Jay-Z is still out here adding to his legacy. This weekend, for instance, he's taking his stadium show to Los Angeles to bless the West Coast with more of his live greatness.

 The show is going to be full of trademark Jay hits. It'll also be full of sports lyrics, because if there's one thing Hov knows, it's sports. From deep dives into Michael Jordan history to NASCAR, scrambling quarterbacks and everything in between, a Jay-Z album might have more sports references than "SportsCenter" does.

 With such a robust history of sports references, we decided to rank his 10 best, most unexpected and clever. As they say, "the list is fluid."

 

 10. "And I sport fly s--- I should win an ESPY" - "Party Life" (2007) 
 This is a little bit of bias, so pardon us. Jay-Z shouting out the ESPYS is just pretty cool. Now he just needs to pull up and host or perform one of these years. When he does, he has our full permission to rap this exact lyric. Heck, he could even win an ESPY for the reference alone. -- David Dennis Jr. 

 

 9. "It's Hov tradition, Jeff Gordon of rap/ I'm back to claim pole position, holla at ya boy" -- "Never Let Me Down" (2004) 
 If there's one NASCAR driver who's going to get referenced in rap songs, it's going to be Jeff Gordon. His rap credentials are certified. It doesn't get more certified than a nod from Hov. As always, there's a double meaning here. In 2004, Jay had taken his short-lived retirement, and this was his claim that he's back to lead the way like he never left. Well, he kind of never did. -- David Dennis Jr. 

 

 8. "You cats is home screaming the fight's on/ I'm in the 1500 seats, watching Tyson/ Same night, same fight/ But one of us cats ain't playing right/ I let you tell it" -- "I Love The Dough" (1997) 

 

 One of rap history's great what-ifs is how much more music Jay-Z and his close friend the Notorious B.I.G. could've made if the latter hadn't been slain in 1997. The Mike Tyson reference here calls to mind Jay and Roc-A-Fella Records' 1995 trip to Sin City to watch Tyson's first post-prison fight against Peter McNeely. This same fight would also live in another Jay-Z classic, "Can I Live." -- Justin Tinsley 

 
 7. "I don't even know y'all name/ I'm too big for ya, the rap LeBron James " -- "Blow The Whistle" (2008) 

 

 Let this next sentence marinate. LeBron James has been playing in the NBA so long that Jay-Z once defended him against ... DeShawn Stevenson and Soulja Boy. Too $hort's "Blow The Whistle" was already a cultural classic and party anthem well outside The Bay by spring 2008. With Jigga jumping on the track, and the subject matter being LeBron during the NBA playoffs, the reach went nuclear. We never did get a response track from Soulja and DeShawn, though. In case you're wondering, too, The King averaged 30 points, 10 rebounds and eight assists in a six-game, first-round defeat of Washington . -- Justin Tinsley 

 
 6. "I told you '96 that I came to take this s--- and I did/ Handle my biz, I scramble like Randall with his/ Cunningham, but the only thing runnin' is numbers, fam" -- "Heart of the City" (2001) 

 

 Jigga held you down six summers, damn.

 Sorry, just had to finish that line. Among the quarterbacks of the past 50 years, one of the most underrated is still Randall Cunningham. He's one of the most beloved forces in Philadelphia Eagles  history. He put together a historic season in 1998 with the Minnesota Vikings alongside Cris Carter and a young rookie named Randy Moss. And, yes, the dude could scramble and make all kinds of plays with his legs. On Hov's timeless classic from a quarter century ago, Cunningham's mention lives on in musical bliss. -- Justin Tinsley 

 

 5. "I'ma stay winnin', rock the custom drop Bentleys/ Never eat at Denny's and party like Lil' Penny" -- "Who You Wit II" (1997) 

 

 Two of the best things Chris Rock ever did were "Everybody Hates Chris" and voicing Lil' Penny -- the charming, boisterous figurine that helped make Penny Hardaway a marketing darling. It's a reference you had to live to really appreciate. But, Hov, what's your beef with Denny's? You ever been there at 3 a.m. after a night of partying? Don't knock it until you try it! -- Justin Tinsley 

 

 4. "More than a street legend, homie, it's Hova/ More than a relief pitcher, I'm the closer/ The Mariano of The Marriott/ If money talks, the whole world's about to hear me out" -- "Go Crazy" (2005) 

 

 Being a legend in New York City is unlike being one anywhere else on the planet. Young Jeezy was the hottest rapper on the planet, and with his seminal 2005 classic "Thug Motivation 101," Jay couldn't resist temporarily pausing his "retirement" to get on the remix of one of the project's standouts. And, buddy, he delivered an absolute masterclass, equipped with a nod to the legendary New York Yankees closer Mariano Rivera. -- Justin Tinsley 

 

 3. "Worry I'm not the Mike Jordan of the mic recordin'/ It's Hovi Baby, you Kobe, maybe, Tracy McGrady/ Matter fact you a Harold Miner/ JR Rider, washed up on marijuana/ Even worse you a Pervis Ellis" -- "Pump It Up (Freestyle)" (2003) 

 

 If there's one thing Jay-Z is going to do, it's belittle his rap competition by making sports comparisons. This one is particularly nasty, as he tossed out these insults to Joe Budden -- over the beat of Joe Budden's song. Here's some lore, as the kids say: Joe Budden was supposed to be one of rap's next big stars, and his big single was "Pump It Up." Jay had heard the rumblings and wanted to remind everyone that he was still king of the mountain. So while dropping this freestyle over the "Pump It Up" beat, he made it known he was one of the GOATs and Joe was, well...all respect to Pervis Ellis. -- David Dennis Jr. 

 

 2. "Jiggaman is Diesel when I lift the 8 up" -- "Lyrical Exercise" (2001) 

 

 This one gets a healthy nod simply for the fact it took us so long to even understand what was going on here. The song, "Lyrical Exercise," is full of double entendres as he relates gym workouts to, well, any number of violent or illegal activities. For instance, "I spot ya, I lift the weight of ya watch of ya arm" is pretty straightforward. This lyric, though? Is not. At first blush, it's about holding up a weapon. However, it's actually a reference to this picture of Shaq (Diesel) lifting up teammate Kobe Bryant (No. 8). Whoa. It took the internet more than a decade to put this together, too. -- David Dennis Jr. 

 
 1. "I ball for real/ Y'all n---as is Sam Bowie/ And with the third pick, I made the Earth sick/ MJ, Him Jay, fadeaway perfect" -- "Hola Hovito" (2001) 
 

 Leave it up to Jay-Z to offer some real draft analysis in the middle of a verse. Of course, this is a reference to one of the biggest NBA draft blunders of all time when the  Portland Trail Blazers  picked Sam Bowie over Michael Jordan in 1984. And the rest, as they say, is history. Jay is making the comparison here that all these other rappers are busts and he's the real MJ. -- David Dennis Jr.

title: David Andrews' blood clot diagnosis illuminates what's going on with Jalen Hurts
summary: The former NFL center tells ESPN about his experience as it might provide a window into the Eagles QB's situation.
full_text:
Philadelphia Eagles  quarterback  Jalen Hurts ' recent diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli has placed a national spotlight on blood clots , stoking an interest in further education around the subject as well as ways to improve the handling of them in professional sports.

 The discourse has even reached the political spectrum, with U.S. Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware penning a letter to NFL commissioner Roger Goodell seeking clarity on league blood clot protocol.

 Hurts joined a list of athletes who have been diagnosed with blood clots, including Serena Williams, Victor Wembanyama , Chris Bosh and  New England Patriots  defensive tackle Christian Barmore .

 

 The Eagles didn't have to look far for another example of an athlete who had been diagnosed with blood clots after learning Hurts would miss the rest of the 2026 NFL season : Carolina Panthers right tackle Taylor Moton made his return to the lineup last week against Philadelphia after being diagnosed in June with multiple blood clots in his right lung.

 "It was really emotional," Moton said of his return.

 "Prayers up to [Hurts]. I hope that everything is OK with him and praying for a speedy recovery for him."

 Every individual case is unique, but learning about other players' experiences can be illuminating when trying to understand what happened with Hurts and what's next. That certainly seems to apply when it comes to the story of David Andrews , the two-time Super Bowl champion with the New England Patriots who manned the center position for Tom Brady and others from 2015 to 2024.

 Andrews shared his story with ESPN detailing the events around a blood clot diagnosis that forced him to sit out 2019.

 

 

 Like Hurts, Andrews' story involves a long flight overseas and discomfort in his calf.

 Andrews had traveled to Israel with Patriots owner Robert Kraft and a handful of his teammates in June 2019. He slept for most of the flight, went out that night, then worked out with fellow lineman Joe Thuney the following morning.

 Andrews noticed his calf was sore after running but thought little of it. He was probably dehydrated or sprinted too hard, the thinking went.

 "Football players are used to pain, right? It's just kind of standard operating procedure," he said.

 The next sign that something was off came later in the summer right before training camp. His energy was lower than normal, his workouts felt more difficult, and he was struggling to breathe. But his wife had recently come down with a bad cold and congestion and he figured he had as well. Then came back pain when he was out to dinner a few nights later. He coughed up blood on the first day of training camp and notified the trainers. A subsequent X-ray appeared to reveal something in his lungs, and he was diagnosed with pneumonia, he said.

 His stamina wasn't improving as the 2019 regular season approached. Andrews labored during their third preseason game against the Panthers and remembers being yelled at by his offensive line coaches. Finally, at his wife's urging after hearing him wheezing while they lay in bed, he went to see a pulmonologist who discovered "a bunch of blood clots in my lungs."

 He was immediately transferred to the emergency room. His hematologist ran a battery of tests, checking for anything from cancers to HIV. A scan ultimately revealed a deep vein thrombosis in his leg that had been scarred over.

 "So then she started asking questions like, 'When was the last long flight you went on?' And I told her about Israel. She's like, 'Well, did you notice anything in Israel?' And I was like, 'Well, you know, I had this calf pain but I thought I just kind of tweaked my calf.' She's like, 'Oh my goodness!'"

 

 Andrews' young family -- he has two boys and a girl, ages 5, 2, and 6 months -- were bustling in the background as he spoke on the phone.

 He was put on anticoagulants and missed the 2019 season. There was some talk about having him on the medication for three months and seeing where things stood then, but during his discussions with coach Bill Belichick, he concluded there was no way he'd be able to train strenuously enough during that time to be ready to play football late in the season if he was cleared.

 He was placed on injured reserve and ended up taking blood thinners for six months. 

 The good news was that he wasn't also dealing with an injury and therefore didn't have to worry: What if I'm not the same player when I get back? 

 Then again, the benefit of rehabbing from a physical injury is there's a sense of control in that you work to achieve specific markers and can see the progress as you go along.

 "This is literally just letting your body heal and sitting around, which I found very frustrating at times," he said.

 After a series of tests at the six-month mark -- Andrews' doctors wanted to make sure his heart wasn't strained from having the clots for as long as he did, he said -- as well as an ultrasound. Andrews announced he was cleared to return in April 2020.

 Andrews played the 2020 season and four more years after that with no issues. Sixty-four of his 121 career starts came after being treated for blood clots in his lungs.

 However, there was some management involved as he played those last five seasons. He underwent a test to see how long the anticoagulant stayed in his system (about 24 hours) so he could take preventative measures when traveling long distances. Before West Coast or international flights, he said he would take a blood thinner after practice on Friday and then again after the game.

 "The only time it technically affected me is when we played in Germany in '23, because on that trip, like most teams we leave on Thursday night after practice, so I took a blood thinner and I just couldn't practice Friday morning," Andrews said.

 The thought of having a recurring blood clot would creep into his mind every once in a while, like if he happened to tweak his calf, but there's also a certain surrendering necessary when playing such a physical sport and "you can't live your life in that kind of fear."

 Andrews said he went back on blood thinners after his retirement in 2025  as a precaution. High-impact activities are not recommended when on anticoagulants but outside of giving up rigorous weight training ("One day I was looking at myself in the mirror like, 'Why are you squatting over 405 pounds?'" he said), he is living his life as normal.

 Andrews said he is also supposed to wear a bracelet indicating he is on blood thinners so emergency workers would be alerted in the event of an accident. He hinted he might not always be a model patient and does run into a problem every now and again ("I cut myself with my pocket knife the other day and bled like a stuck pig," he said) but generally has not faced many issues.

 "I like to deer hunt, and I like to play golf and turkey hunt," said Andrews, who still lives in the Foxborough, Massachusetts, area. "It's not like I'm riding bulls or dirt bikes and stuff."

 ESPN reporters Mike Kaye and Mike Reiss contributed to this story.

title: What's led to Titans' recent success? Under center
summary: Titans run the ball better from under center, so why not put it into practice more?
full_text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- The Tennessee Titans ' passing offense is one of the least explosive attacks in the NFL this season. A look at the numbers shows there may be more opportunities if the Titans ran more plays from under center.

 Tennessee (1-5) ranks next to last in passing plays of 20 yards or more (10). Only the Arizona Cardinals (0) have fewer passing plays of 40 yards or more than Tennessee (1). Finding ways to stretch the field could open things up for other parts of the offense.

 Tennessee has had 363 offensive snaps this season. Of those, 200 have come from shotgun formation with seven plays resulting in an explosive pass completion. By comparison, three of the 163 plays from under center led to a pass completion of at least 20 yards. 

 "I think it really simplifies what we want to get out of the defense, the certain looks that we want to get in and out of," quarterback Cam Ward said. "I think it just helps everybody get in the rhythm, whether it's the run game or passing the ball. So I think the more that we do that, it's going to continue to help us."

  

 Under-center dropbacks (three, five, or seven steps) allow the quarterback's timing to be married to the receiver's routes. It opens up the full route tree and allows for more deep passing concepts. 

 It also helps the run game as it's less predictable. Running backs get a wider view because they're lined up deeper in the backfield behind the quarterback instead of beside him in shotgun.

 Offensive linemen get an advantage from under center as well because they can get to their spots more easily since it takes a tick longer for the quarterback to take the snap before dropping back and handing it to the back. The benefit is the offensive line gets time to reach their spots to make their blocks, and the back can see the play developing better, making it more likely for a positive run gain.

 The Titans have had 10 explosive runs (10 yards or more), all of which resulted in a first down this season. Eight of the 10 came from under center. Ward had one of the two explosive rushing plays from shotgun, but it was a scramble, so it wasn't a called run play. Simply put, the Titans have run the ball better from under center this season.

 Success in the run game not only makes an offense less predictable; it also helps the passing game. Offenses also utilize hard play-action fakes from under center because it helps move defenders out of position, opening up larger passing windows. That's especially the case against zone defense, where linebackers have their eyes locked on the quarterback so it's easier to move them closer to the line of scrimmage and sneak an in-breaking route behind them.

 "When teams go under center and pass, it's more play-action passes, more deep out-breakers, deep-in breakers," rookie linebacker Anthony Hill Jr . said. "It puts us in a lot more conflict because our drops that are normally 11 to 12 yards, now we're thinking 14 to 16. So those extra three or four steps could be the difference between a 20-yard gain and an interception."

 Second-year receiver Elic Ayomanor 's 41-yard catch is Tennessee's longest play of the season. It was the result of a play-action pass from Ward that started under center. This is one way to make the game easier for a young quarterback like Ward who's in his second season.

 "It's fun because it's harder for those guys when we have a true play-action fake," Ward said. "It's hard for those guys to see the ball. So it could get them out of their shell or whatever they're trying to show, but it also allows our guys to get wide open."

 

 Sometimes it can help pass protection, especially in possible run situations where a pass rusher can't just be concerned with going after the quarterback. 

 "I think play-action is good in general," offensive coordinator Brian Daboll said. "Whether it's from underneath or from the shotgun, it causes some indecision with the defensive line so they're not teeing off on you."  

 Not all situations allow for true under-center play. Down-and-distance has an impact. Take last week's 26-20 win over the Colts for instance. The Titans faced third-and-long (seven yards or more) six times, all of which were from shotgun. There's a time and place for everything. 

 "It's important offensively to try to stay balanced the best you can, whether that's shotgun underneath, run pass, complimenting the runs with the run actions, quick dropback, intermediate dropback, shot plays," Daboll said. "Being under center gives you a lot of advantages relative to, is it run? Is it play action pass? Is it a naked?

 "We've done some drop back pass out of that. And then in shotgun, you have to do a good job of where you set the back, how you set the back. Again, It's all week to week obviously for us of what we think we need to do."

 The next week's test will come against a defense  allowing the seventh-fewest points per game at 20.1 points, as Tennessee will host the AFC North-leading Cleveland Browns  (4-2) on Sunday (1 p.m. ET, CBS) at Nissan Stadium. It also might be a task for the passing game, as the Browns allow the eighth-fewest passing yards at 205.2.
